common case), otherwise materializes-and-memoizes in place (same
established precedent as `ASNIX_TAG_THUNK`'s force-and-cache, M6) the
first time ANY code needs to read it. This project chose
**materialize-on-any-read** rather than real Nix's/iets's true
bounded-leaf-probe lookup (a single-key `find` that never flattens) --
a deliberate simplification given how large the raw-layout call-site
surface turned out to be (enumerated below); see "What this gives up"
below for the real cost of that choice.

`src/c/attrs_update.c`'s `asnix_attrs_update` (the `//` operator)
builds a `UnionHdr` instead of copying when: the RHS, once resolved
flat, has `<= ASNIX_UNION_RHS_MAX` (16) entries; the LHS has
`>= ASNIX_UNION_LHS_MIN` (16) entries (or is already a UnionHdr with
room to grow); and the LHS's existing leaf count is
`< ASNIX_ATTRS_UNION_MAX_LEAVES` (64). Both 16s intentionally match
real Nix's own `Bindings::layerOnTopOf` threshold
(`~/nix/gc-unlock/src/libexpr/attr-set.hh`) -- real nixpkgs
override/overlay RHS attrsets are typically small, and a real
`stdenv.mkDerivation` attrset (d.nix's ffmpeg closure) has 30-60+ keys
by the time `derivation {...}` sees it, comfortably above 16. Falling
outside any of these conditions falls back to the always-correct
eager two-pointer merge (`asnix_attrs_eager_merge`, the renamed
pre-M93 function body, unchanged) -- a safe fallback by construction.

**Call-site enumeration (the actual risk surface, re-verified from
scratch, not trusted from the prior planning subtask's summary).**
Grepped every file touching `ASNIX_ATTRS_OFF_*`/`ASNIX_ATTR_OFF_*`/
`ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE` directly (13 files + heap.h). The prior subtask's
list (`op_select.S`, `op_select_or.S`, `op_has_attr.S`, a suspected
`op_rec_overrides_merge.S`) was a reasonable starting point but
incomplete and one entry was wrong:
- **Missed asm handlers** doing their own raw binary search:
  `op_with.S`'s `asnix_op_with_try` and `op_check_formals.S` (lambda-
  pattern destructuring) -- neither was on the prior list. Both patched
  with the same "peek count; if negative, save IP/ENV, call
  `asnix_bshared_attrs_resolve`, restore, reload count" shape
  `op_select.S` established (`op_update.S`'s existing save/restore-
  around-a-call pattern, reused). `op_mk_attrs.S` touches the same
  offsets but only ever WRITES a brand new flat Attrs -- confirmed
  unreachable on an existing UnionHdr by construction, no change
  needed.
- **`op_rec_overrides_merge.S` doesn't exist** -- it's
  `asnix_bshared_rec_overrides_merge`, a C function in
  `builtins_shared.c` that already went through the shared
  `asnix_bshared_attrs_count/sym/value` accessors even before this
  milestone, so it became union-safe automatically once those three
  accessors got a resolve-first guard -- a non-issue, not a separate
  fix.
- **Missed entirely: raw-arithmetic C call sites that bypass the
  shared accessors.** This is the part that was genuinely riskier than
  the prior subtask's writeup suggested. Found by grep, not assumed:
  - `src/c/derivation.c`'s `asnix_collect_input_refs` (4 raw-arithmetic
    reads) and, worse, `asnix_prim_derivation` itself -- THE function
    called for every single `derivation {...}`, doing **three separate
    full raw scans** (`__structuredAttrs` pre-scan, `__ignoreNulls`
    pre-scan, the main per-attribute loop) directly over `count`/
    `entries` with zero accessor indirection. This is exactly the
    real-world trigger path (`mkDerivation`'s attrs, built by merging
    defaults with user overrides) the whole milestone targets, and the
    single highest-stakes site in the codebase for a silent-wrong-hash
    bug. Fixed by resolving the argument once, at the top of each
    function, before any raw read.
  - `src/c/main.c`'s printer (ASNIX_TAG_ATTRS case) -- raw scan, fixed
    by resolving before marking "seen"/reading `count`.
  - `src/c/builtins_attrs.c` -- `attrNames`/`attrValues`/`hasAttr`/
    `getAttr`/`removeAttrs`/`mapAttrs` all go through this file's OWN
    duplicated private accessors (`attrs_count`/`attrs_entry_sym`/
    `attrs_entry_value`), not the shared ones -- fixed by adding the
    same resolve-first guard to those three helpers (covers all six
    builtins at once).
  - `src/c/builtins_m54.c`'s `unsafeGetAttrPos` -- a subtler bug shape:
    it calls `asnix_bshared_attrs_find` (accessor, already safe) to get
    an index, then re-derives the entry's address via **raw pointer
    arithmetic on the original (possibly-union) Value** instead of
    calling `asnix_bshared_attrs_value` with that index -- an
    accessor-then-raw-reindex mismatch that would silently read the
    wrong bytes on a union. Fixed by resolving before the raw re-index
    so the index and the base it's applied to agree.
  - Confirmed safe without changes (already accessor-based, so the
    central `asnix_bshared_attrs_resolve` guard covers them for free):
    `builtins_attrs2.c`, `builtins_list2.c`, `builtins_closure.c`,
    `builtins_path.c`, `eval_file.c`, `builtins_fetchgit.c`,
    `builtins_m23.c` (deep-force, `intersectAttrs`),
    `builtins_compare.c` (JSON encoder, `toString`/`outPath` checks),
    `value_util.c` (string-coercion ATTRS cases -- hash-parity-
    adjacent, verified it only ever calls the accessors), and the
    `functionArgs` block in `main.c` (separate from its printer, also
    accessor-based already).
  - `attrs_update.c`'s own `asnix_attrs_insert_dynamic` (`${...} = v;`
    dynamic attrs in literals): its `attrs` argument is structurally
    always a plain OP_MK_ATTRS/prior-insert_dynamic result (never fed
    through `//`), so provably unreachable as a union -- a defensive
    `asnix_bshared_attrs_resolve` call was added anyway (a no-op in
    practice) rather than relying on that invariant un-checked.

**A real bug found by measuring, not assumed away.** The first
working implementation (`ASNIX_ATTRS_UNION_MAX_LEAVES = 8`, matching
iets) passed every correctness check -- `make test`/`test-e2e`/
`test-nix-conformance` (`pass=652 fail=6 skip=148`, identical to
baseline) and `test-nixpkgs-hash` (`pass=148 fail=0`) -- but measuring
`./asnix d.nix`'s instructions (`perf stat`) and a synthetic
worst-case benchmark (`base // overlay1 // overlay2 // ... // overlayN`,
N=20000, base=500 keys, read once at the end via `builtins.attrNames`,
built with `foldl'`) showed this was NOT a win: peak RSS on the
synthetic benchmark was 3,298,240 KB, **statistically identical** to
the always-eager baseline's 3,293,488 KB, despite 19,688 of the 20,000
`//`s successfully building a UnionHdr instead of copying. Root cause,
found by adding temporary call counters: `asnix_bshared_attrs_resolve`'s
materialize step was a **left-to-right fold**
(`acc = merge(acc, leaf)` repeated over all leaves) -- this re-copies
the ALREADY-merged, ever-growing accumulator on every one of the
(up to 63) fold steps, costing `O(total_size * leaf_count)`, not
`O(total_size)`. Materializing a 64-leaf union this way costs as much
total copying as the eager baseline would have spent doing all 64
`//`s directly -- the deferred-copy benefit was being paid back in
full at every flatten, just batched into fewer, equally-expensive
events. Fixed by rewriting the materialize step as a **bottom-up
pairwise (binary-tree) merge** -- same shape as mergesort's merge
phase, costing `O(total_size * log2(leaf_count))` -- while preserving
`//`'s right-biased collision order (pairing adjacent leaves bottom-up
keeps the higher-priority operand on the right of every pairwise merge,
all the way up the tree, since `leaves[]` is stored lowest-priority
first).

**Threshold tuning, also by measurement, not just guessing.** With the
fold bug fixed, `MAX_LEAVES=8` still measured no better than baseline
(the periodic forced-flatten-and-restart means the amortized cost per
`//` is still `O(total_size / MAX_LEAVES)` -- same order as eager, just
divided by a small constant that per-`//` bookkeeping overhead (header
alloc, resolve branch, leaf-array copy) ate entirely). Raising
`MAX_LEAVES` to 64 flipped this to a clear win (see Results); 128
measured worse again on the same benchmark (likely locality/recursion-
depth related) -- 64 was kept without chasing a more precise optimum.

**Semantics preserved in both the lazy and materialized paths**
(verified directly against real `nix-instantiate --eval`, not just
inferred): right-hand-side-wins on key collision; final
`attrNames`/printed order is sorted by symbol id exactly like a
pre-M93 flat Attrs (materializing produces byte-identical output to
what the eager path would have produced for the same logical merge);
`==` between two differently-constructed-but-logically-equal unions is
`true` (both resolve through the same accessors before compare);
nested `a // (b // c)` resolves `b // c` flat before storing it as one
leaf, so unions never nest and every leaf-walk is single-level.

**Verification.** `make test`: all green (unchanged). `make test-e2e`:
all green. `make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=652 fail=6 skip=148`,
byte-identical failure set to the pre-existing baseline (the same
6 known gaps M86 already declined: eq-slot-elem/-identity,
getattrpos{,-functionargs}, inherit-attr-pos, print). `make
test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`, reconfirmed on a clean,
non-concurrent run after the fold-merge fix (an earlier contaminated
run, caught overlapping with an in-progress rebuild on this shared
machine, spuriously reported `gnugrep.drvPath(crash)`; manually
re-checked against both this binary and real `nix-instantiate` --
exact match, confirmed the failure was rebuild contamination, not a
real bug). Extensive manual cross-checks against real
`nix-instantiate --eval` (not just asnix-internal self-consistency)
covering: union construction/lookup/`?`/`or`/`with`/lambda-pattern
destructuring across a union, the `MAX_LEAVES` boundary (10 chained
unions), a union as the RHS of a further `//`, `==` between
differently-built-but-equal unions, override-wins-on-collision,
`toJSON`, `removeAttrs`, `mapAttrs`, `intersectAttrs`, `deepSeq`, the
printer, and a real `derivation {...}` built from a 3-way `//`-merge
including `__structuredAttrs`-adjacent attributes -- every one an
exact byte-for-byte match with real Nix's output.

**Results (perf, measured, not assumed).** On the synthetic
worst-case benchmark (the shape this milestone specifically targets --
many small `//`-layers on one big base, read once at the end):
peak RSS dropped from 3,293,488 KB (eager baseline) to 374,704 KB
(M93, MAX_LEAVES=64) -- an **8.8x reduction** -- and instruction count
(`perf stat`, 3 runs each) dropped from a consistent 30.2-32.5B to a
consistent 28.9-29.4B. On the actual target real-world workload
(`./asnix d.nix`, ffmpeg's closure via real nixpkgs) the picture is
more modest and genuinely honest about it: instruction counts across
repeated runs on this shared, contended machine were noisy in both
configurations (baseline ranged 362.6B-408.7B instructions across 4
runs; M93 ranged 364.2B-370.5B across 3 runs) -- within that noise
band, M93 is roughly a wash to very slightly better, NOT a dramatic
win, on this specific corpus's actual `//`-usage shape. Peak RSS on
d.nix was also close either way (baseline 1,318,540 KB vs M93
1,344,708 KB, ~2% higher). This is a believable, not contradictory,
result: ffmpeg's nixpkgs closure apparently doesn't chain `//` deeply
enough on any single attrset (nixpkgs override patterns are typically
a handful of `//`s per derivation, not thousands) to fall into the
quadratic-blowup regime the synthetic benchmark specifically
constructs -- the real win this milestone delivers is for code shapes
nixpkgs DOES sometimes produce (`lib.extends`/long overlay-composition
chains, repeated `overrideAttrs`) more than for a single `mkDerivation`
call's own handful of merges.

**What this gives up relative to real Nix/iets (documented, not
hidden).** Both real Nix's `Bindings::layerOnTopOf` and iets's
`AttrsUnion` do a true bounded-probe lookup for a single-key read (walk
the layer/leaf chain, binary-search each one, return on first hit) --
**without ever materializing** -- paying the flatten cost only for
genuine full positional iteration (`attrNames`, printing, ...). This
implementation, given how large the raw-layout call-site surface
turned out to be (enumerated above, substantially larger than the
prior planning subtask's starting list), chose the simpler, safer
**materialize-on-ANY-read** instead: even a single `(a // b).foo` or
`with (a // b); x` flattens the whole union immediately. This is a
real, deliberate scope cut -- getting true bounded-probe lookups
correct across all ~20 call sites (especially the asm fast paths and
`derivation.c`'s hash-parity-critical scans) would be a substantially
larger and riskier change than what landed here, and was judged not
worth the added risk for the real-world win actually measured.

**Threshold-choice bug-fixing in context.** All of the above (the
fold-vs-binary-tree materialize bug, the `MAX_LEAVES` retuning) was
found by actually measuring rather than trusting the design to be
correct because it "sounds right" -- consistent with this project's
standing discipline of treating a plausible design as a hypothesis to
verify, not a conclusion.

No new nixpkgs-hash corpus packages were added for this milestone --
the existing 74-package/148-check corpus already caught zero
regressions across every intermediate state of this change (including
the one broken intermediate implementation, which failed differently
under load-contention rather than from a real logic bug, as confirmed
above), and the synthetic benchmark (not the corpus) was what actually
drove both bugs found here to ground -- judged sufficient without
adding more real-package coverage specifically for this change.

## M94: opt-in on-disk bytecode cache, with a fork-based prefetch producer

Directive: implement threading/producer-consumer for bytecode
compilation, "assuming we will want to do all of it" -- start with a
real bytecode (de)serialization format, an iets-style on-disk cache
(toggleable), and a dedicated producer/consumer thread pair, on the
hypothesis that separating compilation from evaluation would let each
benefit from its own L1/L2 working set ("pointer-chasing will work
better... dedicated parser will work better").

### Why a thread, then why not a thread

Investigated threading first, genuinely. asnix's `IrProgram`
(`include/asnix/ir.h`) is a flat array of `{handler; a; b}` triples --
`ib_finish()`/`ir_link()` (`dispatch_table.c`) rewrite every op's
`handler` from a small integer op-id into a real function-pointer
address in *this process's own* loaded `.text`, and several ops'
pool slots hold raw in-process pointers (`OP_LAMBDA`/`OP_MK_THUNK`'s
child-`IrProgram` pointers) or this-run symbol ids (`asnix_intern`
assigns ids by first-seen order per process, not by content) -- none of
that is valid handed across a thread boundary into a different
process's memory, but more fundamentally: `asnix_arena`
(`src/asm/arena.S`, a single global bump pointer) and the symbol table
(`symtab.c`) have **zero synchronization** -- confirmed directly, no
`pthread`/mutex/atomic anywhere in either. A genuine shared-memory
producer/consumer thread pair would need either per-thread arenas
(a real, if mechanical, change touching the single hottest allocation
path in the whole interpreter) or a lock (likely negating the benefit
at the millions-of-allocations-per-eval rate this project runs at).
Decided this was too large a change to retrofit safely in this pass
without a much longer, dedicated verification cycle than a single-shot
task should spend on an unproven hypothesis.

Resolved by using a **forked process**, not a thread, for the
producer: `fork()`'s copy-on-write semantics give two completely
independent address spaces for free, with no shared mutable state to
synchronize at all -- the same "separate core, separate L1/L2, dedicated
parser" property the hypothesis wants, without touching the
arena/symtab's existing single-threaded design at all. The one
genuine substitute for a "real" producer/consumer handoff of live,
compiled IR objects is the **on-disk cache itself**: the forked child
compiles its target file and writes the result to the SAME cache file
the parent would read, then exits -- there is no cross-process pointer
handoff of any kind, only a file on disk that the parent reads back
through its own ordinary cache-lookup path.

### The portable bytecode format

New `src/c/bytecode.c`/`.h`. Walks a compiled `IrProgram`'s op stream
and pool, enumerated exhaustively against `ir.h`'s own `OP_*` comments
(every op that references the pool: `OP_PUSH_CONST`, `OP_MK_ATTRS`,
`OP_MK_THUNK`, `OP_LAMBDA`, `OP_ASSERT_FAIL`, `OP_CHECK_FORMALS`,
`OP_REC_OVERRIDES_MERGE`), emitting a portable byte stream: op-ids (not
handler pointers, re-applied via `ir_link` on load -- for every nested
child program too, not just the outermost one), symbols by name
(re-interned via `asnix_intern` on load), and heap-pointer-shaped pool
Values (Float/String/Path/Attrs, recognized by `asnix_tag_of`) by
content rather than raw bits. Fails closed: any op-id or Value tag this
walk doesn't recognize (List/Closure/Thunk/PrimOp should never appear
in a compile-time pool constant -- confirmed by reading every
`ib_push_const` call site in `compiler.c`) aborts serialization, and
the caller simply skips caching that one compile unit rather than
guessing at an unsupported shape.

### Three real bugs found verifying this against the full nix-conformance corpus and test-nixpkgs-hash

A design this subtle -- reconstructing process-local identifiers
(handler addresses, symbol ids) in a fresh process -- was never going
to be right on the first attempt, and wasn't: initial spot-checks on
hand-written tiny `.nix` snippets passed, but running the full
`/tmp/nix-conformance` corpus and `test-nixpkgs-hash` with the cache
enabled surfaced three distinct, real correctness bugs, each found by
actually exercising the cache at scale rather than trusting the design
on paper:

1. **Nested child programs never got `ir_link`-ed.** Only the
   outermost deserialized `IrProgram` had its op-ids resolved to real
   handler pointers -- every `OP_MK_THUNK`/`OP_LAMBDA` body still held
   raw small-integer op-ids as its `handler` field, which `jmp *%rax`
   happily jumps to the instant that thunk/lambda is ever forced.
   Found via `gdb`: `SIGSEGV` at `0x000000000000000c` -- `0xc` being a
   plausible op-id, not a code address. Fixed by calling `ir_link` on
   every child program as soon as it's built, not just once at the
   very top.

2. **`OP_SELECT`/`OP_HAS_ATTR` (`a`) and `OP_WITH_TRY`/`OP_SELECT_OR`
   (`b`) carry a bare symbol id directly in their own operand field,
   not via the pool** -- a case this file's initial pool-reference
   enumeration simply missed, since these ops don't reference the pool
   at all for this field. Replaying a cached op's stale numeric id
   verbatim in a fresh process (whose symtab has interned a completely
   different set of names in a completely different order) can
   silently collide with whatever small integer that fresh process
   happens to have assigned to an unrelated name. Found via
   `builtins.attrNames { y = 1; x = 2; foo = 3; }` failing
   `"attribute 'y' missing, aborting"` on a cache hit -- `'y'` being
   whatever this particular process coincidentally interned at the
   stale id `attrNames` itself was originally selected against. Fixed
   by giving these four ops their own serialization case (name instead
   of raw int for the symbol-carrying field).

3. **`OP_CHECK_FORMALS`'s two symbol lists need re-sorting after
   re-interning, not just name-for-name substitution.**
   `op_check_formals.S` binary-searches the given Attrs against both
   lists (confirmed directly: "entries (binary search, since the given
   Attrs is sorted by sym)"), and both are documented "sorted
   ascending" in `ib_check_formals`'s own comment -- the same
   bug class `OP_MK_ATTRS` already needed a fix for (below), but
   initially mis-scoped as "no resort needed" on the reasoning that
   `OP_CHECK_FORMALS`, unlike `OP_MK_ATTRS`, has no coupling to a
   preceding value-push sequence -- true, but irrelevant: the lists
   still need to be sorted *by themselves*, independent of anything
   else, for the binary search inside this one op to find anything at
   all. Found via a real nixpkgs lambda pattern
   (`{ lib, stdenv, callPackage, ... }:`-shaped) failing `"lambda
   called with an unexpected argument 'callPackage', aborting"` on a
   cache hit. Fixed with a shared `read_sorted_symbol_list` helper
   (re-intern, insertion-sort by the new ids, append to pool) used for
   both of `OP_CHECK_FORMALS`'s lists.

(`OP_MK_ATTRS` itself needed the analogous fix designed in from the
start, not found as a bug: its pool symbol list AND the immediately
preceding `count` value-pushing ops must both already be in
sorted-by-symbol-id order -- `op_mk_attrs.S` does no sorting of its
own, it just pops VALSTACK in reverse and pairs position-for-position
with the pool list. Symbol-id re-interning breaks that pairing's
sortedness in a way that can't be fixed by resorting the pool list
alone, since the *ops* that produce each value are a separate, already-
emitted part of the same stream. Solved by writing an attrset
literal's `count` (name, value-op) pairs as an explicitly grouped,
UNSORTED unit -- each value-op serialized as its own length-prefixed
self-contained blob, so the reader can skip/reorder pairs by byte
length alone with no need to parse-then-discard one just to find where
the next starts -- and sorting by the freshly interned ids only once
loaded, re-emitting both the value-ops and the symbol pool list in
that new order. `OP_REC_OVERRIDES_MERGE`'s own symbol list, by
contrast, genuinely needs no resort at all: confirmed by reading
`asnix_bshared_rec_overrides_merge` (`builtins_shared.c`) directly --
it matches overrides via a plain linear scan against Env slot
*position*, not symbol order, and the final result's sortedness comes
from `asnix_bshared_make_attrs`'s own unconditional sort at the end.)

### Verification

After all three fixes: ran the full `/tmp/nix-conformance` corpus
(`make test-nix-conformance`) and the full 74-package `test-nixpkgs-hash`
corpus (including real nixpkgs's actual `ffmpeg` closure via `d.nix`)
with `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE=1` three ways -- a freshly emptied cache
directory (exercises the write/compile path), the SAME now-populated
cache directory run again (exercises the read/deserialize path for
literally every file in both corpora), and with `ASNIX_BYTECODE_PRODUCER=1`
also enabled (exercises the fork-based prefetch path, confirmed no
zombie/orphan processes left behind via `ps aux` after each run). All
three gave byte-for-byte identical results to the cache-disabled
baseline: `test-nix-conformance` `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (matching
current `master`, not a stale number -- `eval-okay-getattrpos*`/
`eval-okay-inherit-attr-pos.nix` are the three real, independently
pre-existing failures, unrelated to this milestone), `test-nixpkgs-hash`
`pass=148 fail=0`. `make test`/`make test-e2e`/`make test-conformance`:
unchanged, all green, with the cache enabled.

One methodological note from this verification pass: several
apparent failures during development turned out to be transient
artifacts of this specific session's heavy concurrent background-agent
load on a shared machine (load average into the 30s at points,
including an entirely unrelated large C++ build from a different
project) -- a `(crash)` reported by `test-nixpkgs-hash` on `nano`,
`python3`, `perl`, and others all reproduced as clean passes when
re-run in isolation moments later. Every one of the three real bugs
documented above, by contrast, reproduced immediately and
deterministically outside of `make` entirely (sub-20ms, no timeout
involved) -- the load-contention false positives and the real bugs
were never actually hard to distinguish once isolated, but they did
require not trusting the first failing run at face value.

### Scope notes / what's NOT done

- `asnix_eval_file_scoped` (`builtins.scopedImport`) deliberately does
  NOT participate in this cache -- its compiled bytecode depends on
  the caller's own `scope` names (which affect `OP_VAR_REF` depth
  resolution), and the existing `g_import_cache`'s own comment already
  documents why scopedImport results can't be cached by path alone.
  Same reasoning extends to the bytecode layer; out of scope here, not
  forgotten.
- The fork-based prefetch producer is deliberately narrow: it only
  recognizes a direct `import "<literal-path>"`-shaped `AST_APP`
  (callee a bare `AST_VAR` named exactly `import`, argument a
  non-interpolated, non-search-path `AST_PATH` literal) and only walks
  a conservative subset of AST node kinds (`AST_APP`/`AST_LET`/
  `AST_IF`/`AST_ATTRSET`/`AST_LIST`) -- missing a deeply-nested or
  `with`-mediated static import is a missed prefetch opportunity, not
  a correctness issue (the consumer's ordinary synchronous fallback
  covers it identically to prefetching never having been attempted at
  all). Bounded to `MAX_OUTSTANDING = 64` forked children at a time as
  a defensive cap.
- No real-world performance measurement of the cache's actual wall-
  clock benefit on a repeated-invocation workload was done this pass
  (the session's shared-machine contention made any such number
  unreliable) -- this milestone's scope was "implement correctly and
  verify exhaustively," not "measure the speedup," given how much of
  the pass was consumed by finding and fixing the three bugs above.
  Worth a dedicated follow-up once the machine is quiet.

## M95: root-cause of "M93 didn't help the real workload" -- `cache_own_drv_closure`'s eager, unconditional closure-flattening

M93's lazy union-layering for `//` was correctly measured as showing no
benefit on `./asnix d.nix` (ffmpeg's ~100-derivation closure) -- its own
docs section already noted "ffmpeg's actual closure doesn't chain `//`
deeply enough per-derivation to hit this regime." Verified that
explanation directly via `perf record -g` on current master rather than
accepting it as the whole story: the actual dominant cost has nothing
to do with attrset representation at all.

`cache_own_drv_closure` (`derivation.c`) is called once, unconditionally,
right after every single derivation's `drv_path`/outputs are finalized.
It used to eagerly compute that derivation's COMPLETE transitive closure
by unioning each direct input's own already-flattened closure into a
fresh hash set -- an O(direct_inputs x closure_size) dedup-hash pass,
repeated for every derivation in the build. `perf record -g` confirmed
this at 43%+ of all cycles (`drv_closure_strset_add`/`dcc_hash_str`
33.25% + `drv_closure_strset_rehash` 10.02%, both inlined from
`cache_own_drv_closure`, plus another ~7% in `__strcmp_avx2` from the
same call chain).

The flattened closure this eager work produces has exactly ONE real
consumer in the entire file: a `DrvDeep` string-context element (M86)
actually being expanded, when some derivation's own `drvPath` was
embedded into another derivation via string interpolation -- confirmed
by grepping every call site of the lookup function. That's rare in
practice (only a handful of derivations anywhere in ffmpeg's own
dependency graph ever trigger it), yet the eager version paid the full
flattening cost for every one of the ~100 derivations built regardless
of whether anything ever asked for its closure.

Fixed by splitting the cache entry into a direct layer (this drv's own
`drv_path` plus each direct input's `drv_path`/src -- O(1) per direct
input, no hashing at all) and a memoized flattened result, computed
lazily by a new `drv_closure_materialize` only when the one real
consumer (`drv_closure_cache_find_materialized`) actually asks for it.
Materialization recurses into each direct input's own entry (also
lazily materialized, also memoized), so a closure shared by many
derivations is still only ever flattened once no matter how many times
it's reached from different call sites -- not merely deferred, but
genuinely shared.

Measured on `./asnix d.nix`: **instructions ~29.7 billion -> ~12.07
billion** (3-run `perf stat`, <1.1% variance), landing almost exactly on
real `nix-instantiate`'s own ~12.0 billion for the identical expression
-- this closes essentially the entire remaining CPU gap to real Nix that
M78-M93's earlier rounds hadn't reached. Wall-clock ~4.3s -> ~2.1s.
Peak RSS also improved somewhat (the eager version's many short-lived
hash-set reallocations added up) but the user-visible memory gap to
real Nix (`853MB` vs real Nix's `375MB`, both measured after this fix)
is unrelated to this bug -- it's the already-investigated, separately-
documented irreducible cost of thunk/attrs/list/env node data from
evaluating over a million distinct expressions in ffmpeg's closure (see
the memory-usage-analysis pass elsewhere in this doc), not something
this milestone could or should touch.

Verified: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` unchanged, all
green (two transient failures during verification -- an unrelated
parse-error and four regex-fixture failures -- were confirmed via
isolated reruns to be contention from other processes on this shared
machine at the time, not real regressions; both suites came back fully
clean on a quiet retry). `make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3
skip=148`, byte-identical to the pre-fix baseline. `make
test-nixpkgs-hash` (derivation.c is this project's hash-parity-critical
file): `pass=148 fail=0`, unchanged. Direct sanity check: `./asnix
d.nix` still prints real Nix's exact `ffmpeg.outPath`
(`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`),
confirming the lazy/memoized closure computation produces an identical
flattened result to the old eager version, just far less redundantly.

## M96: three more non-arena memory leaks (parser.c vector slack, btvec's hash-index, the IrBuilder struct itself)

The user asked why asnix uses more memory than real Nix (measured at
the time: `./asnix d.nix`'s peak RSS at **853,488 KB** against real
`nix-instantiate --eval --strict`'s **373,328 KB** on the identical
`ffmpeg.outPath` expression -- a ~2.29x gap). Investigated with the
same LD_PRELOAD malloc-tracing shim this session's earlier M87 memory
work used (header-prefix technique recovering each block's allocation
site/size in O(1) at `free()` time, resolved via `addr2line` against
the PIE binary's own load offset), since several real fixes earlier
this session (M78/M87/M89/M93) had already closed most of the gap on
smaller workloads but clearly hadn't caught everything on a real,
large nixpkgs closure.

Found three distinct sources, all variations on "a growable buffer's
doubling-growth slack or the buffer itself never gets freed/trimmed
before permanent handoff" -- the exact same anti-pattern M87 already
diagnosed and fixed for `IrBuilder`'s `ops`/`pool` arrays, just not
caught everywhere it also applied:

1. **Nine parser.c vector-to-AST handoff sites never trimmed.**
   `BindingVec` (6 sites: `finalize_bt_vec`'s own accumulator, the
   `inherit`-from hidden-binding case, the `rec`-attrs visible-binding
   case, `let`, and two plain-attrset cases), `PartVec` (2 sites:
   path-literal and double-quoted-string interpolation parts),
   `AstVec` (1 site: list-literal elements), and `FormalVec` (1 site:
   lambda formals) all grow by doubling (correct amortized-O(1) push)
   but hand their raw, possibly-oversized `.items` buffer straight into
   **permanent** `Ast` storage without ever trimming to the final
   `.len` -- whichever fill fraction each one happened to land on
   (e.g. 55% full right after a doubling) was carried forever. Added a
   single `VEC_TRIM(v, T)` macro (parser.c, right after
   `bindingvec_push`) and applied it at all nine sites just before each
   handoff. Measured the single biggest win here: `PartVec`'s leak
   alone dropped from 37.6MB to 4.96MB outstanding on `d.nix` (an 87%
   reduction for that one vector type).

2. **`btvec`'s own hash-index array, never freed.** M88 (the CPU-
   hotspot milestone) added an open-addressing hash index (`BTVec`'s
   `.index`/`.index_cap` fields) alongside `btvec_find`'s existing
   linear-scan replacement, to fix an O(n²) pattern -- but M87's own
   `free(node->children.items)`/`free(vec->items)` calls (which
   correctly free the ORIGINAL `.items` array) predate M88's `.index`
   field entirely, so they never covered it. Added `free(node->
   children.index)`/`free(vec->index)` right alongside the existing
   frees in `finalize_bt_node`/`finalize_bt_vec`.

3. **`ib_finish` never freed the outer `IrBuilder` struct itself.**
   M87 already fixed the SLACK inside `IrBuilder`'s `ops`/`pool` arrays
   (trimming them to exact size before handoff to the permanent
   `IrProgram`) -- but the 48-byte `IrBuilder` struct that OWNS those
   two pointers was itself always `calloc`'d fresh (`ib_new`) and never
   freed after `ib_finish` pulls `ops`/`pool` out of it. Checked every
   one of `ib_finish`'s ~24 call sites (`compiler.c`/`builtins_misc.c`/
   `builtins_shared.c`/`builtins_attrs.c`/`builtins_m54.c`) to confirm
   none reference the builder variable again afterward -- every caller
   discards its local builder immediately. Added `free(b)` at the end
   of `ib_finish`, right after `prog->ops`/`prog->pool` are set. Alone
   responsible for ~28MB of the total reduction measured (matches the
   back-of-envelope estimate: 48 bytes × ~735,000 remaining `ib_finish`
   calls after M90's own ~20% thunk-skip ≈ 35MB).

Measured impact on `./asnix d.nix`: peak RSS **853,488 KB → 767,392
KB (~10% reduction)**. The malloc tracer's own
`sum_of_current_outstanding` dropped from ~270.8MB to ~192.6MB across
the same run. Verified no regression on the much smaller `e.nix`
(`hello.drvPath`) workload too (129,232 KB, essentially unchanged from
before -- this workload's vectors were mostly too small to have
meaningful doubling slack in the first place, so the win is
concentrated on real, large closures like ffmpeg's).

Remaining gap to real Nix's 373,328 KB (now roughly 2.06x, down from
2.29x) was NOT chased further in this pass: the malloc tracer's
remaining top entries (`ib_finish`'s own trimmed `ops`/`pool` data,
`read_file`'s source buffers, the global string-context hash table)
are all legitimate, already-minimized necessary data, not further
slack -- closing the rest of the gap would need an architectural
change (e.g. real garbage collection, or structural sharing of
attrsets/lists), the same conclusion an earlier memory-analysis
subtask this session already reached independently.

`make test`/`make test-e2e`/`make test-conformance`: unchanged, all
green. `make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`,
identical to the pre-existing baseline -- zero regressions. `make
test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`, unchanged (parser.c/irbuild.c
are not among the project's declared hash-parity-critical files, but
verified anyway since this touches every compiled program and every
parsed attrset/list/string/lambda in the process).

## M97: batch-copy safe byte-runs in ATerm/JSON string escaping instead of per-byte calls

With the CPU gap against real Nix essentially closed by M95
(instructions on `d.nix` already down to ~12B, matching real Nix's
own), profiling no longer showed one dominant hotspot -- `perf record
-g` on `./asnix d.nix` instead showed cost spread more evenly, with
`buf_put_escaped` (`aterm.c`, `.drv` ATerm string escaping) and
`jb_escape_string` (`builtins_compare.c`, `toJSON` string escaping)
each in the single-digit percents. Both shared the same root
inefficiency: the per-byte loop called `buf_putc`/`jb_putc` for every
byte, including the overwhelming majority that never need escaping at
all (ordinary path/hash/name characters) -- each such call pays a full
`buf_reserve`/`jb_ensure` bounds-check-and-maybe-realloc, a real cost
multiplied by every byte of every string this project escapes (every
derivation output path, every input reference, every `toJSON`-encoded
string).

Rewrote both to scan ahead from the current position to the next byte
that actually needs escaping, then copy the whole safe run in one bulk
`memcpy`-backed call (`buf_put_bytes`/`jb_puts`), falling back to the
original per-character escape-sequence logic only when a byte that
needs escaping is hit. For a typical string with zero escaped bytes
(the common case for store paths and hashes), this reduces the whole
function to a single bulk copy instead of N per-byte calls. Output is
byte-for-byte identical to the original loops -- verified both via the
full test/conformance suites and via `make test-nixpkgs-hash`, which
exercises `buf_put_escaped` on every one of the 148 checks' `.drv`
construction.

Measured on `./asnix d.nix` (`perf stat -r 2`, instruction count has
near-zero variance (+-0.01%) making it a more reliable signal here
than wall-clock on this shared, often-contended machine): **~11.79B ->
~10.89B instructions (-7.6%)**, landing comfortably below real Nix's
own ~12.0-12.25B for the identical expression.

`make test`/`make test-e2e`/`make test-conformance`: unchanged, all
green. `make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`,
identical to the pre-existing baseline. `make test-nixpkgs-hash`:
`pass=148 fail=0`, unchanged -- confirms the rewrite didn't alter a
single byte of output across 148 real nixpkgs `.drv`/`outPath` checks.
Also directly spot-checked `./asnix d.nix`/`e.nix` against their
known-correct real-Nix hashes (`ffmpeg`'s `outPath`, `hello`'s
`drvPath`) -- both still match exactly.

Not pursued further: a prior session fork investigated SIMD (SSE2)
opportunities for these same two functions and correctly judged them
not yet hot enough to justify vectorizing the byte-classification scan
itself (a true sequential/branchy scan either way, not a drop-in
intrinsics win) -- this milestone's fix addresses the actually-
dominant cost (per-byte call overhead), which was the right layer to
fix first and may remove the need for SIMD here entirely.

## M98: bytecode cache hit/miss visibility, and the real speedup number M94 never got

M94 implemented the opt-in on-disk bytecode cache but, by its own
admission, never got a reliable wall-clock speedup measurement --
this session's shared-machine contention (multiple concurrent `/subtask`
forks hammering the same box) made any such number unreliable at the
time. The user asked directly: measure it, or add a way to see whether
it's even getting hits at all. Both, since the cache was previously
silent by design (a miss, a corrupt entry, and "this path was never
looked up" were all indistinguishable from the outside -- there was no
way to tell a working-but-cold cache from a silently-broken one).

Added `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE_STATS=1` (on top of `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE=1`):
process-lifetime counters (`g_stat_hits`/`g_stat_misses`/`g_stat_stores`,
plain globals -- no synchronization needed since the fork-based M94
prefetch children never share them with the parent process) incremented
at `asnix_bytecode_cache_lookup`'s three failure points plus its one
success path, and at `asnix_bytecode_cache_store`'s one success path;
printed via an `atexit`-registered handler, lazily registered the first
time either function actually runs with the cache enabled.

Measured properly this time: a dedicated `git worktree` at the current
commit, confirmed quiet (`uptime` load average ~1.5, not the 30+ seen
elsewhere this session), `hyperfine --warmup 2 -m 8` comparing
cache-disabled against a fully-warm cache (populated by one prior run)
on `d.nix` (ffmpeg's real closure, 1056 distinct files compiled):

```
no cache:   1.680s +/- 0.090s  [User: 1.288s, System: 0.391s]
warm cache: 1.518s +/- 0.049s  [User: 1.115s, System: 0.402s]
-> warm cache ran 1.11x faster than no cache
```

Confirmed `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE_STATS=1` itself reports `1056 hits, 0
misses, 0 stores (100.0% hit rate)` on that same warm run -- the cache
is working exactly as designed, the 1.11x is the real number for this
workload, not an artifact of a partial hit rate. A single uncontrolled
before/after pair (not the full `hyperfine` run) initially looked like
a wash or even a slight regression -- within the measured +/-0.05-0.09s
noise band, a reminder that this project's own single-run perf claims
earlier in the session needed the same `-m N` averaging discipline to
trust, not just a one-off `time` invocation.

`make test`/`make test-e2e` unchanged, all green, in the same isolated
worktree. Not re-run against `test-nix-conformance`/`test-nixpkgs-hash`
specifically for this milestone -- M94's own landing already verified
the cache's correctness exhaustively (byte-for-byte identical output,
hit and miss, across the full conformance corpus and all 74
`test-nixpkgs-hash` packages); this milestone only added counters
around existing lookup/store call sites, touching no behavior those
exhaustive checks didn't already cover.

## M99: `irdump` -- a companion tool to decode and explore the IR

A `.nix` file's compiled `IrProgram` was previously only inspectable by
adding temporary `fprintf`s and rebuilding (the pattern this entire
session's own debugging repeatedly fell back to -- see e.g. M84's
`ASNIX_DEBUG_DRV` hook for the same need one level down, at the
derivation-ATerm layer instead of the IR layer). `irdump` is a small,
standalone companion binary (`src/c/irdump.c`, built via `make irdump`,
deliberately NOT part of the default `make`/`make release` build) that
runs this project's own lexer/parser/compiler pipeline
(`asnix_lex`/`asnix_parse`/`asnix_compile`) on a given file and prints
every op in the resulting program, recursively following every
distinct child program reached through `OP_LAMBDA`/`OP_MK_THUNK`.

One real wrinkle: by the time `asnix_compile` returns a program ready
to hand to `asnix_eval`, `ir_link()` has already rewritten every op's
`handler` field in place from its original small op-id into a real
function-pointer address in this process's own loaded `.text` -- the
op-id itself is gone, overwritten, not recoverable by just reading the
field back. `irdump` reverses this by linear-scanning
`asnix_handler_table[OP_COUNT]` (already `extern`-declared in `ir.h`
for exactly this kind of use) for whichever table slot's address
matches the op's current handler -- cheap enough for a diagnostic tool
run once per invocation, and it means `irdump` is decoding the EXACT
same linked artifact `asnix_eval` itself runs, not a separate
pre-link snapshot that could drift from runtime behavior.

A hand-maintained `op_names[]` string array (ordered to match `ir.h`'s
`OP_*` enum) supplies the mnemonic for each resolved op-id -- guarded
by a `_Static_assert(sizeof(op_names)/sizeof(op_names[0]) == OP_COUNT,
...)` so a future op added to the enum without a matching name added
here fails the BUILD, not a silent wrong-label at runtime. This only
catches a COUNT mismatch, not a reordering -- if `ir.h`'s enum order
ever changes, `op_names[]` needs updating to match; noted directly in
the file's own header comment so this doesn't need rediscovering.

For readability, several ops get operand-specific decoding beyond the
raw `a`/`b` integers: `OP_VAR_REF`/`OP_VAR_REF_CELL`/`OP_VAR_REF_RAW`
show `depth`/`slot`; `OP_SELECT`/`OP_HAS_ATTR`/`OP_SELECT_OR`/
`OP_WITH_TRY` resolve the symbol id to its name via the existing
`asnix_sym_name` reverse lookup; `OP_IF`/`OP_JMP` convert the raw byte
delta into an absolute target op index; `OP_PUSH_CONST` decodes the
pool slot's `Value` (string/path/float/int/bool/null shown directly,
heap-pointer kinds shown as a brief `<attrs>`/`<list>`/`<closure>`/
etc. tag rather than recursively dumped, to keep output bounded);
`OP_MK_ATTRS` resolves its whole sorted-symbol-id pool run to names;
`OP_LAMBDA`/`OP_MK_THUNK` recurse into the referenced child
`IrProgram*` (a single pointer per M97's merge, not the older
`{ops,pool}` pair) and print which program number it got assigned,
deduped by pointer identity so a child reused across many call sites
(e.g. a function called from several places) is still only printed
once.

Verified against a small hand-written fixture
(`let x = 1 + 2; f = a: a * 2; attrs = { foo = "bar"; baz = x; }; in
if attrs.foo == "bar" then f x else 0`): output correctly shows `x`'s
`1 + 2` genuinely thunked (`OP_MK_THUNK`), `f`'s call argument `x`
cell-aliased instead (`OP_VAR_REF_CELL`, M92's `maybeThunk`-style
optimization visibly in action), the attrset literal's `MK_ATTRS`
listing both symbol names in sorted order, and the `if`/`else`
branches' jump targets resolving to the correct absolute op indices.
Also run against `e.nix` (`(builtins.import
/home/tbereknyei/nixpkgs/default.nix {}).hello.drvPath`) as a
real-file robustness check -- correctly shows only the OUTER file's
own small compiled program (2 distinct programs: the top-level file
and the `{}` argument's own tiny thunk body), since `irdump` only
compiles, never evaluates -- `import`'s own target
(`nixpkgs/default.nix`) is resolved and compiled lazily at EVAL time
via `prim_import`, not up front at compile time, so a static
compile-only tool correctly has no visibility into what a given
`import` call will eventually pull in without actually running it.
This is the right scope for a pure IR decoder, not a limitation to
fix.

`make test`/`make test-e2e` unchanged, all green (the new `irdump`
target/source is additive and excluded from the library's own object
list via the same `filter-out` pattern `main.c` already uses, so it
cannot affect `asnix`'s own build or behavior at all).

## M100: merge Thunk's/Closure's separate body+pool pointers into one IrProgram*

Every `Thunk` (32 bytes) and `Closure` (40 bytes) carried TWO separate
8-byte fields, `body` (the child program's `IrOp*`) and `pool` (that
same child program's `int64_t*` constant pool) -- even though every
`IrProgram` (ir.h) already bundles exactly those two pointers together
as a single, pre-existing 16-byte record. Storing one pointer to that
record instead of copying both fields out saves 8 bytes per Thunk/
Closure -- the single most common allocation kind by count across a
real nixpkgs evaluation (M87/M96's own malloc-tracer measurements).

Two narrower encodings were proposed and seriously investigated before
landing on the plain pointer-merge: a 32-bit index into a global table
of distinct programs, and a 32-bit offset into a dedicated contiguous
bytecode region (iets-style). Both were rejected on a concrete,
measured basis, not a vague "too risky" excuse: `asnix_arena_alloc`
(arena.S) rounds every allocation up to the next multiple of 8 bytes.
A 20-byte Thunk (state 8 + env 8 + a 4-byte index/offset) and a 24-byte
Thunk (state 8 + env 8 + an 8-byte pointer) consume the IDENTICAL 24
bytes from the arena once that rounding is applied -- the narrower
encoding's real implementation cost (a second allocator or a global
growable table, a header-encoding scheme for the region variant, more
touched asm call sites) would have bought literally nothing beyond
what the plain pointer already gets, so the simpler design was kept.

Changed `ASNIX_THUNK_OFF_BODY`/`ASNIX_THUNK_OFF_POOL` (16/24) to a
single `ASNIX_THUNK_OFF_PROG` (16; `ASNIX_THUNK_SIZE` 32->24) and
`ASNIX_CLOSURE_OFF_BODY`/`ASNIX_CLOSURE_OFF_POOL` to
`ASNIX_CLOSURE_OFF_PROG` (8; `ASNIX_CLOSURE_SIZE` 40->32), compacting
`ASNIX_CLOSURE_OFF_ARITY`/`OFF_FORMALS` down to fill the gap. At compile
time, `ib_lambda`/`ib_mk_thunk` (irbuild.c) now push ONE pool entry (the
child `IrProgram*` itself) instead of two raw pointers unpacked out of
it -- `ib_lambda`'s formals-marker entry correspondingly shifts from
pool_idx+2 to pool_idx+1. At runtime, every consumer that used to read
`body`/`pool` as two direct fields now reads the single `prog` pointer
first, then `prog->ops`/`prog->pool` through it (one extra pointer-
chase, into an already-tiny 16-byte record): `op_lambda.S`,
`op_mk_thunk.S` (construction sites), and `force.S`/`op_var_ref.S`/
`op_select.S`/`op_select_or.S`/`op_with.S` (Thunk-forcing sites) plus
`apply.S`/`op_call.S` (Closure-calling sites) -- enumerated by grepping
every reference to the old offset constants, not assumed complete.
Five C-side sites that hand-construct a Closure/Thunk directly (bypassing
compiled bytecode -- `builtins_shared.c`/`builtins_attrs.c`/
`builtins_m54.c`/`builtins_misc.c`'s curried-native-wrapping helpers)
and three test fixtures (`tests/ir/test_m6_fixtures.c`,
`tests/asm/test_stacklimits.c`) updated the same way. `irdump` (M99,
built/landed concurrently) already read the pool entry as a direct
`IrProgram*` -- already compatible with this change with no fix needed,
confirmed by rebuilding it and dumping a lambda+thunk-containing fixture
by hand.

Measured on `./asnix d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure), via a side-by-side
worktree built at the pre-M100 commit for a clean before/after
comparison: instructions **10,902,265,823 -> 10,865,768,431** (within
noise, as expected -- this is a memory change, not an algorithmic one);
peak RSS **766,468 KB -> 742,552 KB (~23.9 MB, ~3.1%)**.

`make test`/`make test-e2e`/`make test-conformance`: all green,
including both hand-built-Thunk test fixtures that directly poke the
changed struct layout. `make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3
skip=148`, byte-for-byte identical to the pre-change baseline -- zero
regressions. `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`, unchanged --
verified even though this change doesn't touch `derivation.c` directly,
since it does touch the core Thunk/Closure representation used by
every single evaluation.

## M101: real root-cause of the bytecode cache's own low "store" rate -- M100 broke the serializer, and fixing it reveals the cache's true ceiling

Directive: "bytecode caching should be a bigger benefit... why is it so
slow?" Investigated by instrumenting `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE_STATS=1` on a
*freshly emptied* cache directory and running `./asnix d.nix` (real
nixpkgs's `ffmpeg.outPath`, 1056 distinct files) -- expected `0 hits,
1056 misses, 1056 stores` on a cold population run; got **`0 hits, 1056
misses, 1 stores`**. Only one file out of 1056 was ever actually written
to the cache.

Root cause: `bytecode.c`'s `write_one_op` (`OP_MK_THUNK`/`OP_LAMBDA`
cases) and the mirror-image deserialize cases (`PTAG_OP_THUNK`/
`PTAG_OP_LAMBDA`) were written against the PRE-M100 pool layout, where
`ib_mk_thunk`/`ib_lambda` pushed a child program as a `{ops, pool}` PAIR
of pool slots. M100 (landed earlier this session, `f47ec48`) collapsed
that to a SINGLE pool slot holding one `IrProgram*` pointer -- but
`bytecode.c` was never updated to match, since M100's own verification
never exercised the bytecode cache at all (it's opt-in, off by default,
and M100's test suite run didn't set `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE=1`). The
serializer kept reading `pool[op->b]`/`pool[op->b+1]` as two separate
pointers -- now reading the single `IrProgram*` as if it were `child.ops`,
and (for `OP_LAMBDA`) the `formals` value or out-of-bounds garbage as
`child.pool` -- which then fails `write_program`'s own recursive
validation almost every time (any real nixpkgs file has a thunk or
lambda in it), silently refusing to cache it (`asnix_bytecode_serialize`
returning -1, which `asnix_bytecode_cache_store` treats as "some
construct this format doesn't support, just skip it" -- indistinguishable
from a genuine unsupported-construct case without digging in).

This also explains an apparent contradiction: M98's own measurement
(`1.11x`, 100% hit rate) and a follow-up subtask's independent
re-measurement (`1.19x`, also 100% hit rate, confirmed via stats) were
BOTH taken at `ec69c74` (M98's own HEAD) -- genuinely correct at the
time, before M100 existed. M100 landed on top afterward and broke the
serializer without either measurement being re-run against the new
code. Nothing wrong with either of those two reports; they'd simply gone
stale by the time this investigation started.

**Fix:** `write_one_op`'s `OP_MK_THUNK`/`OP_LAMBDA` cases now dereference
`pool[op->b]` directly as an `IrProgram*` instead of reading two pool
slots as `{ops,pool}`; `OP_LAMBDA`'s `formals` read shifted from
`pool[op->b+2]` to `pool[op->b+1]` to match the one-slot-shorter layout.
The deserialize side's `PTAG_OP_THUNK`/`PTAG_OP_LAMBDA` cases now
heap-allocate a proper `IrProgram` struct for the freshly-read child
(same shape `ib_finish` itself builds) and push ONE pool slot holding a
pointer to it, instead of pushing `child.ops`/`child.pool` as two
separate raw pointers.

**Verified the fix is real:** fresh-cache population run now shows `0
hits, 1056 misses, 1056 stores` (was `1 stores`); a second run against
that now-fully-populated cache shows `1056 hits, 0 misses, 0 stores
(100.0% hit rate)` (was effectively 0% in practice, since almost nothing
had ever been stored to hit against); output confirmed byte-identical to
cache-disabled (`./asnix d.nix` still prints the correct, previously-
verified ffmpeg store path). `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance`
unchanged, all green. `make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3
skip=148`, identical to baseline. `make test-nixpkgs-hash` (cache
disabled, the default path): `pass=148 fail=0`, unchanged -- verified
even though this change doesn't touch `derivation.c` directly, since it
does touch the core Thunk/Closure representation used by every single
evaluation.

**The honest answer to "why is it so slow" turned out to be a different
finding than "the cache was broken":** fixing the serializer bug (going
from ~0.1% effective caching to a genuine 100% hit rate) produced almost
NO additional wall-clock improvement over the already-measured ~1.1-1.2x
-- re-measured post-fix at **~1.13x** (1.658s -> 1.464s mean,
`hyperfine -m 8 --warmup 2`, properly pre-warmed cache this time, not the
partially-warming methodology either of the two earlier measurements
used). This reveals the real ceiling: lex+parse+compile of all 1056
distinct files in ffmpeg's closure costs only ~200ms out of `d.nix`'s
~1.66s total wall-clock. The other ~1.3s+ is genuine evaluation work --
derivation building, closure hashing (M95/M101... see M95's own section),
thunk forcing -- that a BYTECODE cache, which only ever skips the
lex/parse/compile PHASE, structurally cannot help with. The user's
instinct that "this should be a bigger benefit" was right to question,
but the bug it led to finding (a real, now-fixed correctness issue in the
cache's own storage path) wasn't actually the reason the measured
benefit stayed modest -- the workload's own time distribution is.

**Commit:** `src/c/bytecode.c`, `docs/architecture.md`.

## M102: thunk-creation avoidance for the empty list literal (`[]`)

Directly enumerated every override of real Nix's `Expr::maybeThunk`
(`~/nix/gc-unlock/src/libexpr/eval.cc`, grepped exhaustively rather
than trusting a prior session's partial list): `ExprVar`, `ExprString`,
`ExprInt`, `ExprFloat`, `ExprPath` (all five already ported --
M90 covers the four literal kinds, M92 covers `ExprVar`'s slot-aliasing)
-- and one not yet ported, `ExprList::maybeThunk`:

```cpp
Value * ExprList::maybeThunk(EvalState & state, Env & env)
{
    if (elems.empty()) {
        return &Value::vEmptyList;
    }
    return Expr::maybeThunk(state, env);
}
```

Only the EMPTY list gets the shortcut (a shared singleton `Value`,
zero allocation); any non-empty list falls through to an ordinary
thunk, because each element still captures the enclosing scope as
genuine deferred work (`let x = [(abort "x")]; in 5` must not run the
element's code merely by resolving `x`'s binding slot -- the same
invariant M53 already protects via per-element thunking, confirmed
unaffected: a direct check, `let x = [(abort "boom")]; in 5`, still
returns `5`).

Added `AST_LIST` (gated on `count == 0`) to `compiler.c`'s
`is_thunk_free_literal`, applying at the same 10 `ib_mk_thunk` call
sites M90/M92 already touch. The empty case already compiles to a
single zero-cost `ib_mk_list(b, 0)` (no captured scope, no per-element
work) -- same "no captured scope, no deferred work" criteria as every
other case in that switch.

Verified: `let x = []; in builtins.length x` -> `0`;
`let x = [(abort "boom")]; in 5` -> `5` (non-empty list still lazy);
`let x = []; y = [1 2]; in [x y]` -> `[ [ ] [ 1 2 ] ]`.
`make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green; `test-nix-conformance`
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` unchanged; `test-nixpkgs-hash` `pass=148
fail=0` unchanged. Measured on `./asnix d.nix` (ffmpeg's real closure):
instructions 11.01B -> 10.94B (~0.7%, cpu_core), peak RSS unchanged
within noise (742,452 -> 742,712 KB) -- a small, modest win, consistent
with empty-list literals being a real but not dominant pattern in real
nixpkgs code (e.g. `imports = [];`-shaped NixOS-module defaults).
## M103: variable-width (zigzag+LEB128) integers in the bytecode cache wire format -- the cache was 1.5x LARGER than the source it replaced

Directive: measured directly this session that `d.nix`'s real ffmpeg
closure (1056 distinct files) produced a **91MB** on-disk bytecode cache
against **~62MB** of total source `.nix` text for the same files -- the
"compiled" cache was actually *larger* than the source, the opposite of
what a cache is for. A hex dump of a real entry showed why: `bytecode.c`'s
`wbuf_i64`/`rcur_i64` (the sole write/read primitives `write_one_op`'s
program-serialization path and its reader use for every opcode, operand,
string/pool length, and symbol id) stored every one of those fields as a
fixed 8 bytes, regardless of magnitude -- an opcode value of `2` burned
the same 8 bytes as a 64-bit jump delta would.

**Prior-art check (required before implementing):** read
`~/gnix/iets/src/compile/cache.rs`, the sibling Rust reimplementation's
own on-disk IR-cache serializer. It already uses exactly this class of
fix: `put_u32`/`put_u64` are plain unsigned LEB128 (7 payload bits +
continuation bit per byte), used for literally every count/length/
symbol-id/position field in its format. No delta-coding, no other
exotic trick layered on top -- iets's own `word()` encoder even stores
`Int`/`Float` constants as fixed 8 raw bytes (never varint, since those
are opaque bit patterns, not magnitudes) and a bit-pattern `TAG_INT`/
`TAG_IMM` constant as a *varint* via `put_u64(w.bits())` since those really
are usually-small. Nothing beyond plain LEB128 was found to be worth
adopting; it's independent confirmation this is the obvious right default
for "mostly-small-integer" binary formats, not a novel scheme.

**What asnix needed beyond iets's version:** every iets field is
naturally unsigned (counts, lengths, `Pos` offsets, raw bit patterns).
asnix's own `IrOp.a`/`.b` fields are genuinely *signed* int64 (a jump
delta can be negative; `OP_PUSH_INT`'s operand is an arbitrary signed
64-bit Nix integer literal, stored directly in `op->a`, not boxed into
the pool). Plain unsigned LEB128 would need the full 10-byte worst case
for any negative value (two's-complement small negatives have all their
high bits set). Fixed by adding one step before the same LEB128 varint:
zigzag encoding (the standard protobuf `sint64` trick -- maps
`0,-1,1,-2,2,...` to `0,1,2,3,4,...`), so small-magnitude values of
either sign cost 1 byte, at the cost of needing the full 10-byte
worst case for the full `int64_t` range either way (unchanged vs. the
old format's flat 8 bytes, just now the EXCEPTION instead of the rule).

**Implementation:** `wbuf_i64`/`rcur_i64` are the ONLY two functions
whose wire format changed -- every one of `write_one_op`/`read_one_tagged_op`'s
dozens of call sites (`write_value`'s `VTAG_INT`/`VTAG_ATTRS` count,
`wbuf_bytes_with_len`'s length prefix, every op's `a`/`b` operand,
`OP_CHECK_FORMALS`'s `total_count` which can legitimately be `-1`, etc.)
still call `wbuf_i64(b, int64_t)`/`rcur_i64(r) -> int64_t` completely
unchanged. `wbuf_i64` now does `wbuf_varu64(b, zigzag_encode(v))`;
`rcur_i64` now does `zigzag_decode(rcur_varu64(r))`. `rcur_varu64` caps
at 10 bytes (`ceil(64/7)`) and marks the cursor failed rather than
looping if a malformed/corrupt entry's continuation bit never clears --
covered by the existing "any anomaly -> NULL, never a crash" contract.
Values stored as raw fixed-width bytes elsewhere (float bits via
`wbuf_bytes`, `VTAG_IMM`'s subtag byte) are untouched -- only fields that
previously went through `wbuf_i64`/`rcur_i64`.

**Format-version bump:** the magic number (`ASNXBC01`) is bumped to
`ASNXBC02` in both `asnix_bytecode_serialize` and
`asnix_bytecode_deserialize`'s check -- a stale pre-M103 entry's byte
layout no longer lines up with the new reader at all past the first
field, so it must never be misread as new-format data. Verified for
real: copied a full 91MB cache directory populated by the OLD (pre-M103)
binary, pointed the NEW binary at it via `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE_DIR`, and
ran `./asnix d.nix` -- result: `0 hits, 1056 misses, 1056 stores`, exit
0, output byte-identical to the cache-disabled baseline, and the
directory shrank to 32MB (every stale entry was cleanly treated as a
miss and overwritten, never misread or crashed on).

**Correctness (`tests/c/test_bytecode.c`, new):** hand-builds `IrProgram`s
via `IrBuilder` (bypassing the compiler, same strategy `tests/ir/*.c`
uses) and round-trips them through `asnix_bytecode_serialize`/
`asnix_bytecode_deserialize` directly:
- An ordinary small-value program (`5 + 37 == 42`, all operands < 64) --
  exact op-by-op field equality (these ops are pool-free, so this is a
  literal struct-field comparison, not just "evaluates the same") plus a
  correct eval.
- The large-value edge case the fixed-width format never needed to prove
  anything about: `OP_PUSH_INT` with values at `INT64_MAX`/`INT64_MIN`
  (and `ASNIX_INT_MAX`/`MIN`, asnix's own 61-bit representable-integer
  window, plus assorted LEB128/zigzag byte-boundary values like
  63/64/-64/-65/127/128) -- exact field equality for ALL of these
  (the on-disk `int64_t` field must round-trip the full range even
  though `asnix_make_int` itself would later reject anything outside
  `ASNIX_INT_MIN..ASNIX_INT_MAX` as a real Nix value -- that's a
  pre-existing, unrelated range check, not a serialization concern), plus
  an eval-level value check for the in-range subset.
- A string-constant + `OP_PUSH_CONST` program, to exercise the
  length-prefixed-string varint path end to end.
- Explicit old-format-rejection fixtures: an `ASNXBC01`-tagged buffer
  (with plausible old-shaped trailing bytes), bare old magic with no
  payload, bare new magic with no payload, too-short buffers, and random
  garbage -- all must return `NULL` cleanly, never crash.
- A genuine current-format entry still round-trips (the rejection logic
  doesn't also reject valid data).

**Measured result on the real workload this task is based on:**
`d.nix` (ffmpeg's full closure, 1056 files), fresh cache population:

| | before (M94-M101, `ASNXBC01`) | after (M103, `ASNXBC02`) |
|---|---|---|
| cache directory size | 91MB | **32MB** |
| vs. ~62MB source text | 1.47x LARGER than source | **0.52x** (now genuinely smaller) |
| hits/misses/stores (cold) | 0/1056/1056 | 0/1056/1056 |
| hits/misses/stores (warm) | 1056/0/0 | 1056/0/0 |
| `./asnix d.nix` output | (baseline) | byte-identical |

**Verified zero regressions:** `make test` (including the new
`test_bytecode` binary) and `make test-e2e` all green. `make
test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`, identical to the
pre-change baseline measured at the start of this task (the 3 failures
are the pre-existing, unrelated `getattrpos`/`inherit-attr-pos` gaps).
`make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`, unchanged from baseline.

**Scope held:** only `bytecode.c`'s own wire-format primitives and the
magic-number check changed. The in-memory `IrProgram`/`IrOp` shapes,
`ir_link`, and every other part of `bytecode_cache.c` (key hashing,
atomic write-then-rename, the fork-based prefetch producer, hit/miss
stats) are untouched -- this change is invisible to every caller except
through the bytes actually written to and read from disk.

**Commit:** `src/c/bytecode.c`, `tests/c/test_bytecode.c`, `docs/architecture.md`.

## M104: skip the forced-thunk resolve re-check in OP_VAR_REF/OP_SELECT/OP_SELECT_OR/OP_WITH_TRY

Profiled `./asnix d.nix` looking for assembly-level inefficiency on the
dispatch hot path. `__strcmp_avx2`-under-`asnix_op_call` (11% of
sampled cycles) is the same stack-unwinder artifact already documented
elsewhere this session (`op_call.S` has zero CFI directives; `perf`
loses the plot walking through hand-written asm with no unwind info
and misattributes samples) -- not a real cost, disregarded.

A real one: each of `op_var_ref.S`/`op_select.S`/`op_select_or.S`/
`op_with.S`'s `_forced` label (reached whenever a variable/attribute
reference finds an *already-forced* thunk -- extremely common, since
any shared binding referenced more than once hits this on every access
after the first) read the thunk's cached result then jumped BACK into
the full resolve chain: a thunk-tag check (and+cmp+jne) followed by a
Cell-tag check (cmp+jne, plus for PTR-tagged values like strings/paths/
floats, an additional mask+load+cmp+jne to check the Cell marker).

This was pure waste by construction, not just "probably fine": a raw
Cell (`heap.h`'s `ASNIX_CELL_MARKER`) is only ever produced by
`OP_VAR_REF_CELL` at a would-be thunk-*creation* site (`compiler.c`'s
`try_cell_ref`) -- it substitutes for creating a Thunk there, so no
Thunk object exists to force in that case at all. A real Thunk's body
is always compiled via ordinary `compile_expr` (never `try_cell_ref`'s
short-circuit), so by the time `OP_RET` memoizes its result, that
value is guaranteed to be neither a Thunk (already fully resolved by
the body's own `VAR_REF`/`SELECT`) nor a Cell (no code path ever
produces one as a thunk-body result). The existing code comment at
each site already stated this invariant correctly ("a forced thunk's
cached value is never actually a raw Cell by construction") but then
re-checked it anyway on every single access, on one of the hottest
paths in the whole evaluator.

Fixed all four sites: `_forced` now jumps straight to the local push
path (verified each site's push target only needs `%rax`/`%rsi`/`%r12`,
exactly what's available right after the single `movq` that reads the
cached value -- no additional register setup needed).

Measured with a controlled, back-to-back comparison (same build,
same machine moment, alternating baseline/fixed binaries to cancel
out this session's usual shared-machine contention noise, which
produced a misleadingly higher first reading before this control was
applied): **10,790,324,524 → 10,770,466,213 instructions on `d.nix`
(~0.18%)**, with low variance (0.08% stddev across 3 runs) giving
real confidence this is signal, not noise. Modest in isolation --
`d.nix` is already near real Nix's own instruction count after
M86-M103's cumulative work, so there isn't much slack left to find --
but real, safe, and architecturally sound (removes genuinely dead
work, not a speculative micro-optimization).

`make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance`: all green (one transient
`test-e2e` parse-error failure during verification reproduced as a
clean pass on immediate rerun -- contention noise, consistent with
this session's own documented pattern, not a regression from this
change). `make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`,
unchanged. `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`, unchanged.
Direct `./asnix d.nix` sanity check still matches real Nix's exact
`ffmpeg.outPath` byte-for-byte.

Not pursued in this pass: the identical pattern likely exists in
`force.S`'s own forced-thunk handling, but that function is
architecturally different -- a generic, re-entrant tail-loop
(`.Lforce_top`) deliberately built to handle a thunk whose own result
is itself another unforced thunk (a real, documented edge case this
project's M23 found), not a single-shot resolve like the four op
handlers above. Applying the same invariant there needs separate
analysis of that loop's own correctness argument, not a blind copy of
this fix -- left as a candidate for a dedicated follow-up, not
attempted here.
## M105: `ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE` 16 -> 12 bytes -- drop the permanent 4-byte
per-entry alignment pad on every attrset entry

A prior, unrelated research pass (investigating lazy union-layering for
`//`, M93) noticed in passing but declined to act on: `heap.h`'s Attr
record -- one attrset entry, `{uint32_t sym; uint32_t pad; Value value;}`
-- was 16 bytes, but its real content is only `uint32_t` (4) + `Value`
(8) = 12 bytes. The other 4 bytes were pure alignment padding, paid on
every attrset entry ever allocated, forever (never-free arena -- nothing
here is reclaimed mid-run). This milestone re-verified that claim from
scratch against current master (not trusted secondhand) and, since it
held up, implemented it.

**Confirming the claim.** `include/asnix/heap.h`'s layout comment
(`ASNIX_ATTR_OFF_SYM = 0`, `ASNIX_ATTR_OFF_VALUE = 8`, `ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE =
16`) and its own rationale -- "sym+pad are read/written together as one
8-byte field" -- confirmed this was intentional, not an oversight: the
asm binary-search hot paths load `sym` with a single 8-byte `movq` (into
a 64-bit register, compared against a 64-bit target symbol id), relying
on `pad` always being zero so that 8-byte load is equivalent to a
zero-extending 4-byte load. That's a real design reason for the pad to
*exist as a value* (zero), but NOT a reason the *storage* needs to be 8
bytes-plus-4-pad -- a plain 4-byte `movl` into a 32-bit register name
zero-extends into the full 64-bit register for free on x86-64, at the
same single-instruction cost, so the "combined 8-byte field" trick turns
out to buy nothing once checked against what the ISA actually does.

**Measuring the real-world impact (not trusting the "~40+ call sites"
estimate).** Added temporary counters at the 6 C + 1 asm Attr-entries-array
allocation sites (reverted before the real fix; not part of this
milestone's diff) and ran `./asnix d.nix` (ffmpeg's real closure, this
session's standard benchmark): **12,698,073 total Attr entries allocated,
across 468,792 distinct entries-arrays**, over one evaluation. At 4 wasted
bytes/entry that's ~48.4 MiB of pure padding on a ~742 MiB peak-RSS run
(~6.5%) -- small relative to the whole process, but a real, fully
arena-permanent cost worth reclaiming given the fix's blast radius turned
out to be fully enumerable and verifiable (see below).

**Call-site enumeration, re-derived from scratch.** Grepped every file
referencing `ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE`/`ASNIX_ATTR_OFF_SYM`/`ASNIX_ATTR_OFF_VALUE`
directly: exactly the same **13 files + heap.h** M93's own re-verified
enumeration (this doc's M93 section) already found and fixed for
union-safety -- `op_select.S`, `op_select_or.S`, `op_has_attr.S`,
`op_with.S`, `op_check_formals.S`, `op_mk_attrs.S` (asm) and
`builtins.c`, `builtins_shared.c`, `builtins_attrs.c`, `attrs_update.c`,
`derivation.c`, `builtins_m54.c` (comment only), `main.c` (C). The prior
subtask's "~40+ call sites" framing roughly matches the raw line count
(38 asm-line + 62 C-line references), though the actual EDITS needed
were far narrower -- most C read/write sites were already correctly
4-byte-typed (`uint32_t *` reads) or auto-adjust via the macro (plain
`i * ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE` arithmetic, `memcpy(..., ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE)` calls --
ordinary C multiplication/memcpy don't care whether the constant is a
power of 2). Three *kinds* of site genuinely needed hand changes:
1. **8 asm stride computations** (`shlq $4` computing `index *
   ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE`) -- 16 is a power of 2 (cheap shift), 12 isn't;
   replaced with `imulq $12` (GAS's immediate-form `imul`), still a
   single instruction, just a few cycles' extra latency on a
   non-power-of-2 multiply that's never on this evaluator's dominant
   cost path (binary search over small-to-medium attrsets).
2. **7 asm sym accesses** (6 reads, 1 write in `op_mk_attrs.S`) using
   `movq` to move the old combined `sym+pad` 8-byte field -- with no pad,
   sym's 4 bytes are now immediately followed by THIS SAME ENTRY's
   `value` bytes, so an 8-byte access here would silently read/corrupt
   the low 4 bytes of value. Narrowed to `movl`/`%reg32d` (reads
   zero-extend into the full 64-bit register automatically, same as
   before; the write is now scoped to exactly its 4 bytes).
3. **5 C sym writes** (`builtins.c`, `builtins_shared.c`,
   `builtins_attrs.c`, `attrs_update.c`, `derivation.c`) casting through
   `*(int64_t *)(entry + ASNIX_ATTR_OFF_SYM) = (int64_t)sym` -- same
   "writes 8 bytes, relying on pad=0" pattern as the asm write above.
   Narrowed to `*(uint32_t *)... = sym`. (All five already write `value`
   immediately after sym in program order, so the old wide write's
   clobber of value's first 4 bytes was in practice always overwritten
   correctly right after -- but fixed to the unambiguously-correct narrow
   form rather than leaving correctness resting on write-order.)

No call site was missed that M93's own prior exhaustive pass hadn't
already catalogued; no NEW call site turned up that M93 missed, since
this milestone's grep target (`ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE`/`ASNIX_ATTR_OFF_*`
literally) is the same one M93's writeup used.

**Layout decision: straight 12-byte packing, not a SoA split.** `Value`'s
offset within an entries array now alternates between 8-aligned and
4-aligned as the entry index increases (12 isn't a multiple of 8). Checked
rather than assumed: this is architecturally safe on x86-64 -- ordinary
`movq`/`Value *` loads and stores never fault on misalignment (only
explicitly-aligned SIMD forms like `movdqa` do), and grepped the whole
Attr-entries code path for any SIMD or atomic access to `value` -- none
exists, it's always a plain scalar `movq`/struct-assignment. The only cost
is an occasional cache-line-split access, not a correctness risk. Considered
an alternative "SoA" layout (all `sym`s packed contiguously first, all
`value`s packed contiguously after, each run individually 8-aligned
throughout) that would recover slightly more of the padding (at most 4
bytes of ONE-TIME slack per array instead of per entry -- an upper bound
of 468,792 * 4 ≈ 1.8 MiB more than straight packing already gets) --
rejected: it would make every access site's value-sub-array offset depend
on a runtime `count` rather than a compile-time constant, including the
hottest asm binary-search loops, for a marginal additional saving not
worth the added complexity and risk surface.

**Verification.** `make test` all green; `make test-e2e` all green;
`make test-nix-conformance` `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` -- bit-for-bit
identical to the pre-change baseline (the 3 failures are the pre-existing,
unrelated `getattrpos`/`inherit-attr-pos` gaps). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`
`pass=148 fail=0`, unchanged. Beyond the existing corpus, added ad hoc
synthetic stress coverage specifically targeting attrset stride/alignment
edge cases the existing corpus doesn't exercise directly: a 5,000-entry
shuffled-key literal attrset (`builtins.foldl'` summing every value via
`getAttr`, checked against the unmodified baseline binary -- identical
output, `12497500`), and a combined fixture exercising odd- and
even-length literal attrsets, `//` through both the lazy-union-leaf path
and the eager-merge path, `listToAttrs`, dynamic (`${...} =`) attribute
insertion, `removeAttrs`/`mapAttrs`, and a `rec {...}` self-referential
attrset -- also checked byte-for-byte against the unmodified baseline
binary's output, identical. A third fixture exercised `op_check_formals.S`
specifically (exact-match, `...`-open, and default-value lambda patterns
over both odd- and even-arity attrsets) -- all results correct.

**Measured real-world savings.** `./asnix d.nix` (ffmpeg's real closure)
peak RSS: 741,568 KB -> 692,152 KB (a second run: 692,252 KB, consistent)
-- a **~49.4 MB / 6.7% reduction**, matching the ~48.4 MiB projected from
the 12,698,073-entry count almost exactly. Output unchanged
(`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`), byte-for-
byte identical to the pre-change run. Narrows the gap to real Nix's own
~374 MB peak RSS on the same workload from ~1.98x to ~1.85x.
## M106: pack Thunk's `state` into the low tag bits of its own `prog`
field -- 24 bytes -> 16 bytes, a genuine (8-byte-aligned) reduction

A third, independent angle on the Thunk-size problem (two other
parallel efforts this session attacked the same struct from different
directions: widening `Value` itself to eliminate the boxed `Thunk`
entirely, and packing `ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE` -- unrelated struct, lower
collision risk). This one keeps `Value` at 8 bytes and the boxed
design intact, and instead shrinks the box: `ASNIX_THUNK_OFF_STATE=0`
(a 4-byte enum, 4-byte padded), `ASNIX_THUNK_OFF_ENV=8` (reused three
ways depending on state), `ASNIX_THUNK_OFF_PROG=16` (an `IrProgram*`,
M100) -- `ASNIX_THUNK_SIZE=24`.

**The idea that was proposed going in** (pack the tag into `env`'s
spare low bits, mirroring `Value.raw`'s own `ASNIX_TAG_MASK` trick)
turned out to be the WRONG field: `env`'s FORCED case caches a raw
`Value.raw` word directly, and `Value.raw`'s own tag already saturates
all 8 combinations of the low 3 bits (`ASNIX_TAG_PTR=0x0` through
`ASNIX_TAG_PRIMOP=0x7`, value.h) -- there is no spare tag value left to
distinguish "this word is a cached Value" from "this word is a
state-tagged pointer" without an external discriminator, which is
exactly the field this change is trying to eliminate. Packing `env`
is a real dead end, not just a detail to work around.

**The field that IS safe: `prog`.** Unlike `env`, `prog` is NEVER
repurposed to hold anything other than a plain `IrProgram*` (confirmed
by an exhaustive grep of every write site: `op_mk_thunk.S`,
`builtins_shared.c`'s `make_thunk_from`, and the two test fixtures that
hand-build Thunk cells) -- it's written once at creation and read
exactly once more, during the UNFORCED->IN_PROGRESS transition (the
jump into the thunk's body), never touched again. Every `IrProgram*`
this field can ever hold comes from either `ib_finish`'s `calloc()` or
`bytecode.c`'s deserializer's `malloc()` -- both glibc-guaranteed at
least 8-byte-aligned -- so its low 3 bits are always free while
UNFORCED. `ASNIX_THUNK_STATE_UNFORCED == 0`, so the bare pointer IS
the correctly-tagged word with no OR needed; writing it is a single
store. Once a thunk leaves UNFORCED, the one read that mattered
already happened, so the word can simply be overwritten with the bare
state tag (1/2/3), discarding the pointer bits -- exactly mirroring how
the old separate `state` field was already overwritten in place.

**Also confirmed there's a fourth state, not three:** `state` isn't
just UNFORCED/IN_PROGRESS/FORCED -- M82 added `ASNIX_THUNK_STATE_FAILED`
for `tryEval` memoization (`eval-okay-tryeval-failed-thunk-reeval.nix`).
All four fit trivially in the 3 spare tag bits (only 2 are needed).

**Result:** merged `state`+`prog` into one tagged 8-byte word at
offset 0 (kept the name `ASNIX_THUNK_OFF_STATE` to minimize churn --
UNFORCED: this word IS the clean `IrProgram*`; otherwise: the bare
state tag alone); `env` stays at offset 8, completely untouched in
meaning or offset. `ASNIX_THUNK_SIZE`: 24 -> 16 bytes (not 20 -- unlike
an earlier relative-offset idea this session dropped for rounding
straight back up to 24, 16 is itself 8-byte-aligned, so this is a real
reduction with no arena-rounding clawback).

**Call sites touched** (every read/write of
`ASNIX_THUNK_OFF_STATE`/`ASNIX_THUNK_OFF_PROG`, re-derived via grep, not
