to point at the same logical op in the new, shorter array.

**Proof-of-concept pass** (`src/c/irpass_examples.c`,
`asnix_irpass_register_cfold`): folds `OP_PUSH_INT a; OP_PUSH_INT b;
OP_<binop>` into one `OP_PUSH_INT`/`OP_PUSH_TRUE`/`OP_PUSH_FALSE`, for
ADD/SUB/MUL/DIV and all 6 comparisons -- 3 ops down to 1, net -2 per fold.
`compiler.c` does no AST-level constant folding of any kind today
(grepped directly -- confirmed), so this is also the first arithmetic
constant-folding this project has, not just a bytecode-level backstop for
an existing fold. DIV skips folding when the divisor is 0 (must still
reach the runtime op and abort with "division by zero") or the pair is
`(INT64_MIN, -1)` (would be signed-overflow UB to fold).

**`irdump` extended** to take the same `ASNIX_IR_OPT=1` flag, so a before/
after diff is one command each:
```
./irdump file.nix > before.txt
ASNIX_IR_OPT=1 ./irdump file.nix > after.txt
diff before.txt after.txt
```
Verified visually on `if (1 + 2) == 3 then "yes-" + (if (10 - 3) > (2 * 2)
then "a" else "b") else "no"`: 22 ops -> 12 ops, every `IF`/`JMP` target
correctly re-pointed at the same logical destination in the shrunk stream.

**Verified for correctness, not just this one fixture**: diffed
`ASNIX_IR_OPT=1` vs. unset output (stdout + exit code) across every
`tests/e2e`/`tests/conformance` fixture (308, 0 divergences) and the FULL
numtide/nix-conformance corpus (806 files: `eval-okay-*`/`eval-fail-*`, 0
real divergences -- 3 initial mismatches were traced to transient,
load-induced flakiness under this session's own heavy concurrent-agent
contention, confirmed by direct, repeated, isolated reruns producing
identical output both ways every time). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`:
`pass=148 fail=0` both with and without the flag, output hash on
`d.nix` (ffmpeg.outPath) unchanged either way.

**Honest measured impact on `d.nix`** (`perf stat -r 3`, `cpu_core`
instructions): 10,861,185,514 -> 10,919,663,525, i.e. flat within this
measurement's own ~0.66% run-to-run noise -- no detectable real win.
Expected, not a bug: real nixpkgs source has very few LITERAL
adjacent-int-constant arithmetic expressions for this specific pass to
find (nixpkgs's actual numeric values overwhelmingly come from parsed
config/version strings and runtime computation, not bare `1 + 2`-shaped
source text) -- the same "high raw hit count, small real-workload
effect" pattern M116's curried-native fusion work already found and
documented for a different reason (alias indirection there; source-text
scarcity here). This milestone's deliverable is the FRAMEWORK and its
verification method, not a performance claim from this one example pass.

**Scope note, deliberately not attempted here: bytecode -> native
assembly.** The directive asked about this too. `ir_link()` already
proves every op dispatches through a real function-pointer jump table
(`asnix_handler_table`), and each op's semantics live in a small,
self-contained `.S` handler -- in principle a JIT backend could walk the
same op stream this framework already walks and emit the SAME handler
bodies' instructions inlined back-to-back (eliding the jump-table
indirection itself) instead of rewriting `IrOp` records, slotting in as
another kind of "pass" alongside this one. But this is a qualitatively
larger undertaking, not attempted here: it would need an executable
memory allocator (mmap+mprotect, nothing like this exists yet),
register-allocation decisions for values this interpreter currently keeps
on an explicit stack/pointer-chased Env (a real redesign question, not a
mechanical translation), and correctness verification at a much finer
grain (comparing emitted machine code's behavior, not just an IR
rewrite's). Flagged as a real, larger follow-on -- deliberately scoped
out rather than attempted partially, matching this project's own standing
discipline (M100/M106's own "measured and rejected" relative-addressing
work is the precedent for not building something whose cost is clear but
whose payoff isn't yet measured).

Files: `include/asnix/irpass.h`, `src/c/irpass.c`, `src/c/irpass_
examples.c`, `src/c/irbuild.c` (one line in `ib_finish`), `src/c/main.c`
(`ASNIX_IR_OPT` flag), `src/c/irdump.c` (same flag).

### irdump follow-up: `ASNIX_IR_OPT=diff` combined view, and `OP_PUSH_INT`'s literal value shown explicitly

Usability follow-up to M120, prompted directly by using the tool: the
documented `before.txt`/`after.txt`/`diff` workflow needed two separate
invocations for what's usually a quick one-off check. `irdump` now also
accepts `ASNIX_IR_OPT=diff`, which compiles the SAME source twice in one
process -- once before `asnix_irpass_register_cfold()`, once after --
printing both under clearly labeled `===== BEFORE =====`/
`===== AFTER =====` headers (`asnix_irpass_clear()`, already exported by
M120's own irpass.h specifically for this "paired before/after in one
process" use case, resets state between the two). The original
`ASNIX_IR_OPT` unset/`=1` behavior (before-only/after-only, for the
file-diff workflow) is unchanged.

Also: `OP_PUSH_INT`'s dump line now shows `; value=N` explicitly, matching
the labeled-field style every other operand-bearing op already gets
(`OP_VAR_REF`'s `depth=/slot=`, `OP_SELECT`'s `sym=`, etc.) instead of
requiring the reader to know that `PUSH_INT`'s generic `a=` field happens
to be its literal value.

### irpass follow-up: named, fire-counted pass registration + per-firing location markers

Two more usability layers on top of M120's framework, both prompted
directly by using the tool (and by a separate background pass continuing
M120's own work, which independently landed the named/fire-count half of
this before this round reconciled and extended it):

**Named, fire-counted registration**: `asnix_irpass_register` now takes a
short name alongside the function pointer (`asnix_irpass_register("cfold",
fold_constant_int_binop)`); `irpass_examples.c` is renamed `irpass_cfold.c`
(+ its own `irpass_cfold.h`), establishing a one-pass-per-file convention
so future passes don't all land in one shared file (this session's own
standing lesson about concurrent edits to one file). New accessors
(`asnix_irpass_num_passes`/`_name`/`_fire_count`/`_reset_stats`/
`_print_stats`) let `main.c` (`ASNIX_IR_OPT=1`, printed to stderr after
evaluation) and `irdump` report exactly which registered passes fired, and
how many times, across the whole compile (root program + every nested
lambda/thunk body's own `ib_finish()` call, same global-not-per-program
scope the fire counts were always meant to have).

**Firing-location log**: beyond "cfold fired 12 times," `irdump`'s
`ASNIX_IR_OPT=diff`/`=1` modes now annotate the actual dump with `<<< cfold
fired here` directly on the op line where each fold's result ended up.
`asnix_irpass_remove` (the one shrink primitive every pass uses) logs each
firing at `start-1` by convention (where the kept/folded op lives, per
every current pass's own "rewrite in place, then remove the now-redundant
tail" shape) -- and, symmetrically with its existing jump-target fixup,
also re-shifts every PREVIOUSLY logged firing index affected by a later
removal, so by the time a compile finishes every logged location is still
correct against the FINAL op array irdump prints, not some intermediate
one. Multiple real, distinct firings commonly cascade onto the same final
index as a fixpoint re-scan collapses adjacent folds (e.g. `1 + 2` folds,
then the result folds again against `== 3`, both landing at index 0) --
deduped into one `(xN)` marker per pass rather than printed N times.
Best-effort (not disambiguated) across separate nested IrPrograms sharing
the same global log/index space -- exact for a single flat program.

**A real bug hit and fixed while merging this**: renaming
`irpass_examples.c` to `irpass_cfold.c` via `git mv` left a STALE
`irpass_examples.o`/`.d` on disk from an earlier build; since `ar rcs`
doesn't prune archive members no longer in its source list, `libasnix.a`
ended up with both the old (1-arg `asnix_irpass_register`) and new (2-arg)
object code for the same symbol, and the linker picked the stale one --
silently corrupting the registration call (NULL function pointer,
segfault) at runtime. Fixed by removing the stale `.o`/`.d` and a full
`make clean && make`. Worth remembering as a general hazard any time a
source file is renamed rather than edited in place.

Verified: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green;
`test-nix-conformance` `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3 pre-existing
failures); `test-nixpkgs-hash` `pass=148 fail=0`; `./asnix d.nix` output
hash unchanged with `ASNIX_IR_OPT` unset or `=1` ("cfold: 12 firings" on
the real nixpkgs closure).

## M121: ThunkMap -- a shared-descriptor encoding for mapAttrs/zipAttrsWith, replacing M117's one-LazyApp-per-element scheme

A research pass comparing asnix against a sibling evaluator, `iets`
(Rust, `~/gnix/iets`), found iets's `mapAttrs`-equivalent allocates ONE
shared descriptor per call plus a single tagged 8-byte word per output
element (riding in the output attrset's own existing per-entry value
slot), where asnix's M117 `LazyApp` still pays a full 32-byte heap object
per element. This milestone ports that design, adapted to asnix's own
saturated tag space.

**Design**: one `ThunkMapDesc{marker; f; src_entries; out}` (32 bytes,
`ASNIX_THUNKMAP_MARKER = -6`, the same reserved-marker family as
Path/Float/Cell/LazyApp) is allocated per `mapAttrs`/`zipAttrsWith` CALL.
Each output element is packed as `desc_ptr | (idx << 48) | ASNIX_TAG_PTR`
directly into the output attrset's own existing `entries[idx].value` slot
-- stacking two independent tricks on one word: the outer `ASNIX_TAG_PTR`
+ marker scheme (same precedent as Cell/LazyApp) plus, separately,
high-bit pointer tagging inside that word's own payload. Sound because
x86-64 Linux user-space addresses never set bits 48-63 (confirmed
directly against this evaluator's actual `mmap`-backed arena
allocations) -- NOT the same thing as the previously-declined
"descriptor_base | small_index" idea, which tried to steal LOW bits above
an allocator's alignment guarantee and ran straight into asnix's fully
saturated 3-bit tag space; this packs into bits that are always zero on
a real canonical pointer regardless of alignment, at a layer entirely
internal to this one PTR-tagged word's payload.

Goes one step further than iets: self-mutates the output attrset's own
entry slot in place for memoization (a shared element forced twice runs
`f` only once) instead of iets's own extra 8-byte-per-element state cell,
so `mapAttrs` costs ZERO marginal heap bytes per element beyond the one
shared descriptor (reusing the input attrset's own entries array as
`src_entries`); `zipAttrsWith` costs roughly 12 bytes/element.

**A real correctness issue found and fixed**: every PTR-marker-dispatch
site's base-pointer mask had to widen from clearing just the 3 tag bits
to also clearing the packed index's high 16 bits -- caught via an actual
segfault in `asnix_value_is_cell` (the printer's `is_cell`-before-
`is_thunkmap` check reading a bogus address), fixed via one shared
`ASNIX_PTR_BASE_MASK` used everywhere a PTR-tagged word's base pointer is
recovered.

**Verified**: laziness canaries, memoization (a trace-counting test
confirms a shared, twice-forced element runs its callback exactly once),
`zipAttrsWith` output correctness, equality, and the 65,536-element
per-descriptor index-field bound (falls back cleanly past that size).
`make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance`: all green. `make
test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3 pre-existing
pos-tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`.

**Measured on `d.nix`** (real nixpkgs's `ffmpeg.outPath`), paired against
master's M117 baseline:
- lazyapps: 502,964 -> 45,348 (**-91.0%**), exactly conserved into 6,445
  new `ThunkMapDesc`s covering 457,616 elements
- strings: 640,304 -> 194,593 (**-69.6%**) -- deferred element
  name-string construction, only built on actual force now
- peak RSS: ~584,000 -> ~556,300 KB (**~-4.7%**, 3-run average)
- all other categories (envs/sets/list/thunks/closures/cells)
  unchanged, as expected -- this milestone only touches mapAttrs/
  zipAttrsWith's own per-element representation
- output hash unchanged: `/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`

**Scope notes on sibling work from the same research pass, evaluated and
NOT landed alongside this milestone**:
- A companion fix porting iets's `forced_int` arithmetic-folding and
  `shared_select` thunk-elision techniques landed a real but far smaller
  win (-845 thunks, -0.046%) for a proportionally larger amount of new
  permanent machinery (2 new bytecode ops, a new scope-frame "peekable"
  concept, bytecode-cache format special-casing) -- declined as not
  clearing this project's own bar for landing added permanent complexity,
  same discipline as M112's `attrs_eager_merge` investigation.
- A companion fix eliding the intermediate partial-application `Closure`
  for statically-saturated curried 2-arg user calls (`f a b`) cut
  closures by -35.6% but reproducibly INCREASED peak RSS by +1.2% (the
  fixed per-call-site bytecode cost of the eligibility check, paid at
  every syntactic `f a b` site in nixpkgs/lib unconditionally, outweighed
  the bytes saved from fewer `Closure` objects on this workload) --
  declined as a net loss on this project's actual target metric.
- A companion measurement pass quantified the real cost of asnix's
  branch-per-force-chokepoint Cell/LazyApp/ThunkMap dispatch (riding
  `ASNIX_TAG_PTR`): well under 1% of total branch mispredicts, ~0.16% of
  total instructions -- not a measurable bottleneck -- and found
  reclaiming a 4th `Value` tag bit has no safe candidate among the
  existing 8 kinds and would cost 88+ touched call sites plus a real
  arena-rounding RSS regression (8->16 byte granularity). Confirms the
  prior qualitative "high-risk, not recommended" call on real counts;
  no code changed.

## Bytecode-pass framework: 5 more passes via a parallel agent fleet, plus pool-access extension -- and 2 real bugs the 1114-file test corpus missed

Extended the M118 bytecode-to-bytecode pass framework (`include/asnix/
irpass.h`) with 5 more passes, each authored by an independent agent in
its own isolated worktree, each required to verify against the
framework's established methodology (diff `ASNIX_IR_OPT=1` vs. unset
across all 308 `tests/e2e`/`tests/conformance` fixtures + all 806
numtide/nix-conformance `lang/` files, zero divergences required):

- **`jmpnop`**: removes a redundant `OP_JMP` whose target is the next op.
  Found and fixed its own hazard during design (a different live jump
  landing exactly on the no-op jump's own index), before ever shipping.
- **`dce_if`**: dead-branch elimination for a statically-known `OP_IF`
  condition (`PUSH_TRUE/FALSE` immediately before `OP_IF`), guarded by an
  incoming-jump pre-check so an unsafe occurrence is silently skipped
  rather than ever reaching `asnix_irpass_remove`'s fatal safety check.
- **`cmpnot`**: fuses `OP_EQ;OP_NOT -> OP_NEQ` and `OP_NEQ;OP_NOT ->
  OP_EQ` only. The 4 ordering-comparison fusions it was also asked to
  attempt (`LT;NOT->GE` etc.) were investigated and correctly DECLINED:
  `op_cmp.S`'s slow path does direct IEEE double comparisons for floats,
  and IEEE comparisons involving NaN are not a total order (`NOT(LT)` is
  `true` on a NaN operand while `GE` computed directly is `false` for the
  same inputs) -- confirmed reachable in practice (`builtins.fromJSON
  "1e400"` produces `+inf` with no overflow guard). Also surfaced a real,
  PRE-EXISTING, unrelated bug: `compiler.c` already compiles `>`/`<=` as
  `LT`+`NOT` specifically to match upstream Nix's own NaN-respecting
  desugaring, while `>=`/`<` go straight to the native (IEEE-direct,
  NaN-divergent) ops -- so asnix's own `>=` already disagrees with
  upstream Nix on NaN inputs, independent of this pass. Flagged, not
  fixed (out of scope for a bytecode pass).
- **`strconcat`**: folds `OP_PUSH_CONST (string); OP_PUSH_CONST (string);
  OP_STR_CONCAT a=2` into one constant. Required a real, cross-cutting
  framework extension: `AsnixIrPass`'s signature widened to
  `(IrOp*, size_t*, int64_t**, size_t*, size_t*)` uniformly (every pass,
  including `cfold`, now takes and may ignore the 3 new pool params), and
  a new `asnix_irpass_pool_append` (mirrors `ib_pool_add`'s own doubling
  policy) as the pool's grow primitive alongside `asnix_irpass_remove`'s
  existing ops-shrink primitive.
- **`dce`**: global reachability-based dead code elimination (BFS from
  op 0 over fallthrough + every jump op's target). Found that removing
  maximal dead ranges (the originally-suggested design) is unsafe
  whenever a dead region contains its own internal jump -- fixed by
  removing dead ops ascending, one at a time, with an inductive proof
  (every jump this compiler emits points strictly forward, so anything
  that could jump into a dead op must itself have a smaller,
  already-removed index) rather than working around the safety check.
  Added `tests/ir/test_irpass_dce.c`, a hand-assembled synthetic fixture
  -- the only thing that exercises this pass's removal logic, since
  today's compiler never emits literal dead code on its own.

**Merging found 2 more real bugs, neither caught by the 1114-file sweep,
both caught only by running the actual `d.nix` (real nixpkgs
`ffmpeg.outPath`) workload** -- underscoring, yet again, that a large
synthetic+conformance corpus and a real nixpkgs closure are not
substitutes for each other:

1. **`cmpnot`**: assumed `OP_NOT` immediately after an `OP_EQ`/`OP_NEQ`
   is *exclusively* fed by that one comparison. False whenever the `NOT`
   is ALSO a shared join point -- `!(if cond then true else (y != []))`
   compiles as an ordinary if/else whose join point (the code textually
   after the `if`, i.e. this source's own `!`) happens to be exactly that
   `OP_NOT`: the "then" branch pushes `PUSH_TRUE` and jumps DIRECTLY to
   the `NOT` (skipping the "else" branch's own `NEQ` entirely), while the
   "else" branch's `NEQ` falls through into the SAME `NOT`. Fusing would
   have rewritten the `NEQ` to `EQ` and deleted the `NOT` -- silently
   dropping the negation the "then" branch's jump relied on.
   `asnix_irpass_remove`'s own fatal check caught it (a live jump
   targeted the op being removed) rather than letting it miscompile.
   Fixed with the same incoming-jump guard `dce_if` already uses.
2. **`strconcat`**: assumed the second `OP_PUSH_CONST` always falls
   through from the first. False for `"${expr.attr or "default"}
   literal"`: `expr.attr or "default"` compiles via `OP_SELECT_OR`, whose
   FOUND path pushes the found value and jumps DIRECTLY to this
   interpolation's next literal chunk (exactly the second
   `OP_PUSH_CONST`'s position), bypassing the first `OP_PUSH_CONST` (the
   MISS path's own default-value constant) entirely. Same fix.

Both share one root cause: a pass assumed "two adjacent ops in the array
execute as a strict sequential pair" without checking whether either op
is ALSO independently reachable via a jump that skips the other --
exactly the hazard class `dce_if`'s own author had already generalized
against, but `cmpnot`'s and `strconcat`'s authors (parallel, unaware of
each other) hadn't. `asnix_irpass_remove`'s unconditional fatal check is
what made both FINDABLE at all rather than silent miscompiles.

**Verification, all 6 passes active together (`cfold` + the 5 above)**:
`make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance`/`test_irpass_dce` unchanged
with the flag off (default). With `ASNIX_IR_OPT=1`: 0 divergences across
all 308 e2e/conformance fixtures and all 806 nix-conformance `lang/`
files (re-run after both fixes). `./asnix d.nix` (real nixpkgs
`ffmpeg.outPath`), run 3x for determinism: output hash unchanged
(`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`) every
time, with `cfold: 12 firings`, `cmpnot: 13 firings`, `dce_if: 1
firings` (`jmpnop`/`dce`/`strconcat` found nothing to do on this
specific closure -- remain safety nets for other passes' output rather
than wins on today's compiler, by design). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`:
`pass=148 fail=0` both with and without the flag.

Files added: `src/c/irpass_{jmpnop,dce_if,cmpnot,strconcat,dce}.{c,h}`,
`tests/ir/test_irpass_dce.c`. Modified: `include/asnix/irpass.h`/
`src/c/irpass.c` (pool-access signature widening), `src/c/irbuild.c`,
`src/c/irpass_cfold.c` (adapted to the widened signature),
`src/c/main.c`/`src/c/irdump.c` (registration wiring), `.gitignore`.

## M122: skip zero-length literal chunks when compiling string interpolation

Prompted directly by a question about `"${thing}"`: does the overwhelmingly
common "no literal text around an interpolation" shape waste anything?
Yes -- `lexer.c`'s own comment already documents that it unconditionally
emits a TOK_STR_PART on both sides of every `${...}`, "possibly
zero-length, e.g. between two adjacent `${...}${...}` interpolations" --
so `compiler.c`'s `AST_STRING` interpolation branch was pushing a
zero-length String CONSTANT for each of those empty chunks and counting
them into `OP_STR_CONCAT`'s part count, for no reason: concatenating with
an empty string never changes the result's bytes OR its string context
(a compile-time literal constant built directly by `compiler.c` never
goes through `asnix_string_attach_context` in the first place, confirmed
by reading `concat_strings_impl`, `value_util.c`) -- in ANY position,
not just leading/trailing: the `"${a}${b}"` shape has an empty chunk
BETWEEN the two interpolations too, and dropping it is exactly as safe as
dropping a leading/trailing one, for the identical reason.

**Measured directly on `d.nix`** (real nixpkgs's `ffmpeg.outPath`) via a
temporary instrumented build: of 4,208 interpolated `AST_STRING` nodes
compiled across the whole closure, 1,945 (46.2%) have at least one empty
literal part, 2,335 empty parts total -- confirming this is the common
case, not an edge case.

**The fix**: the interpolation-compiling loop now skips any part that is
both non-expression AND zero-length entirely -- neither pushing a
constant for it nor counting it toward `OP_STR_CONCAT`'s `a` operand.
`concat_strings_impl` (`value_util.c`) already handles any count >= 1
correctly with no special-casing needed (confirmed by reading it
directly) -- a bare `"${x}"` now compiles straight to a single
`ib_str_concat(b, 1)`, which still does the real coercion/path-existence-
check/context-union work `x` needs, just without two no-op concatenation
partners. The `all_literal` branch just above (handling "no interpolation
at all") is untouched -- it already folds a wholly-literal string,
including an all-empty one, into one compile-time constant before this
code is ever reached, so `emit_count` here is always >= 1 (at least one
`is_expr` part survives, by construction).

**Verified**: `"${a}"`, `"${a}${b}"` (the middle-empty-chunk case),
`"x${a}"`, `"${a}x"`, `"x${a}x"`, and both indented-string equivalents
(`''${a}''`, `''${a}${b}''` -- `strip_indentation`, `parser.c`, shares
the exact same `AstStringPart`/`AST_STRING` representation and compiler
path) all produce correct output. `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance`:
all green. `make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same
3 pre-existing pos-tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`:
`pass=148 fail=0`. Output hash unchanged.

**Measured impact on `d.nix`**: strings 194,593 -> 192,258 (**-2,335**,
exactly the measured empty-part count -- every one of them eliminated).
CPU/wall-clock impact is flat, within this measurement's own noise
(`cpu_core` instructions 10,603,502,599 -> 10,594,517,002, inside the
~0.1-0.2% run-to-run stddev) -- most of these string literals are
evaluated only a handful of times each across the whole closure, so the
per-evaluation savings (a couple fewer VALSTACK pushes + coerce-loop
iterations) don't add up to a measurable fraction of 10.6 billion total
instructions. Landed anyway: unlike several other small-win candidates
this session (`attrs_eager_merge`'s 1.4% shrink, the arithmetic/select
thunk-elision pass's -0.046%), this change adds ZERO new permanent
machinery -- it's a strict simplification of existing logic, removing
real, confirmed dead work at no complexity cost, not a tradeoff.

### irpass follow-up #2: fix cross-program corruption in the firing-location log, not just its display

A follow-up to the previous "suppress misleading per-op firing markers for
multi-program files" fix -- that commit only gated the DISPLAY symptom.
Digging further (prompted directly by a question about whether location
info had been lost entirely for real files, which overwhelmingly compile
to more than one program) found a deeper, real bug in the underlying log
itself, not just how it's shown.

**The bug**: `asnix_irpass_remove`'s shift-fixup loop ("keep every
already-logged firing location valid against the new, shorter array")
iterated the ENTIRE global `g_firings` list, unconditionally, on every
call -- but that list accumulates entries from EVERY program's own
`ib_finish()`-triggered `asnix_irpass_run` call, and different programs'
op arrays independently start their own indexing at 0. So a LATER
program's own removal could silently decrement an EARLIER, already-
finished program's already-correct `op_index` whenever the raw integers
happened to fall in its shift range -- not just a display artifact, a
real logged-location corruption that the previous fix's blanket
suppression merely hid from view rather than preventing.

**The fix**: `asnix_irpass_begin_program()` (new) is called by
`ib_finish()` immediately BEFORE its own `asnix_irpass_run` call, snapshotting
the firing-log length into `g_program_firing_base`. The shift-fixup loop
now only touches `g_firings[g_program_firing_base .. g_nfirings)` --
exactly this program's own slice, never an earlier program's. Once that
call returns and `prog` is allocated, `asnix_irpass_mark_program(prog)`
(new) records `{prog, g_program_firing_base, g_nfirings}` into a small
side table, and `asnix_irpass_firing_belongs_to_program(i, prog)` (new)
lets a caller with a specific `IrProgram*` in hand -- irdump, dumping one
program at a time -- filter the global log down to exactly that program's
own entries. Both new calls are unconditional in `ib_finish()` (cheap
bookkeeping either way) but true no-ops whenever zero passes are
registered, preserving the framework's "byte-for-byte identical by
default" guarantee for every real production run.

`irdump`'s per-op `<<< fired here` markers now filter through
`asnix_irpass_firing_belongs_to_program` instead of the blanket per-file
suppression -- correct for every program, not just files that happen to
compile to exactly one. Verified directly on the 5-program file that
exposed the original issue: the two real firings now show up on exactly
the two op lines that have them (programs #1 and #4), with zero markers
on the three programs that never fired, and the single-program regression
case (6 passes all firing on one flat program) still shows every marker
correctly. Verified the shift-fixup fix doesn't affect the REAL
interpreter (not just irdump) either: `ASNIX_IR_OPT=1 make
test-nix-conformance` across the full 806-file corpus with the whole
6-pass pipeline active gives the identical `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`
baseline, and `ASNIX_IR_OPT=1 ./asnix d.nix` on real nixpkgs's
`ffmpeg.outPath` still produces the byte-identical output hash.

## M123: two bounded speed fixes from a cross-evaluator speed investigation -- lexer token-vector presizing and readDir's d_type fast path

A dedicated investigation comparing asnix against a sibling evaluator,
`iets` (~/gnix/iets, Rust), on real wall-clock/cycle/instruction/page-
fault/syscall terms (not just the object-count comparisons M90-M122
focused on) found a fair, single-threaded (`iets --workers 1 --no-cache`)
gap of ~2.35x wall-clock, ~2.07x instructions, with IPC actually close
between the two (asnix ~1.76, iets ~1.91) -- meaning most of the gap
tracks raw instruction count, not per-instruction inefficiency. One sharp
outlier: page-faults were 6.71x higher in asnix (174,407 vs 25,998)
despite only 1.83x more peak RSS. Two bounded, independently-verified
fixes landed from that investigation; several bigger findings (documented
separately below) did not land here and need their own follow-on work.

**Lexer token-vector presizing** (`src/c/lexer.c`, `asnix_lex`): `push_
tok`'s capacity grew from scratch (0->64->128->...) on every one of the
1057 files a real nixpkgs eval imports -- measured directly (temporary
instrumentation): 24,405,685 source bytes -> 2,836,205 tokens, 3,688 total
reallocs across the whole corpus. Presizing `TokVec` from `strlen(src)/3
+ 32` (a generous margin over the measured ~8.6 bytes/token average)
drops reallocs to exactly 0. Measured (perf stat -r 5, two separate
sessions): wall time 1.893s->1.704s and 2.199s->1.920s, consistently
~10-13% faster. Page faults barely moved (174,407->173,303, -0.6%) --
this is NOT a page-fault fix, it's pure saved CPU from fewer realloc/
memcpy calls (glibc's free-list reuse mostly satisfies a growing buffer's
reallocs from already-first-touched heap space, not fresh pages) --
confirmed directly, disproving the "doubling-copy causes extra page
faults" theory the same investigation initially suspected.

**`readDir`'s `d_type` fast path** (`src/c/builtins_m23.c`, `prim_
readDir`): `strace -c` found asnix made 25,388 `newfstatat` calls vs
iets's 6,326 stat-family calls on the SAME real nixpkgs eval, while
`openat`/`close`/`getdents64` counts were nearly identical -- meaning the
actual file-touching work was the same, but asnix paid ~4x more stat
syscalls for it. Root cause, confirmed via a full path trace: 92% of
those calls were to `pkgs/by-name/*` -- nixpkgs's `by-name-overlay.nix`
does a two-level `builtins.readDir` over ~759 shard directories and
~20,000+ package directories, and `prim_readDir` called `lstat()`
unconditionally on every entry, ignoring the `d_type` field `getdents64`/
`readdir` already populates for free on ext4/btrfs/xfs/tmpfs/overlayfs.
Fix: trust `ent->d_type` (DT_DIR/DT_REG/DT_LNK map directly to the same
strings an lstat-based check would produce; DT_BLK/DT_CHR/DT_FIFO/DT_SOCK
map to "unknown", matching the old code's own S_ISDIR/S_ISREG/S_ISLNK-only
coverage), falling back to the original `lstat` path only when `d_type ==
DT_UNKNOWN` -- correct on every filesystem, faster on the common ones.
Measured: `newfstatat` calls 25,388 -> 12,965 (49% reduction), output hash
unchanged.

**Verified** (both fixes combined): `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance`
all green. `make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3
pre-existing pos-tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148
fail=0` (one transient `ruby.outPath(crash)` on a run taken under heavy
concurrent-agent machine load, reproduced clean standalone and on a full
rerun -- this session's familiar contention-flakiness pattern, not a real
regression). Output hash on `d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`. A clean
wall-clock before/after on THIS machine right now was inconclusive (3
other background workflows were actively running, consuming real CPU) --
trusting the originating investigation's own controlled, isolated
measurements above rather than re-litigating under worse conditions.

**Bigger findings from the same investigation, NOT landed here -- flagged
for follow-on work, not forgotten**:
- **Lex/parse/compile is estimated ~8x slower per byte than iets's own
  pipeline**, accounting for roughly HALF of the entire cycle gap --
  `asnix_eval_file`'s own subtree is 43.9% of all cycles (16.9% compile,
  10.6% lex, 9.9% parse). Root cause for the parser's own share:
  `parser.c`'s binary-operator precedence chain is 15 separate, mostly-
  non-inlined C functions deep for every leaf expression
  (`parse_expr->...->parse_atom`), vs iets's single `parse_op(min_bp)`
  precedence-climbing function (~4 calls/leaf). Rewriting this is
  correctness-sensitive (associativity, the `parse_not`/`->`-desugaring
  insertion points) and was deliberately NOT attempted as part of this
  milestone -- flagged as the single biggest remaining lever, needing its
  own dedicated milestone with full conformance-suite gating.
- **The 6.71x page-fault outlier remains largely unexplained** after
  ruling out the doubling-copy theory (disproven above) and porting iets's
  own `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` hint (measured zero effect on this host --
  `/proc/self/smaps_rollup`'s `AnonHugePages` stayed `0 kB` with or
  without the hint, in both the real binary and an isolated
  microbenchmark; transparent huge pages are evidently not being granted
  for anonymous mappings on this shared, contended machine). A SEPARATE,
  follow-up architectural investigation found iets ALSO calls
  `madvise(MADV_POPULATE_WRITE)` on its arena chunks (not just
  `MADV_HUGEPAGE`) -- a distinct mechanism that bulk-pre-faults a whole
  region in one syscall regardless of huge-page availability, which was
  NOT what got tested here. Worth a focused, narrow follow-up
  specifically on `MADV_POPULATE_WRITE` before concluding this lead is
  fully dead.
- **`asnix_attrs_eager_merge`'s own `//`-merge memcpy** was 17.11% of the
  page-fault profile -- identified, not root-caused or attempted.
- A real, independently-measured `masked_hash_cache_find` O(n)->hash-index
  fix in `derivation.c` (not from this investigation -- found sitting
  uncommitted in one of its worktrees, left untouched, flagged for its
  own author to land) and a real `asnix_copy_path_to_store` lstat-caching
  fix (found via a shared-stash collision mid-investigation, recovered
  and pushed back for its original author) are both real, complementary,
  already-measured fixes waiting to be landed by whoever owns them --
  combined with this milestone's `readDir` fix, `newfstatat` was observed
  to drop as low as 2,772 (9.2x off the original 25,388) when briefly
  combined in one worktree.
- An `-O2`->`-O3` build-wide flip measured a real but small ~4.9%
  instruction reduction (byte-identical output) with zero page-fault
  change (confirming faults track allocation pattern, not codegen) --
  not shipped as part of this milestone (a build-wide flag change
  deserves its own explicit decision, not bundling into a code fix).
  A matching LTO build hit a real structural blocker (GCC's LTO plugin
  vs. the hand-written `.S`-files-in-a-static-archive link step) requiring
  Makefile restructuring, out of scope here.
- Process-startup overhead, link-time settings (PIE/dynamic, stack
  protector), and the always-on `ASNIX_SHOW_STATS` counter-increment cost
  were all investigated and ruled out as contributing to the gap (asnix's
  own bare-startup latency is already 10-30x FASTER than iets's, if
  anything an argument in asnix's favor, not a lead).

## M124: cache-aware existence-check skip for repeated Path-literal coercion (`asnix_copy_path_to_store`)

A second fix from the same cross-evaluator speed investigation (M123),
found via a full syscall path trace: the SAME local path (e.g. nixpkgs's
`pkgs/stdenv/generic/source-stdenv.sh`/`default-builder.sh`, referenced as
a Path literal inside `make-derivation.nix`'s body) is coerced fresh on
every single `stdenv.mkDerivation` call reachable from a build -- measured
directly: 4,616/2,587/1,945 redundant `lstat`s for just those three files
building ffmpeg from real nixpkgs. `asnix_copy_path_to_store` (`nar.c`)
already memoizes the actual NAR-hash+copy work by literal path, but every
CALLER (`value_util.c`'s `asnix_coerce_to_string_for_derivation` and
`coerce_to_string_for_interp`) still paid its own unconditional existence-
check `lstat` first, before ever reaching that memoized function -- so the
cache hit happened too late to save the syscall.

**The fix**: a new read-only lookup, `asnix_copy_path_to_store_cache_
lookup` (`nar.c`/`nar.h`), exposes the SAME cache `asnix_copy_path_to_
store` already maintains, letting a caller skip its own redundant
existence-check `lstat` when the exact literal path was already
successfully copied earlier in this process -- existence can't change
mid-run for a path this project only ever reads, never writes. Both call
sites in `value_util.c` now check the cache first and only fall back to a
real `lstat` on a cache miss (preserving the original behavior exactly
for `check_path_exists=1, copy_to_store=0`, where there's no copy-cache
to consult in the first place).

**Measured**: combined with M123's own `readDir` `d_type` fix,
`newfstatat` drops to 2,772 -- a 9.2x reduction off the original 25,388,
closing nearly all of the stat-count gap against the comparison
evaluator's own 6,326.

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green. `make
test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3 pre-existing
pos-tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0` (one
transient `gnutar.outPath(crash)` on a run taken under heavy concurrent-
agent machine load -- reproduced clean standalone and on a full rerun,
this session's familiar contention-flakiness pattern). Output hash on
`d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged.

## M125: collapse the 9-level binary-operator precedence chain into one precedence-climbing loop

Directed follow-up to M123's speed investigation, which found `parser.c`'s
binary-operator chain was a 15-level non-Pratt recursive-descent cascade
(`parse_expr -> ... -> parse_atom`), with 9 of those levels being
nothing but a trivial "lhs = parse_NEXT(p); if/while (match(op)) {...}"
for a single precedence tier each (`parse_impl -> parse_or -> parse_and
-> parse_eq -> parse_cmp -> parse_update -> parse_not -> parse_add ->
parse_mul -> parse_concat`), paying all 9 call/ret pairs for every single
leaf expression regardless of whether it touches any of these operators
at all. A comparison evaluator (iets) does the equivalent work with one
`parse_op(min_bp)` precedence-climbing function (~4 calls/leaf).

**The fix**: those 9 levels collapsed into one table-driven climbing
loop, `parse_binop(Parser *p, int min_prec)`, plus a `BinOpInfo` table
(token, precedence, associativity, AST-node-shape) and a `parse_binop_
primary` helper that checks for the `!` prefix (whose own operand reaches
down through `+`/`-`/`*`//`++` at `PREC_ADD` and tighter, exactly
matching the original `parse_not`-calls-`parse_add` nesting) before
falling through to the unchanged `parse_has_attr` (and everything
tighter: unary `-`/negate, application, select, atom, which keep their
own real, non-table grammar as separate functions). `parse_impl` keeps
its name as the single external entry point (`parse_expr` is its only
caller), now just delegating to `parse_binop(p, 0)`.

**A real bug found and fixed during this rewrite**: the first draft
treated every `non_assoc` operator (`==`/`!=`, `<`/`>`/`<=`/`>=`) as
"break the whole loop after firing once," which incorrectly rejected
`1 == 2 && true` (should parse as `(1==2) && true` -- `&&` is a
perfectly valid, looser continuation) and `1 < 2 == 3` (should parse as
`(1<2) == 3` -- a DIFFERENT non-assoc operator at a different precedence
is not blocked by an earlier one). Caught immediately by the project's
own `tests/e2e/ops_precedence_add_eq_and.nix` fixture. Fixed by tracking
only the precedence VALUE of the last-fired non-assoc operator and
blocking only an exact repeat at that same precedence (`1==2==3`,
`1<2<3`, or mixing the 4 mutually-exclusive comparison operators with
each other, correctly still rejected) while leaving every other
precedence free to continue in the same loop -- verified by re-deriving
and manually tracing both the failing and the originally-intended cases
before re-testing, not just patching until the suite went green.

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green.
`make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` -- EXACT match to
the pre-existing baseline (same 3 pos-tracking failures), a strong signal
given this rewrite touches every single binary-operator expression in
the whole 806-file real-world corpus. `make test-nixpkgs-hash`:
`pass=148 fail=0`. Output hash on `d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged.

**Honest note on performance measurement**: this milestone landed under
unusually heavy concurrent load on this shared machine (two OTHER
background agents' own `asnix` processes pegged at 100-200% CPU during
measurement). Three separate `perf stat` comparison attempts gave
contradictory results (one showing ~18% fewer instructions, another
showing a few percent MORE) -- too noisy to certify a clean number right
now. The structural case for a real win stands regardless (the common
leaf-expression case genuinely drops from up to 9 nested call/ret pairs
to 1-2, a deterministic reduction independent of runtime values, and
matches the exact technique a faster comparison evaluator already uses)
-- but the actual measured wall-clock/instruction delta should be
re-taken on a quiet host before being cited as a specific number.

### irpass follow-up: `jmpthread` -- generalized jump-threading, by far the highest-firing pass in the pipeline

A new pass, `jmpthread` (`src/c/irpass_jmpthread.c`): when any jump-bearing
op (`OP_IF`/`OP_JMP`/`OP_WITH_TRY`/`OP_SELECT_OR`/`OP_SELECT_DYNAMIC_OR`)
targets an op that is ITSELF an unconditional `OP_JMP`, redirects the
first jump's own delta to point straight at the chain's final
destination, collapsing the jump-to-a-jump hop(s) entirely. This is
exactly the shape `jmpnop.c`'s own header comment anticipated ("a nested
`if` inside an outer `if`'s then-branch... could in principle after a
future pass shrinks the else-branch" create a jump whose target is
itself just a jump") -- `dce_if` collapsing a dead branch, or `jmpnop`/
`dce` removing ops, routinely leaves what used to be a two-step jump as a
jump directly to another jump.

Unlike every other pass in this framework, `jmpthread` never calls
`asnix_irpass_remove` at all -- it only rewrites an operand (the jump
delta) on the jump-bearing op itself, which needs no incoming-jump safety
guard (nothing else's index or target is affected, only where THIS one
jump lands when taken). It resolves a whole chain in one call (follows
target -> target's own target -> ... until a non-`OP_JMP` is reached)
rather than one hop per fixpoint iteration, with a defensive `*len+1`
hop-count cycle guard (this compiler's forward-jump-only invariant --
see `dce.c`'s own exhaustive argument -- means a real cycle can never
arise, but the guard costs nothing and avoids ever looping forever if
that invariant is somehow violated in the future).

**Measured on `d.nix`** (real nixpkgs's `ffmpeg.outPath`): `jmpthread:
405 firings` -- by far the highest-volume pass of the whole pipeline
(cfold: 12, cmpnot: 13, dce_if: 1), confirming the "chain-creation is
exactly what other passes expose" hypothesis this pass was built around.
Verified: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green;
`test-nix-conformance pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3 pre-existing
failures); `test-nixpkgs-hash pass=148 fail=0`; output hash unchanged
with `ASNIX_IR_OPT=1`.

### irpass follow-ups: `streq`, `notfold`, `deadframe` -- three more correctness-complete passes, zero yield on this workload

Three more passes from the same fleet that produced `jmpthread`, landed
together since none touch each other's code:

**`streq`** (`src/c/irpass_streq.c`): extends `cfold`'s `PUSH;PUSH;binop`
pattern to string equality -- folds `OP_PUSH_CONST idx1; OP_PUSH_CONST
idx2; OP_EQ`/`OP_NEQ` into `OP_PUSH_TRUE`/`OP_PUSH_FALSE` when both pool
entries are genuine Strings, reusing `strconcat.c`'s exact "genuine
string" tag check. Confirmed via `op_cmp.S`/`asnix_bshared_value_eq`:
string equality is a pure length-then-`memcmp`, no context lookup at all
(unlike `strconcat`'s union-of-contexts), so this fold needs no context
handling whatsoever.

**`notfold`** (`src/c/irpass_notfold.c`): folds `OP_PUSH_TRUE;OP_NOT` ->
`OP_PUSH_FALSE` and the mirror case. Explicitly NOT the same as a general
"NOT;NOT elision on an arbitrary value," which a prior session correctly
declined (`OP_NOT`'s own runtime type check on an unknown operand must
not be silently skipped) -- this is safe specifically because
`PUSH_TRUE`/`PUSH_FALSE` are always genuine booleans by construction, so
the two ops being folded ARE the entire "operand computation," with
nothing else's type check being bypassed. Confirmed via `ir.h`'s `OP_*`
enum: there is exactly one `NOT` op and no dedicated boolean and/or
opcodes (`&&`/`||` compile via branch-shaped `OP_IF`/`OP_JMP`), so there's
no other `NOT`-adjacent pattern in this IR to fold.

**`deadframe`** (`src/c/irpass_deadframe.c`): removes a dead `OP_FRAME_
ALLOC a=0 ... OP_FRAME_EXIT` bracket (keeping the body between them,
which still runs for its own effects) once nothing inside genuinely needs
the frame. NOT a re-do of M114 (which skips emitting the bracket entirely
at compile time for non-rec attrsets) -- the real source here is
`AST_LET`'s own unconditional `ib_frame_alloc(b, n)`, including `n==0`
for a bindings-free `let in body`. The one real subtlety, found and
handled correctly: removing the bracket changes how many real `ENV->up`
hops any `OP_VAR_REF`-family op INSIDE it that reaches PAST it to an
enclosing frame has to walk (confirmed concretely: `let a = 1; in (let in
a)` compiles to an inner zero-slot frame whose own body is a `VAR_REF
depth=1`, reaching the outer frame) -- a `local_nest`-tracking scan
classifies each crossing reference and decrements its depth by one to
compensate, rather than naively assuming "zero slots means nothing to
check."

**Verified** (all three, combined with `jmpthread` and M125's parser
rewrite): `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green;
`test-nix-conformance pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3 pre-existing
failures); `test-nixpkgs-hash pass=148 fail=0`; output hash unchanged.
**Honest firing counts on `d.nix`**: all three fired **0 times** on this
real workload -- real nixpkgs source has no adjacent-constant string
`==`/`!=`, no literal `!true`/`!false`, and (per `AST_LET`'s own
compile-time behavior) presumably no bindings-free `let in body` shape
that survives to this bytecode-level check. Each is still landed as a
correctness-complete, zero-added-risk safety net, matching `dce.c`'s own
precedent (also 0 firings on this benchmark, kept anyway) -- each reuses
100% established safety patterns from the existing 6 passes and adds no
new value-kind, op, or runtime machinery.

## M126: `./asnix --flake DIR[#attr.path]` -- the smallest real slice of flake support, after reading how iets does the whole thing

**The ask**: real Nix flake support in full -- `flake.nix`/`flake.lock`
parsing, the `inputs`/`outputs` schema, input resolution and *locking*,
fetching inputs from git/github/gitlab/tarball/path/registries, and
evaluating `outputs` with the resolved inputs as its argument. Explicitly
scoped as "research first, implement only the smallest safe slice" --
this is one of the largest asks this project has taken on; the honest
finding is that full parity is a multi-milestone effort on its own (see
the scope cuts below), but a genuinely useful, genuinely verified slice
turned out to fit in one pass.

**Research: how iets (`~/gnix/iets`) does it.** Read
`~/gnix/iets/src/flake/{mod.rs,flakeref.rs,call-flake.nix}` (774+702+105
lines) and `~/gnix/iets/src/{source/lock.rs,builtins/fetch.rs}`
(311+783 lines) in full before writing anything. Headline finding: iets's
own flake support, despite shipping a working `FLAKEREF#attr` CLI (the
thing this session's own earlier research had confirmed via `--help`),
is ALSO a deliberately narrow slice, not full parity -- its own doc
comments say so directly:
- The *root* flake reference (what's on the command line / passed to
  `builtins.getFlake`) is **only ever a local path** (`path:`, a bare
  directory, or a git working tree pinned to an exact 40-hex-digit
  `rev`, read straight out of the repository beside it) --
  `parse_flake_ref`'s own comment: *"only a local path is taken"*, and
  every `github:`/`git+https:`/registry-indirect root ref is explicitly
  `Error::Unsupported` ("iets cannot fetch a root flake").
- `flake.lock` must be **complete already** (`source/lock.rs`'s
  `lockfile.cc`-derived `check()`: every node the root reaches must
  already carry a `narHash`/be a resolved relative `path:`) or **entirely
  absent for a flake with no declared inputs** -- iets never writes a
  lock file, never resolves an unlocked input, never consults a flake
  registry at all.
- Once locked, `builtins.fetchTree` (`builtins/fetch.rs`) DOES do real
  network fetching for `github`/`gitlab`/`git`/`tarball`/`sourcehut`/`hg`
  node types (reusing its own `fetch/http.rs`+`source::scm` machinery) --
  so a flake with a *fully-locked* `flake.lock` naming real remote inputs
  genuinely works end to end. The actual evaluation glue is cppnix's own
  `call-flake.nix`, embedded **byte-for-byte verbatim**
  (`include_str!("call-flake.nix")`) rather than reimplemented -- the
  recursive `self`/`result` fixed point, `follows` resolution, and
  per-node `fetchTree` dispatch are all real Nix's own `.nix` source,
  unchanged; iets only supplies the native `fetchTree` primop it calls
  into and the root tree's `sourceInfo`.
- `builtins.parseFlakeRef`/`flakeRefToString` are pure string<->attrset
  syntax with zero resolution -- asnix already has these (M66, below).

**What asnix already had (checked before writing anything new)**:
`builtins.fetchGit` (M82, real, shells out to `git`), `builtins.
parseFlakeRef`/`flakeRefToString` (M66, pure syntax, no resolution), the
M75/M80 NAR-hash + content-addressed-store-copy machinery
(`nar.c`'s `asnix_hash_path_nar_sha256`/`asnix_copy_path_to_store_ext`,
already used by `fetchGit`, `builtins.path`, and fixed-output
derivations) -- and, per `eval_file.c`/`builtins.h`/`builtins_toml.c`'s
own standing comments, confirmed **zero** flake.nix/flake.lock handling,
**zero** `fetchTarball`/`fetchTree`/`fetchMercurial`/`getFlake`, and no
CLI flake-ref support at all.

**The slice actually landed, matching iets's own narrowing one level
further**: `./asnix --flake DIR[#attr.path]` for a flake that declares
**no inputs at all** (or whose `flake.nix` has no non-empty `inputs`
attribute) -- no `flake.lock` is read, consulted, or required; no
network fetch of any kind. This is strictly narrower than even iets's
own "root ref must be a local path" cut (iets still locks/fetches
*declared* inputs via a real `flake.lock`; this milestone has no lock-file
handling whatsoever) -- deliberately, since a *correct* lock-file-driven
input resolution (`follows`, per-node `fetchTree` dispatch, "every
reachable node needs a `narHash`") is exactly the ~1,400-line surface
iets itself needed and is a legitimately separate, larger milestone, not
a one-pass add-on to this one.

**The fix.** New module `src/c/flake_eval.c`/`.h`
(`asnix_eval_flake_outputs`), wired into `main.c`'s existing CLI parser
(`--flake`, alongside `--arg`/`--argstr`/`-A`) and reusing `main.c`'s own
`select_attrpath` (the exact same function `-A` already uses) to apply
the `#attr.path` fragment -- selecting a flake output attribute is
byte-for-byte the same operation as `-A` on any other evaluated file, so
no new selection logic was needed at all. Internals, deliberately
following the SAME "embed a `.nix` snippet rather than hand-roll its
recursive-attrset logic in C" trick M46 already used for
`<nix/fetchurl.nix>` (and that iets itself uses for the real
`call-flake.nix`): a small embedded Nix expression (`CALL_FLAKE_MIN`,
`sourceInfo: outputsFn: let outputs = outputsFn { self = result; };
result = outputs // sourceInfo // { outPath = sourceInfo.outPath; inputs
= {}; inherit outputs sourceInfo; _type = "flake"; }; in result`) is run
through `asnix_eval_expr_source` and applied (two single-arg
`asnix_apply` calls, same curry convention as every other multi-arg call
in this codebase) to a C-built `sourceInfo` attrset and the flake's own
`outputs` value. The `self`<->`result` mutual recursion is ordinary Nix
`let`-recursion (exactly how `rec {}` already works) -- nothing new on
the evaluator side. `sourceInfo` (`outPath`/`narHash`) is built by
NAR-hashing and store-copying `DIR` under the name `"source"`, the exact
same two `nar.c` calls `fetchGit` (M82) already makes, confirmed to be
the right name/shape by checking `builtins.fetchTree { type = "path";
path = ...; }` directly against `nix-instantiate --eval --extra-
experimental-features 'flakes fetch-tree'` (which returns exactly
`outPath`+`narHash` for a plain path input, no `lastModified` at all --
unlike a git-tracked tree).

**Verification methodology.** Since `nix eval`/`nix flake`-family
commands were blocked by this worktree's own sandboxing (any command
whose name is literally `eval` is refused as a potential worktree
escape, regardless of it being `nix eval`, not a shell builtin), ground
truth was established with `nix-instantiate --eval --strict
--extra-experimental-features 'flakes fetch-tree'` instead, by hand-
writing a driver expression that reproduces cppnix's own `call-flake.nix`
logic field-for-field (`sourceInfo = builtins.fetchTree { type = "path";
path = ...; }; outputs = flake.outputs (inputs // { self = result; });
result = outputs // sourceInfo // { ...; _type = "flake"; };`) and
comparing `builtins.attrNames`/individual-field reads against this
project's `--flake` output for the same directory. Confirmed
byte-for-byte identical for all of: the full output attrset's key list
(`_type inputs narHash outPath outputs packages selfKeys selfOutPath
selfType sourceInfo`), `self.outPath`/`self.narHash` (the real NAR hash +
derived content-addressed store path), a plain string output
(`packages.x86_64-linux.hello`), and `self._type`. Also directly
exercised the three documented fatal paths: a non-directory/missing
`DIR`, a directory with no `flake.nix`, and a flake declaring a
non-empty `inputs` attribute (clear, specific error messages, exit 1
each time, no crash).

**New fixtures + Makefile target**: `tests/flake/minimal/flake.nix`
(no declared inputs; exercises `self.outPath`, a plain string output
under `packages.<system>.<name>`, `self._type`, and `builtins.attrNames
self`) plus four `tests/flake/minimal.<case>.{attr,expected}` sidecar
pairs and a new `make test-flake` target (same stdout-diff mechanics as
`test-e2e`/`test-conformance`, just invoking `./asnix --flake
DIR#attr` instead of `./asnix FILE`). The sidecars deliberately live
NEXT TO the flake directory, not inside it -- `self.outPath`'s NAR hash
covers every file the directory contains, so a sidecar living inside the
very directory being hashed would make its own existence change the
value it's testing (caught live: the first version of this fixture put
the `.attr`/`.expected` files inside `tests/flake/minimal/` itself, and
`make test-flake` immediately failed on `selfOutPath` because the
hashed tree now also contained the sidecar files).

**Deliberate, documented scope cuts -- a genuinely separate, larger
milestone, not attempted here**:
- **No `flake.lock` handling of any kind** -- not read, not required,
  not validated. A flake declaring ANY non-empty `inputs` is a hard,
  loud, specific error (`"flake '...' declares input 'X' (and N more);
  flake inputs are not supported yet"`), never a silent wrong-result
  approximation.
- **No input fetching whatsoever** -- no git/github/gitlab/tarball/
  registry/path-input resolution, no `builtins.fetchTree` entry point at
  all (unlike iets, which has one once a lock file resolves a node).
  This is the actual bulk of what full flake support needs (iets's own
  `fetch/`+`source/lock.rs`+`flake/`+`builtins/fetch.rs` alone is
  ~3,400 lines) and is exactly the "needs its own larger multi-milestone
  effort" case flagged up front, not a surprise found mid-implementation.
- **No `follows`, no flake registries, no `nixConfig`, no `builtins.
  getFlake`** -- none of these are reachable at all without input
  fetching existing first.
- **No `.git`/working-tree-aware source for the root flake** -- `DIR` is
  always treated as a plain, ungitted directory (every file in it is
  NAR-hashed, no `.gitignore`/`export-ignore` filtering, no `rev`/
  `lastModified` in the result) -- matching iets's own `path:`-only root
  behavior (though iets ALSO supports a pinned git working tree for the
  root; this milestone doesn't).
- `--flake` is not validated against `--arg`/`--argstr` (real Nix's own
  flake CLI doesn't accept these either); combining them is simply
  harmless here (`auto_call` no-ops on a non-Closure result) rather than
  a hard usage error -- a cheap, deliberate non-issue, not an oversight.

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance`/`test-flake` all
green (new target, 4/4 fixture checks). `make test-nix-conformance`:
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3 pre-existing pos-tracking failures,
confirmed unrelated -- this change touches no existing code path, only
adds a new CLI flag and a new, separately-linked translation unit). `make
test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`.

### M125 follow-up: `-!x`/`-!-x` was a hard parse error, but real Nix accepts it

Found by an independent re-implementation of M125's own precedence-
climbing rewrite (comparing against the landed version): `parse_negate`'s
own recursive operand-parsing (for `-`'s operand, allowing `--x`) only
ever checked for another `-`, never a `!` -- so `-!x` fell through
straight to `parse_app`, which has no `TOK_BANG` case, giving a hard
parse error. Real Nix accepts the syntax (`nix-instantiate --eval
'(-!true)'` evaluates `-!true` as `-(!true)`, failing only at RUNTIME on
`sub`'s own operand-type check, never at parse time) -- confirmed this
asymmetry is real and one-directional: `!-1` already worked correctly
(the top-level `!`-check's own operand recurses through the FULL primary
chain, including `parse_negate`'s own `-`-check), but `-`'s own operand
position never got the matching `!`-check.

**The fix**: `parse_negate` now also checks for a leading `!` in its own
fallthrough (after the `-`-check), mirroring the top-level `!`-handling
in `parse_binop`'s own entry point exactly (same `PREC_ADD` operand
precedence, same `AST_NOT` node shape) -- unreachable when `parse_negate`
is entered directly with a leading `!` already present (the top-level
check would have intercepted that earlier), only live for the specific
"`!` appears as `-`'s own operand" position this asymmetry missed.

**Verified**: `-!x`/`-!-x` now parse and fail at eval time with the
correct error class, matching real Nix; `-a ? "x"` (the precedence
interaction this fix had to NOT break -- `-`'s operand must not swallow
a trailing `?`) still parses as `(-a) ? "x"`, confirmed directly.
`make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance`/`test-flake` all green;
`test-nix-conformance pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3 pre-existing
failures); `test-nixpkgs-hash pass=148 fail=0`. Output hash unchanged.

## M127: register-based-VM investigation -- measured and declined, with the deep architectural answer the user asked for

Follow-up to M123's cross-evaluator speed investigation: asnix is ~2.35x
slower than a sibling evaluator (`iets`) in a fair single-threaded
comparison, with IPC already close between the two (asnix ~1.76, iets
~1.91) -- meaning the gap tracks the ~2.07x instruction-count difference,
not per-instruction inefficiency. The architectural-research thread
(M123's own follow-ups) identified the leading hypothesis for WHERE that
extra instruction volume goes: every asnix op handler (`src/asm/ops/
*.S`) pops operands from and pushes results to a memory-resident
VALSTACK array via `%r12` -- a real memory store+load round trip for
every intermediate value, system-wide -- while `iets`'s recursive
tree-walker keeps intermediates in Rust locals LLVM allocates to real
registers across the call chain, with no equivalent structure.

This milestone is a deliberate, explicitly-scoped two-step investigation
into whether that hypothesis is actually the dominant cause, and if so,
how to close it -- NOT a code change to the production evaluator (no
op handler, compiler codegen, or dispatch-loop file is touched by this
milestone; the artifact is a standalone, unlinked microbenchmark at
`bench/regvm_poc/`, kept for reference, not wired into the build).

### Step 1: stack-top register caching -- no clean fit, found without writing code

The smallest escalation (cache just the top 1-2 VALSTACK slots in spare
registers instead of a full redesign) was checked against this
project's own ABI first. Per `docs/abi.md`'s register table, cross-
checked directly against real usage in all 32 `src/asm/ops/*.S` files:
EVERY callee-saved register (`%rbx`/`%rbp`/`%r15`) is already in active
use by the hottest handlers themselves -- `op_call.S` (every function
application), `op_let.S` (every `let`-binding), `op_frame.S` (every
`rec {}` literal) -- to hold their OWN internal bookkeeping (saved IP,
saved ENV, slot counts) across their own nested calls into `asnix_arena_
alloc`/`asnix_env_arena_alloc`. The ~10 general-purpose registers are
used even more pervasively as primary working registers inside nearly
every handler (`op_var_ref.S` especially -- almost certainly the single
hottest op in the whole evaluator). There is no register sitting idle to
dedicate to an additive cache without first rewriting the handlers that
would matter most -- a real, file-level-verifiable blocker, not an
estimate. No prototype was built; this is a legitimate "don't force it"
outcome, matching this session's own standing bar for declined ideas.

### Step 2: isolated register-based-VM microbenchmark -- real but small win, discounted twice over

Despite step 1's blocker, a genuine proof-of-concept was built anyway
(explicitly requested) to get a REAL measured number rather than stop at
"no clean fit." `bench/regvm_poc/chains.S`/`harness.c` implement the
exact representative chain `(a+b)*(c-d) < (e+f)*(g-h)` (8 `OP_VAR_REF` +
6 arithmetic ops + 1 `OP_LT` -- deliberately chosen to have ZERO
`OP_CALL`/`OP_LET`/`OP_FRAME_*` anywhere in it, i.e. exactly the slice
where step 1's blocker does not apply) two ways: `run_valstack_chain`
(every intermediate through real memory via `%r12`, byte-for-byte
matching `op_arith.S`/`op_cmp.S`/`op_var_ref.S`'s own fast-path
instruction sequences) and `run_regvm_chain` (the same values held in a
fixed set of real registers, `%r8`-`%r11`, for the whole chain via
per-position specialized handler code -- the POC's own README is explicit
that this measures an OPTIMISTIC CEILING, since x86 can't address a
register by a runtime index, so a genuinely *generic* register-VM
dispatch loop would need its own memory-indexed register file anyway,
which is a different addressing scheme for the same memory traffic, not
a way around it).

**Measured** (`perf stat -r 7`, pinned to a confirmed P-core, 200M
iterations/run, cross-run spread <0.2% on cycles):

| metric | VALSTACK | register | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| instructions/iter | 362.1 | 298.1 | **-17.7%** |
| cycles/iter | 55.39 | 51.77 | **-6.5%** |
| wall-clock/iter | ~14.95 ns | ~13.38 ns | **-10.5%** |
| IPC | 6.54 | 5.76 | (VALSTACK is HIGHER) |

Per-iteration instruction counts were independently hand-traced from
both handler chains and matched `perf`'s measured totals to 2 decimal
places -- a strong cross-check that the measurement itself isn't
confused. **The headline finding**: eliminating 100% of this chain's
VALSTACK memory traffic cuts instructions 17.7% but cycles only 6.5% --
a real, repeatable win, not a wash, but far smaller than the raw
instruction delta suggests. VALSTACK's own IPC is actually HIGHER than
the register version's (6.54 vs 5.76): the extra memory ops are nearly
free on this core, because store-to-load forwarding on a tight,
predictable stack access pattern hides most (not all) of the round-trip
latency, with enough out-of-order window to overlap the rest.

**How much of the real ~2.07x gap could this close, even in the best
case?** Measured (not guessed) via `irdump` over all 532 real
`eval-okay-*.nix` fixtures in the nix-conformance corpus (18,064 total op
records): strictly chain-safe ops (`PUSH_*`/arithmetic/comparison) are
only 19.9% of real dispatches; even the generous upper bound (counting
every ambiguous `VAR_REF` as chain-safe, which overstates it) caps the
share at 32.0% -- the other 68%+ are `CALL`/`MK_THUNK`/`SELECT`/
`FRAME_*`/`LAMBDA`/`WITH*`/etc., structurally excluded by step 1's own
blocker. Combining both real measurements: `0.32 x 6.5% ~= 2.1%` plausible
overall cycle reduction, best case -- against a gap that needs roughly
50%+ cycle reduction to close (IPC is already close between asnix and
iets, so there's no slack hiding elsewhere). On the order of 3-4% of the
real gap, even taking the POC's numbers as a fully-realized, zero-
overhead ceiling.

### Conclusion -- the deep architectural answer

**VALSTACK memory traffic was never the dominant real bottleneck it
looked like on paper.** Two independent, compounding, directly-measured
reasons: (1) a modern out-of-order core already hides most of a
predictable stack's store/load round trips (verified: only 6.5% cycle
reduction from removing 100% of the traffic, against a 17.7%
instruction-count reduction), and (2) only a minority (~20-32%, measured
via a real IR-dump histogram, not estimated) of real op dispatches are
even candidates for this treatment in the first place, since every
`OP_CALL`/`OP_LET`/`OP_FRAME_*`/thunk-force site is structurally excluded
by step 1's own register-pressure finding, independent of this POC's
result.

**Register-based VM and full-JIT (the original steps 2/3 of the
escalation) are NOT the lever for closing the asnix-vs-iets gap, on real
measured evidence, not intuition.** The actual biggest identified lever
remains M123's own finding: lex/parse/compile is estimated ~8x slower per
byte than `iets`'s own pipeline and accounts for roughly HALF of the
entire cycle gap on its own (`asnix_eval_file`'s own subtree is 43.9% of
all cycles) -- an order of magnitude bigger than anything available from
the dispatch loop's own memory-traffic pattern, and the correct target
for continued investigation.

Files: `bench/regvm_poc/chains.S`, `bench/regvm_poc/harness.c`,
`bench/regvm_poc/README.md` (full methodology, build/measure commands,
and the reasoning above in more detail) -- kept for reference, not
linked into `make`/`make test`/the production binary.

## M129: table-driven character classification in `asnix_lex` -- replacing isalnum()-chain predicates with one 256-entry lookup

Directed follow-up to M123's speed investigation, assigned specifically to
`asnix_lex` (`src/c/lexer.c`), confirmed as the single hottest function in
the whole binary (6.61% self-time on a real nixpkgs eval). Profiled
directly rather than guessing from source alone: a standalone lex-only
microbenchmark (a small harness linking `lexer.o`, looping `asnix_lex`
over `pkgs/top-level/all-packages.nix`, a real 326KB nixpkgs file, 300+
times) under `perf record -F 999 -g` + `perf annotate asnix_lex` found
`path_char` -- inlined into `try_scan_path`'s per-character scan loop,
which (per the file's own comment) runs on the leading character of
EVERY identifier/number/operator token, not just real path literals, to
rule paths out first -- was ~15-20% of `asnix_lex`'s own self time on its
own, and `try_scan_uri`/`uri_scheme_char` another ~9-10%. Neither
predicate's cost came from the `isalnum()` call itself being slow (the
disassembly confirms gcc hoists glibc's one `__ctype_b_loc()` call out of
the loop, since it's declared `__attribute__((const))` -- no repeated
TLS/function-call overhead per character); the cost is every character of
every token paying a 16-bit ctype-table load plus a bit test for
`isalnum()`, then up to four MORE byte-compares for the `.`/`_`/`-`/`+`-
style extras every one of `path_char`/`ident_cont`/`uri_scheme_char`/
`uri_tail_char` chains on top.

**Checked against iets** (`~/gnix/iets/src/syntax/lexer.rs`): its own
`is_path_char`/`is_uri_scheme_char`/`is_id_char` are the same kind of
short boolean-OR chains asnix already had -- iets does NOT win via a
classification table, it wins via NOT calling its expensive path/URI
scanners unconditionally on every token the way asnix's main loop did
(iets's `next_token` only re-scans for a path/URI after an identifier
once a cheap single-byte peek at the character immediately following the
identifier's own run suggests one might be there -- see `next_token`'s
`b'a'..=b'z' | ...` arm). That guard-based restructuring is a real,
larger lever (effectively doubling the scan of most identifier/number
tokens today, since `try_scan_path`'s own prefix scan and the later
`ident_cont`/digit scan largely re-walk the same bytes) but changes
*which* bytes get scanned under what conditions, with a genuine edge case
to get right (`uri_scheme_char` and `ident_cont` are not the same
character set -- a URI scheme containing `.`/`+`, e.g. a token shaped
like `a.b:foo`, needs the *URI* scan's own character set checked, not an
identifier-run endpoint, to stay correct) -- flagged below as a follow-on,
NOT attempted this milestone, in line with this project's bar for what
ships now vs. what's written up as a plan.

**What shipped instead**: a single `static const unsigned char
CHAR_CLASS[256]` table plus seven `CC_*` bit flags (`CC_SPACE`,
`CC_DIGIT`, `CC_ALPHA`, `CC_IDENT_CONT`, `CC_PATH_CHAR`, `CC_URI_SCHEME`,
`CC_URI_TAIL`), built with plain C11 designated initializers (GNU range
designators for the `0-9`/`A-Z`/`a-z` runs, explicit entries for every
other classified byte). `path_char`/`ident_cont`/`uri_scheme_char`/
`uri_tail_char`/`ident_start` (plus three new small helpers, `cc_digit`/
`cc_space`/`cc_alpha`, replacing the file's remaining bare `isdigit()`/
`isspace()`/`isalpha()` call sites) all became one table load + one `AND`
+ one compare, with the exact same character sets as before -- a pure
speed change, not a grammar change. `<ctype.h>` is no longer included at
all. Every `CC_*` bit was checked for an exact match against the original
`isalnum()`-based bodies across all 256 byte values before this table
replaced them (a throwaway standalone C harness, not shipped -- this file
has no dedicated unit-test binary to extend, and bare `isalnum()` under
the "C" locale is a fixed ASCII fact this project can rely on since it
never calls `setlocale()`).

**Measured** (`perf stat -r 7`, `taskset -c 0` pinned to one performance
core to avoid this host's hybrid P/E-core scheduling noise, two binaries
built from the otherwise-identical tree with only `lexer.c` swapped,
never relying on git-stash for the swap after this same session hit a
live shared-`refs/stash` collision -- see below):
- **Lex-only microbenchmark** (`all-packages.nix` x 300 iterations):
  instructions 5,068,325,003 -> 4,464,488,191 (-11.9%), cycles
  2,114,024,044 -> 1,587,067,876 (-24.9%), task-clock 534.06ms ->
  390.83ms (-26.8%). The cycles/wall win exceeding the instruction-count
  win suggests the table lookup also removes some branch-misprediction or
  dependent-load latency the `isalnum()`-chain paid on top of raw
  instruction count, not just fewer instructions.
- **Full real eval** (`d.nix`, ffmpeg's closure, bytecode cache OFF by
  default so every one of the 1057 imported files genuinely re-lexes):
  instructions 10,225,659,332 -> 10,068,970,206 (-1.5%), cycles
  5,908,661,924 -> 5,802,411,973 (-1.8%), task-clock 1648.35ms ->
  1610.18ms (-2.3%). Consistent with M123's own breakdown (lex is 10.6%
  of total cycles in a real eval): a ~25% cycle cut confined to just that
  slice predicts roughly a 2.6% whole-program cycle cut, matching the
  observed ~1.8% within the expected noise band for a different host/run.

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green.
`make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3
pre-existing pos-tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148
fail=0`. Output hash on `d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.

**A live `refs/stash` collision, hit and recovered mid-milestone**: this
session's shared-stash hazard (documented by several other agents'
"RECOVERED" stash messages this session) was hit directly while trying to
`git stash`/`git stash pop` this very change to get a clean before/after
binary pair -- a concurrent agent's own M128 allocation-instrumentation
WIP (`irbuild.c`/`parser.c`) landed in this worktree's working tree via
the race instead of this milestone's own stashed `lexer.c` change.
Recovered by: pushing the foreign `irbuild.c`/`parser.c` changes back
onto the shared stash with a descriptive message (not dropping or
committing them), then locating this milestone's own entry by content
(`git stash show -p stash@{N} -- src/c/lexer.c`, checked across every
entry in `git stash list` until the one touching only `lexer.c` with the
expected diff turned up) and recovering it with the non-destructive `git
stash apply` (never `pop`/`drop`, to avoid any further irreversible
action on a stack several other concurrent agents were actively reading
and writing). The before/after binaries above were built by manually
swapping `lexer.c`'s contents between the original (`git show
HEAD:src/c/lexer.c`) and the edited version saved to a scratch file
first, specifically to avoid touching the shared stash a second time.

**Follow-on, NOT attempted here -- flagged for its own dedicated
milestone**: the iets-style guard (skip `try_scan_path`/`try_scan_uri`
entirely unless a cheap peek suggests a path/URI might follow an
identifier's own scan, rather than always attempting both scans first)
is a real, likely-larger win on top of this one -- plausibly removing
most of the remaining double-scan of every plain identifier/number token
-- but needs the `uri_scheme_char`-vs-`ident_cont` character-set mismatch
(schemes containing `.`/`+`) handled correctly, which this milestone
deliberately left alone rather than rushing. Also not investigated here
(out of this phase's assigned scope): `asnix_intern` (symtab.c, 3.14%
self-time) and the scattered growable-buffer `_int_malloc` sites M123's
own writeup flagged (IrBuilder's ops/pool arrays, parser.c's PartVec-style
vectors, the AST arena) -- left for whichever milestone picks those up
next (M128, per the in-flight work recovered above, appears to already be
claimed for at least the irbuild.c/parser.c allocation sites).

## M130: `symtab.c`'s `hash_bytes` goes word-at-a-time -- a real but small win, honestly sized

Follow-up to M123's cross-evaluator speed investigation, this time
targeting `asnix_intern` (`src/c/symtab.c`), the symbol table used for
every identifier/attribute name the lexer sees and throughout
parsing/compiling -- 3.14% self-time in M123's profile.

**What's already right, read directly, not guessed**: the table is a
single, unsynchronized, open-addressed hash table with linear probing
(no chaining indirection), rehashing at a 75% load factor with stable
ids across rehashes (`tests/c/test_symtab.c` already covers this). A
temporary counter instrumentation run (`atexit`-gated, `ASNIX_SYMTAB_
STATS`, removed before landing) over the real `d.nix` (nixpkgs/ffmpeg)
benchmark measured 1,833,170 total `asnix_intern` calls, 95.8% hits
(1,755,938) against 77,232 unique symbols, only 14 rehashes total, and
an average of just 0.609 EXTRA linear-probe steps per call at the
table's steady-state ~59% load factor -- collision resolution is cheap
and the table is not the bottleneck. `asnix_intern`'s own lookup already
short-circuits on length before `memcmp` (`g_symbols[id].len == len &&
memcmp(...)`) -- nothing wasteful there either.

**What was real**: `hash_bytes`'s mixing loop processed one byte, one
multiply, per iteration (`h ^= byte; h *= C;`, repeated `len` times).
Every iteration depends on the previous one's result (`h` is a genuine
loop-carried dependency, not independent lanes an out-of-order core can
overlap), so for an identifier of the corpus's own measured average
length (9.12 bytes/call, measured via the same instrumentation summing
`len` across all 1,833,170 calls) the CPU pays 9 fully serialized
multiply-latency steps just to hash one short name. `~/gnix/iets`'s own
`FxHasher::write` (`src/syntax/symbol.rs`) avoids exactly this: it reads
a whole 8-byte word (then a 4-byte remainder, then individual bytes only
for what's left) per multiply, cutting the serial chain length to at
most 2-3 steps for the same input instead of 9.

**Fix**: `hash_bytes` now mixes in 8-byte words via `memcpy` (avoiding
unaligned-access UB, matching `iets`'s own structure) for `len/8`
iterations, one 4-byte word for the next chunk if one remains, and falls
back to the original byte-at-a-time loop only for the final <4-byte tail
-- reads stay bounded to `s[0..len)` exactly as before, so this is safe
for any caller's buffer regardless of alignment. The splitmix64 finalizer
is untouched. Because `hash_bytes` is `static` and only ever feeds the
in-process table (the bytecode cache, M94, persists symbols by NAME and
re-interns on load, never by hash value), changing the hash's output is
invisible outside this file.

**Measured, three ways, all agreeing**:
1. Isolated microbenchmark (`/tmp/bench_hash.c`, not committed --
   one-off, like M127's own throwaway harnesses -- fed the REAL captured
   corpus of all 1,833,170 `asnix_intern` call arguments from a full
   `d.nix` run, 20 reps, `perf stat -r 5`): `cpu_core/instructions/`
   3,865,388,978 -> 2,593,277,657 (**-32.9%**), `cpu_core/cycles/`
   1,412,384,011 -> 1,187,892,691 (**-15.9%**) for the hash function
   alone -- a real, chain-length-bound win, matching the serial-multiply
   theory's prediction almost exactly (expected ~105 -> ~71
   instructions/call matches the measured 105.4 -> 70.7).
2. Scaling that per-call instruction delta (~34.7 instructions/call) by
   the real run's 1,833,170 calls predicts an ~63.6M-instruction drop in
   the full binary.
3. Full-binary `perf stat -r 10 -e cpu_core/instructions/,cpu_core/
   cycles/ ./asnix d.nix`: `cpu_core/instructions/` 10,317,816,273 ->
   10,231,720,417 (**-0.83%**, low noise: +-0.43%/+-0.16%), matching
   prediction #2's order of magnitude closely (86.1M observed vs 63.6M
   predicted -- same ballpark, the gap plausibly from secondary effects
   like code layout/icache, not a different mechanism). `cpu_core/
   cycles/` 5,863,844,884 -> 5,806,951,845 (**-0.97%**, within/at the
   edge of run-to-run noise: +-0.85%/+-0.28%). Wall-clock did not move
   outside noise (1.594s -> 1.587s, both +-~2%).

**Honest sizing**: this is a real, cleanly-explained, zero-risk
micro-optimization of one hot function -- NOT a fix that meaningfully
closes the asnix-vs-iets gap. `asnix_intern`'s total instruction volume
turns out to be a much smaller slice of the real run (~1.8% of all
instructions, back-computed from the measured per-call cost) than its
3.14%-of-cycles profile share suggested, because hashing's latency chain
is largely hidden by the surrounding dispatch loop's own independent
work in the full program, the same "removing instructions doesn't
proportionally remove cycles" pattern M127 already found for VALSTACK
traffic. Landed anyway because the fix is trivial, fully contained to
one static function, adds no new data structure or interface, and the
~0.8% instruction reduction is real and reproducible, not because it
