closes any meaningful fraction of the ~2.07x gap.

**Considered and declined**: a per-call direct-mapped lookup cache in
front of the table, mirroring `iets`'s own `Interner::cache` (a 1024-
entry array trading a hash+compare for a lock/shard lookup). Declined
because `iets`'s cache exists to skip a sharded, `RwLock`-guarded
`HashMap` lookup in a *multi-threaded* interner -- asnix's table has
neither locks nor chaining indirection to skip, and the measured 0.609-
extra-probe-steps/call figure above shows the open-addressed probe itself
is already cheap; a front-cache would add real complexity (another data
structure, another invalidation-free-but-still-reasoned-about path) for
an upper bound of saving well under 1 extra probe step and one `memcmp`
per call -- smaller than this milestone's own hash fix, for more
complexity, not clearing the bar.

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green.
`make test-nix-conformance` (`NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`):
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3 pre-existing pos-tracking failures).
`make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. Output hash on `d.nix`
(ffmpeg's closure) unchanged: `/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.

Files: `src/c/symtab.c` (`hash_bytes` only; `asnix_intern`/`asnix_sym_
name`/the table/rehashing logic untouched).

## M131: clean M125 re-measurement, plus two AST/parser allocation fixes found profiling the compile-only phase in isolation

Continuing M123/M125/M127's cross-evaluator speed investigation, scoped
to the parser (`src/c/parser.c`) and its own AST allocator (`src/c/
ast.c`). Two parts: (1) the clean before/after measurement for M125
itself that its own writeup flagged as never having been taken on a
quiet host, and (2) a further architectural issue found profiling
`parser.c` directly, beyond the already-fixed precedence chain.

**Methodology, used throughout**: a dedicated lex+parse+compile-ONLY
timing harness (`timeit_compile.c`, built directly against `libasnix.a`,
not part of the normal build) that loops over the exact 1057 real `.nix`
files `d.nix` (`(import /home/tbereknyei/nixpkgs/default.nix {}).ffmpeg.
outPath`) imports (collected via `strace -e trace=openat`, matching
M123's own corpus exactly), calling `asnix_lex`/`asnix_parse`/`asnix_
compile`/`asnix_ast_arena_reset` directly with NO evaluation at all --
isolates compile-phase cycles from the eval phase that dominates total
d.nix wall-clock, giving a much cleaner signal than running the whole
binary for changes confined to lex/parse/compile. Cross-checked against
the full real `asnix d.nix` binary (`perf stat`, CPU-pinned via `taskset
-c 2` to one confirmed P-core throughout, plus `hyperfine` as a second,
independent measurement methodology) for an end-to-end sanity check.
Host checked quiet before every measurement (`uptime`/`ps aux`, no
concurrent `asnix`/`iets` processes running) -- load average 1-3
throughout (other background agents' own non-asnix tooling), contrasted
explicitly against M125's own writeup, which landed under two OTHER
agents' `asnix` processes pegged at 100-200% CPU.

**Part 1: M125's own clean re-measurement.** Built the exact pre-M125
and M125 commits (`2f768bb~1`/`2f768bb`, which touches `parser.c` and
`docs/architecture.md` ONLY -- no other file -- confirmed via `git show
--stat`) into separate directories via `git archive`, so the ONLY
difference between the two binaries is the precedence-chain collapse
itself. Measured (`perf stat -r 5-7`, pinned, quiet host):

| | instructions | cycles | wall (perf stat avg) |
|---|---|---|---|
| compile-only harness, 1057 files | -0.54% | -0.79% | -3.57% |
| full `asnix d.nix` (lex+parse+compile+eval) | -0.21% (noise) | -1.14% | -3.46% |

Both measurements agree: a real, repeatable, single-digit-percent win,
much smaller than "9 call/ret pairs down to 1-2 per leaf expression"
might suggest in isolation, but LARGER in wall-clock than in raw
instruction count -- consistent with the win being mostly about reduced
call/return overhead (branch-predictor/return-stack-buffer pressure,
I-cache footprint from 9 separate non-inlined function bodies) rather
than raw instruction volume, matching M123's own observation that
asnix's IPC is already close to iets's (so cycle reduction, not
instruction-count reduction, is the resource actually being saved here).
This closes M125's own flagged gap: a real, trustworthy, quiet-host
number now exists and is small but genuinely positive.

**Part 2: profiling `parser.c` for further hot paths.** `perf record -g`
+ `perf report` on the compile-only harness (built with `-g`, M125-level
binary) surfaced a result the task's own hypothesis (iets's flatter,
less-indirect AST representation) only partly predicted: asnix's AST
node allocator ALREADY uses a dedicated bump arena (`ast.c`'s `asnix_ast_
new`, documented there as "Ast nodes are pure compile-time scratch, ~17%
of peak memory, freed in one shot per file"), not a slower general-
purpose malloc per node -- so the iets-style "flatten the tree into
index-based tables" rewrite this task's own brief suggested checking
turned out to be substantially already-equivalent in spirit (bump-
allocated nodes, not individually malloc'd) and NOT the real gap. Two
bugs/inefficiencies in how that EXISTING design was implemented were
the real finding instead:

**Fix 1 -- `ast.c`'s per-FILE chunk `calloc` was re-zeroing a full 1 MiB
on every single one of 1057 files, usually for far fewer live bytes than
that.** `asnix_ast_new`'s chunk allocator used to `calloc(1, sizeof(
AstChunk))` (1 MiB) whenever a fresh chunk was needed, with a `/* DEBUG:
test zero-init hypothesis */` comment flagging it as an open question.
Confirmed BOTH halves of that question directly: (a) the zero-init
itself IS load-bearing -- `parser.c`'s plain `a: body` lambda case
(`parse_expr`'s `TOK_IDENT && peek2 == TOK_COLON` branch) never sets
`AST_LAMBDA.is_pattern`/`formals`/`has_ellipsis`/`has_as_name` at all,
relying on them defaulting to 0/NULL, so simply switching to `malloc`
would have been a real, silent correctness bug (every ordinary `a: b`
lambda would get garbage `is_pattern`, misrouting through compiler.c's
pattern-destructuring path); (b) but the zero-fill only needs to cover
the bytes a node ACTUALLY occupies, not the fixed 1 MiB chunk size --
`perf report` found `__memset_avx2_unaligned_erms` as a genuine ~5.7%-
of-total-cycles hot symbol in the compile-only harness, NOT eliminated
by `calloc`'s usual "fresh mmap page is already zero, skip the memset"
fast path, because `asnix_ast_arena_reset()` frees every chunk right
after each FILE's own compile (by design, see ast.c's own header
comment -- Ast nodes are reclaimable compile-time scratch), so this
process allocates-then-frees a ~1 MiB chunk roughly once per imported
file. glibc's malloc dynamically RAISES its own internal mmap threshold
every time a chunk at or above the current threshold is freed (`mallopt
(M_MMAP_THRESHOLD)`'s own documented dynamic-adjustment behavior, meant
to stop mmap/munmap thrashing for a workload that repeats the same large
size) -- so after the first one or two ~1 MiB frees, the threshold climbs
past 1 MiB and every SUBSEQUENT same-sized chunk is served from the
ordinary heap instead of a fresh mmap, where `calloc` can no longer
assume pre-zeroed pages and must really `memset` the whole 1 MiB, most
of which the file's own (usually much smaller) AST never even touches.

**The fix**: `malloc` the chunk (no zero-fill promise, so nothing to
skip or fall back to -- sidesteps the dynamic-threshold problem
entirely) and `memset(n, 0, sizeof(Ast))` on exactly the one node being
carved out, inside `asnix_ast_new` itself, preserving the EXACT same
"every node starts fully zeroed" guarantee the correctness audit above
confirmed is needed -- just scoped to the bytes actually used instead of
the whole chunk, strictly less total zeroing for any file that doesn't
fill a whole chunk (the common case for 1057 real files averaging
~23 KB of source each) and no worse for one that does.

**Fix 2 -- `parser.c`'s other growable vectors (`AstVec`/`PartVec`/
`FormalVec`/`AttrSegVec`/`RawIndVec`) each started a fresh malloc-from-
cap-0 for EVERY list literal, string/path interpolation, lambda formals
list, and attrpath/inherit-name segment list in the whole file**, unlike
a comparison evaluator's (iets, `~/gnix/iets/src/syntax/parser.rs`)
`sc_ids`/`sc_elems`/`sc_parts`/`sc_formals`/`sc_names` -- ONE shared,
file-lifetime growable scratch buffer per table kind, reused across
every node via a `mark`/`commit` protocol (push onto the shared stack,
then copy the just-pushed span into permanent storage and roll the
stack's length back down). `perf report`'s self-time breakdown on the
compile harness found the whole malloc-family (`_int_malloc`/`malloc`/
`realloc`/`_int_realloc`/`__libc_calloc2`/`_int_free_merge_chunk`/
`unlink_chunk`) summing to roughly 14% of total self-time, with `BTVec`'s
OWN already-hash-indexed family (`btvec_push`/`insert_attrpath`) only
accounting for ~2.65 points of that -- leaving the bulk attributable to
these simpler, flat, append-then-finalize vector types.

**The fix**: a `SCRATCH_VEC(name, T)` macro (`parser.c`) adapted from
iets's own technique, generating a `_push`/`_mark`/`_commit` trio backed
by one `static` buffer per vector kind, applied to exactly the five
types above. Each `_commit(mark, &count)` copies the span pushed since
`mark` into a freshly `malloc`'d exact-size array (preserving this
project's existing "every Ast node owns its own permanent, exact-size
array" output shape, unlike iets's single ever-growing flat table
indexed by `(start,len)` -- that bigger representation change was
deliberately NOT adopted, see below) and rewinds the shared buffer's
length back down, so only the single largest node of each kind in the
WHOLE file ever forces a real `realloc` -- every other node of that kind
reuses already-grown capacity for free.

**Safety argument (the one real subtlety, verified against every call
site actually converted, not assumed)**: sharing one buffer across the
whole file is sound exactly because recursive-descent parsing is
strictly LIFO -- a NESTED use of the same vector kind (e.g. a list
literal nested inside another list literal's own element expression, or
an attrpath-sugar binding's value expression that itself contains
another binding block) always completes its own full push...push...
commit cycle and shrinks the shared length back down BEFORE the
enclosing use's own next push, simply because that's how a call that
hasn't returned yet works. The one discipline this places on every call
site: never dereference a stale pointer captured before a call that
might recurse into the SAME macro instance (a nested `_push`'s `realloc`
can move the buffer) -- audited specifically for `parse_binding_stmt`'s
attrpath-sugar `segs` (which parses the binding's VALUE expression,
`parse_expr`, strictly BETWEEN collecting `segs` and finally reading
`segs_items` -- fixed by moving the `_commit` call to AFTER `parse_expr`
returns, not immediately after the collection loop as the naive
translation would do) and `inherit`'s `names` (no such gap -- everything
between the collection loop and `free` is pure tree manipulation, no
parser recursion, so committing right after the loop is safe). **NOT
applied** to `BTVec`/`BindingVec`/`DynBindingVec`: those have an
irregularly-nested, TREE-shaped (not flat), incrementally mutated-and-
reopened lifetime (`reopen_attrset_into` can populate several different
BTNode-owned `DynBindingVec`s in a non-LIFO interleaved order within one
block's own parse) where the same safety argument does NOT hold --
converting those would need a materially bigger, riskier change (either
re-deriving the family's own O(1) hash-index scheme against a shared
backing store, or the full iets-style flat-table-with-`Range`
representation change) and was deliberately left alone, flagged below
as a real but out-of-scope follow-on, not attempted here.

**Measured** (compile-only harness, 1057 files, `perf stat -r 5`, quiet
host, pinned):

| | instructions | cycles | wall (harness internal "best") |
|---|---|---|---|
| + ast.c fix only | +0.13% (noise) | -4.83% | -5.35% |
| + both fixes (full) | -1.60% | -6.72% | -7.12% |

(percentages relative to the M125-level baseline; the scratch-vec fix's
own marginal contribution, full vs. ast.c-fix-only: instructions -1.73%,
cycles -1.99%, wall -1.87% -- smaller than the ast.c fix alone, but real
and in the same direction, not noise).

**Full end-to-end `asnix d.nix` (lex+parse+compile+eval combined)**,
both fixes together vs. the same commit with neither (`perf stat -r 7`,
pinned, quiet host):

| | instructions | cycles | page-faults | wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| neither fix | 10,259,392,435 | 5,797,927,153 | 173,322 | 1.549s (±1.79%) |
| both fixes | 10,214,974,464 (-0.43%) | 5,679,358,453 (-2.05%) | 171,866 (-0.84%) | 1.444s (-6.78%, ±0.10%) |

Cross-checked with `hyperfine` (15 runs, 2 warmups, same pinning):
`after` measured 1.03x +- 0.03 faster than `before`, matching direction
and rough magnitude, with a notably tighter variance in the "after"
binary (±0.006s vs ±0.036s) -- a believable side-effect of removing a
cost that was itself contingent on glibc's own internal dynamic-
threshold state, which is exactly the kind of thing that varies run to
run.

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green.
`make test-nix-conformance` (`NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`):
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` -- exact match to the pre-existing baseline
(same 3 pos-tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: one run showed
`pass=147 fail=1` (`clang.outPath(crash)`), reproduced clean standalone
(`./asnix -A clang.outPath`/`-A clang.drvPath` both rc=0, correct output)
and on a full rerun (`pass=148 fail=0`) -- this session's familiar
transient-contention flakiness pattern, not a real regression, per the
exact same pattern M123/M124/M125 all independently hit and confirmed.
Output hash on `d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.

**Not attempted, flagged for follow-on work**: converting `BTVec`/
`BindingVec`/`DynBindingVec` (attrset/let/rec binding lists, the single
largest remaining concentration of parser-side malloc-family overhead
after this milestone, per the ~2.65-points-of-14% breakdown above) to
the same shared-scratch technique, OR the bigger iets-style flat-table-
with-`Range`-indices `Ast` representation change (which would also
subsume this fix and the existing bump-arena design into one coherent
scheme) -- both are real, visible, NOT yet root-caused-away opportunities,
but each is a materially bigger, riskier change (the former needs a new
non-LIFO-safe sharing scheme or a rederived hash-index; the latter
touches every single `Ast*`-typed field across `ast.h`/`compiler.c`/
every builtin that walks an AST) than this milestone's own bar for a
same-session landing -- left as explicit, scoped-out future work rather
than forced.

## M132: initial capacities for `IrBuilder.ops`/`.pool` and the parser's growable vectors tuned 8/16->24, measured directly

Continuing the M123/M128/M131 allocation-pattern sweep across lex/parse/
compile, this milestone targets the one remaining class of leftover
`realloc` traffic: every one of these vectors already amortizes to O(1)
per push and (for the ones with a permanent-storage lifetime) already
trims to exact final size before handoff -- the only thing left on the
table is how many times each one actually pays a growth-realloc before
reaching its real final size.

**Measured** (temporary counter instrumentation, same convention M123
used for the lexer's `TokVec` fix, removed before landing) across a real
nixpkgs eval (`d.nix`, ffmpeg's closure, 1057 imported files):
`IrBuilder.ops` (old cap 16): 585,631 builders created, averaging 5.3 ops
each, but 30,367 (5.2%) exceeded 16 and paid a growth-realloc anyway.
`IrBuilder.pool` (old cap 8): 80,658 growth-reallocs -- a much worse
29%-of-pool-using-builders tail, since several of this project's own
emitted-ops sequences (e.g. every `ib_lambda`/`ib_rec_overrides_merge`
call) pack 2 pool entries per source construct. `AstVec`/`BindingVec`/
`BTVec` (old cap 8, parser.c): 23-25% regrow rate, ~11-14K growth-
reallocs each. `FormalVec` (old cap 8): 66% regrow rate, 13,806 growth-
reallocs -- real nixpkgs package functions routinely declare well over 8
named formals (e.g. `{ lib, stdenv, fetchurl, ... }:`), so this one was
undersized even at the average, not just the tail. `AttrSegVec`/
`PartVec`/`DynBindingVec`/`RawIndVec`: under 0.2% regrow at their
existing caps -- confirmed not worth touching.

**Fix**: raised the initial capacity to 24 (chosen by testing 16/24/32
directly against the measured regrow counts and picking the point of
diminishing returns, not just doubling blindly) for `src/c/irbuild.c`'s
`ib_emit`/`ib_pool_add`, and for `src/c/parser.c`'s `SCRATCH_VEC` macro's
own shared-buffer growth default (covering `astvec`/`partvec`/
`attrsegvec`/`formalvec`/`rawind` uniformly -- harmless even for the
already-fine `partvec`/`attrsegvec`/`rawind`, since `SCRATCH_VEC`'s
buffer is pure transient scratch, always copied out to an exact-size
allocation by `_commit`, never carried into permanent storage regardless
of how generous the initial guess is) plus `bindingvec_push`/
`btvec_push` (still their own independent per-node growable arrays, not
converted to `SCRATCH_VEC` -- M131's own documented reason: non-LIFO,
tree-shaped lifetime -- but `VEC_TRIM` still trims any slack from the
bigger initial guess before permanent handoff, so this is also a pure
realloc-count reduction, not a permanent-memory cost). Cut measured
growth-reallocs by roughly 50-98% depending on vector (the worst
offenders -- `pool`, `BindingVec`/`BTVec`, `FormalVec` -- saw the biggest
cuts, matching their worse starting regrow rates).

**Measured impact**: instruction count dropped ~0.14-0.15% consistently
across 3 interleaved before/after `perf stat` pairs on the full `d.nix`
eval (a precise, low-noise metric for this kind of change). Cycles/wall-
clock did not move outside this shared machine's noise floor in either
direction -- honestly reported rather than overclaimed. Unlike M123's
`TokVec` fix (few but individually expensive large-buffer reallocs on a
single growing vector per file), these are many independently cheap
tiny-buffer reallocs spread across hundreds of thousands of short-lived
`IrBuilder`/AST-vector instances, so the win is real but small.

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green.
`make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (exact baseline
match). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. Output hash on
`d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.

**Declined**: eliminating each `IrBuilder`'s own *first* allocation
(585,631 of them, unavoidable under the current per-instance malloc/
realloc/free lifecycle) -- not fixable via capacity tuning at all; would
need an inline-small-buffer or shared-arena redesign touching
`irpass.c`'s in-place pool-mutation API and the builder lifetime model.
Flagged below (M133) as a bigger, separately-scoped lever, not attempted
here.

Files: `src/c/irbuild.c` (`ib_emit`/`ib_pool_add` only), `src/c/
parser.c` (`SCRATCH_VEC`'s growth default, `bindingvec_push`,
`btvec_push`).

## M133: lex/parse/compile speed sweep -- consolidated status and the honest overall verdict

Closes out the M123/M128-M132 lex/parse/compile investigation with a
single consolidated accounting, after merging all 4 landed fixes
(lexer `CHAR_CLASS` table, M129; symtab `hash_bytes` word-at-a-time
mixing, M130; AST-chunk malloc+lazy-zero plus the parser's
`SCRATCH_VEC` rewrite, M131; growable-vector initial-capacity tuning,
M132) into one tree and resolving the one real cross-branch conflict
(two independently-dispatched investigations both touched `parser.c`'s
growable-vector capacities -- one via a wholesale `SCRATCH_VEC` rewrite,
the other via a direct cap-8-to-24 tuning of the pre-rewrite per-struct
`_push` functions the first change deleted; reconciled by folding the
cap-24 tuning into `SCRATCH_VEC`'s own growth default instead of keeping
two incompatible vector implementations, per M132 above).

**Ranked causes found this round, with status**:
1. `AstChunk` `calloc`'d per-file but freed every file, paying a real
   full-1MiB `memset` via glibc's dynamic mmap-threshold drift --
   **FIXED** (M131).
2. 5 parser vectors each malloc-from-empty per literal despite provably
   LIFO lifetime -- **FIXED** (M131, `SCRATCH_VEC`).
3. `path_char`/`uri_scheme_char`/etc. ran a full ctype-chain on every
   token's leading character, not just real paths/URIs -- **FIXED**
   (M129).
4. `hash_bytes` was a fully serial byte-at-a-time multiply chain --
   **FIXED** (M130).
5. `IrBuilder.pool`/`.ops`, `FormalVec`, `AstVec`/`BindingVec`/`BTVec`
   initial capacities too small for real nixpkgs shapes -- **FIXED**
   (M132).
6. `scope_find_lexical`'s linear linked-list/`memcmp` scan vs. a
   hashmap-based scope lookup -- architecturally real, but measured
   self-time only 0.40% of sampled cycles on this workload --
   **PLANNED, NOT ATTEMPTED**.
7. `compile_expr` (4.03% self-time) and `asnix_intern` (2.87%
   self-time, called from `compiler.c` once per identifier occurrence)
   driven by re-hashing identifier strings at compile time instead of
   carrying interned `Sym`s on AST nodes from parse time, the way `iets`
   (`~/gnix/iets/src/compile/mod.rs`) does -- the single largest lever
   identified this round (~7% of sampled cycles combined), but touches
   `ast.c`/`parser.c`/`compiler.c` simultaneously and needs a full
   correctness audit of every `AST_VAR`/`AST_SELECT`/binding/formal
   site -- **PLANNED, NOT ATTEMPTED**, flagged as its own dedicated
   future milestone.
8. `iets`'s lexer skips path/URI scanning entirely unless a cheap peek
   suggests one might follow, instead of unconditionally running the
   predicate chain on every token's leading character -- a real,
   likely-larger lever on top of M129's own fix, but has a genuine
   correctness edge case (URI schemes containing `.`/`+` aren't in
   `ident_cont`'s character set) that needs targeted unit-test coverage
   before landing -- **PLANNED, NOT ATTEMPTED**.
9. `IrBuilder`'s malloc/realloc/free-per-instance lifecycle vs. `iets`'s
   bump-`Arena` with in-place-extend-last-allocation -- real design gap,
   but `irbuild.c`'s own allocation-site cycles are under 1% of total
   process cycles, so porting this wouldn't move the needle --
   **INVESTIGATED, RULED OUT**.
10. A per-call `asnix_intern` lookup cache mirroring `iets`'s
    `Interner::cache` -- declined, since `iets`'s cache exists to skip a
    locked/sharded map and asnix's table is unlocked with only 0.609
    extra probe steps/call at steady state -- **INVESTIGATED, RULED
    OUT**.

**Honest overall verdict**: the lex/parse/compile subtree is ~43.9% of
total process cycles per M123's own breakdown; the 4 landed fixes' full-
`d.nix` deltas (lexer -1.8% cycles, parser/AST -2.1% cycles, symtab
-0.97%, allocation-cap tuning noise-level) sum to roughly a 3-4
percentage-point cut of *total* process cycles -- something like an 8-
10% cut of the subtree's own cost once overlap between the fixes is
accounted for. Multiplicatively, this moves asnix from roughly 8x to
roughly 7.2-7.5x slower per byte than `iets` on this phase: real,
verified, zero-regression progress, but nowhere near closing the gap on
its own. The two largest remaining levers (items 6+7 combined, Sym-
carrying AST nodes plus hashmap-based scope resolution; and item 8, the
lexer peek-guard) were both explicitly investigated and deliberately
left for a dedicated future milestone, not because they were ruled out,
but because each is a genuinely separate, riskier, multi-file change
that does not fit this session's bar for a bounded, same-pass landing.

## M134: why iets is still ~2x faster, beyond lex/parse/compile's own internal costs -- the two-phase lex/parse boundary itself, not yet named

Research-only follow-up to M123/M127/M129-M133 (`/subtask` "identify why
iets is twice as fast," no implementation requested or attempted).
M129-M132 sped up asnix's existing lex-then-parse architecture; this
pass instead asked whether the architecture itself, not just its
constant factors, differs from `iets`'s in a way not yet named in this
project's own docs.

**Finding, verified directly against both source trees (not re-derived
from the prior milestones' own numbers)**: asnix's `Token` struct
(`src/c/lexer.h:102-126`) is 56 bytes (`kind` + `int_val` (8B) +
`float_val` (8B) + `start` pointer + `len` + `pos` pointer + 2 int
flags), and every field is written for every token regardless of kind
-- `int_val`/`float_val` are meaningless for the 95%+ of tokens that are
identifiers, punctuation, or keywords, but still get populated.
`asnix_lex` (`src/c/lexer.c:569`) runs as a fully separate phase: it
scans the entire file and writes every token into a `TokVec` array
before the parser sees a single one; `asnix_parse` (`src/c/
parser.c:2009`) then indexes back into that same array
(`p->toks[p->pos]`, `parser.c:648`) rather than pulling tokens on
demand. Two full passes over the same ~159 MB of token data on a real
nixpkgs eval (M123's own measured corpus: 2,836,205 tokens x 56 bytes):
one that writes it, one that reads it back.

`iets`'s `Token` (`~/gnix/iets/src/syntax/lexer.rs:138-142`) is 12
bytes: `kind` (enum tag) + `start: u32` + `end: u32`. No `int_val`/
`float_val` field exists at all -- integer/float/string payloads are
never decoded at lex time; they're parsed lazily from
`self.src[start..end]` only once, exactly when the parser's AST-
building step actually needs that specific token's value. `iets`'s
parser calls `self.lx.next_token()` directly (`parser.rs:212/225/235`)
-- a pull-based, single-token-lookahead design fusing lexing and
parsing into one pass, with no intermediate token array allocated,
written, or re-read at all.

**Why this is additional, not a restatement of M129-M133**: those
milestones (the `CHAR_CLASS` table, `hash_bytes` mixing, the `AstChunk`/
`SCRATCH_VEC` allocator fixes, the growable-vector capacity tuning) all
reduced the constant-factor cost of asnix's existing two-phase lex-then-
parse architecture. None of them touched the phase boundary itself.
This finding says the boundary's existence -- a ~56-byte-per-token
eager array, fully materialized before parsing starts, then fully re-
read -- is itself a real, distinct, previously-unnamed cost with no
counterpart in `iets`'s fused, pull-based, lazily-decoded design.

**Not attempted, by design (a research-only task)**: fusing lex+parse
into one pull-based pass, or shrinking `Token` to a 12-byte offset pair
with deferred int/float decoding, would be a large, correctness-risky
rewrite touching essentially every one of `parser.c`'s 40+ direct
`Token`-field access sites (`.kind`/`.int_val`/`.float_val`/`.start`/
`.len`/`.pos`/the two flag fields) plus every lexer call site that
currently decodes a literal's value eagerly. Flagged here as a
candidate future milestone, scoped as its own dedicated pass with a
correctness audit of every access site, not a one-session bounded fix.
No files changed, no commits made.

## M135: lex/parse fusion, implemented and measured -- a correct, verified, but honestly negative result

Implements the fusion M134 flagged but didn't attempt: `asnix_lex`
running to completion over the whole file, handed to `asnix_parse` as a
pre-filled array, replaced by on-demand lexing interleaved with parsing.
Scoped deliberately narrower than M134's own "shrink Token to 12 bytes
with deferred int/float decode" framing -- that half is a separate,
larger, correctness-risky change (every one of `parser.c`'s 40+ direct
`Token`-field accesses would need auditing); this milestone fuses the
CONTROL FLOW only, keeping the existing 56-byte `Token` and its exact
per-token scanning logic untouched.

**What changed**: `lexer.c`'s `asnix_lex` body (the `for(;;){...}` token-
producing loop) was extracted into `lex_until(src, i, modes, v,
min_len)`, identical per-token scanning code, with one added early-exit
check (`if (v->len > min_len) return;`) so it can stop and resume
anywhere instead of only running to EOF. `asnix_lex` itself is now a
thin wrapper (`lex_until(..., SIZE_MAX)`), preserving its existing
behavior and all existing callers (tests/bench) byte-for-byte. A new
`LexCursor` (lexer.h/lexer.c) bundles the same `(src, i, modes, v)`
state persistently; `lexcur_tok(lc, idx)` is the parser's on-demand
driver -- `static inline`, checking `idx < lc->v.len` first (the common
case: the token's already there) and falling back to a real call into
`lexcur_tok_slow` -> `lex_until` only when lexing actually needs to
advance. `parser.c`'s `Parser` struct now holds a `LexCursor *` instead
of a pre-filled `Token *`/count pair; `cur()`/`peek2()`/
`find_matching_rbrace`'s forward-scanning loop (the one place that
reads arbitrarily far ahead, for `{...}:`-pattern-vs-attrset
disambiguation -- found to be a hard blocker against a simpler, iets-
style single-token-lookahead pull design, since it needs true random
access, not just 1-token peek) all now go through `lexcur_tok` instead
of indexing a pre-filled array directly. `asnix_parse`'s signature
dropped its now-unnecessary `(toks, count)` parameters down to just
`(src)`, creating and freeing its own `LexCursor` internally; all 7
call sites (`eval_file.c` x4, `irdump.c`, `tests/ir/test_m45_codegen.c`,
`bench/microbench_m45.c` -- every one previously doing `toks =
asnix_lex(src,&n); ast = asnix_parse(toks,n,src); free(toks);` back to
back) collapsed to one `asnix_parse(src)` call.

**Why the `static inline` fast path matters, found by measuring, not
guessing**: the first working version routed every `cur()`/`peek2()`
call through a real cross-translation-unit function call into
`lex_until` just to evaluate its own early-return check, even when the
requested token was already lexed (the overwhelmingly common case,
since `cur()` alone is called many times per token position as the
parser decides which grammar rule applies). Measured directly: this
cost a **+10.5% instruction regression** on a full `d.nix` eval (9.98B
-> 11.04B) before any fast path existed. Moving `LexCursor`'s full
struct definition (plus the previously lexer.c-private `LexMode`/
`ModeStack`/`TokVec` types) into `lexer.h` so `lexcur_tok`'s "is it
already there" check could be `static inline` and genuinely inline at
every parser.c call site cut this down substantially (see below) --
this is a real, generally-applicable lesson for any "lazy produce on
demand" refactor: the function boundary SURROUNDING the check matters
as much as the check's own cost once it's called from a hot, high-
frequency, deeply-pipelined caller.

**Measured, after the fast-path fix** (`perf stat -r 7`, `taskset -c 0`
pinned to a confirmed-quiet-relative-to-the-rest-of-this-session P-core,
two binaries built from the otherwise-identical tree with only this
milestone's files swapped, `cpu_core/instructions,cycles` -- low noise,
+-0.01%/+-0.54%):
- Full `d.nix` eval: instructions 9,957,338,035 -> 10,287,423,982
  (**+3.3%**), cycles 5,519,921,354 -> 5,649,162,933 (**+2.3%**),
  wall-clock 1.888s -> 1.859s (-1.5%, inside this measurement's own
  +-1.16%/+-1.17% noise band -- not a confident win).

**Honest verdict: this is a correct, fully-verified fusion that is a
small net REGRESSION, not an improvement, on real asnix workloads --
and the reason why is itself the useful finding.** `asnix_parse`
unconditionally consumes every token up to and including `TOK_EOF`
before returning (it has to: `expect(&p, TOK_EOF, "end of input")` is
the very last thing it does, on every successful parse of a whole
file) -- so for any syntactically valid file, on-demand lexing still
lexes literally every byte the eager version did, in the exact same
order, with the exact same total work. The eager array's `cur()` was a
single pointer-arithmetic load; the on-demand version's `cur()` is that
same load PLUS one bounds comparison and one conditional branch, paid
on every single token access rather than once per token produced (and
`cur()`/`peek2()` are each called several times per token position).
There is no equivalent `iets`-style payoff here because `iets`'s real
win (per M134) isn't "lex on demand instead of eagerly" in the abstract
-- it's a genuinely different Token representation (12 bytes vs. 56)
AND a true single-token-lookahead pull design with no backing array at
all, which this milestone deliberately did NOT attempt (that redesign
is blocked by `find_matching_rbrace`'s need for unbounded forward
random access, a hard architectural fact discovered while implementing
this, not assumed). Fusing just the CONTROL FLOW, while keeping the
same per-token work and the same backing array, trades a free pointer
index for a cheap-but-nonzero bounds check with nothing on the other
side of the ledger to pay for it -- a real, if small, loss.

**Verified** (fast-path version): `make test`/`test-e2e`/
`test-conformance` all green. `make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655
fail=3 skip=148` (exact baseline match, same 3 pre-existing pos-
tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: one run showed `pass=146
fail=2` (`rustc.drvPath(crash)`, `jq.drvPath(crash)`) under confirmed
heavy concurrent-agent load (load average 7.59-14.45 on this 22-core
shared machine during this milestone's measurement window), both
reproduced clean standalone (`rc=0`, correct output) and on a full
rerun (`pass=148 fail=0`) -- this session's familiar transient-
contention-flakiness pattern, not a real regression. Output hash on
`d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.

**Recommendation: do not build on this as-is.** The two things that
would actually need to be true for lex/parse fusion to pay off --
shrinking `Token` so there's real memory-traffic to save, and a true
pull-based design with no backing array at all -- are exactly the two
things this milestone deliberately scoped out, and the second is
architecturally blocked by `find_matching_rbrace` without a design
change (a backtracking-capable lexer position, or restructuring that
one disambiguation to not need forward random access). Landed and kept
anyway, per this session's own M127 precedent for a correct-but-
declined POC, as real, working reference material for whoever
eventually tackles the larger Sym-carrying-AST/Token-shrink milestone
M134 already flagged as the one lever in this area with real headroom
(~7% of sampled cycles) -- fusing control flow alone, this milestone
now shows directly, is not that lever on its own.

Files: `src/c/lexer.c`/`lexer.h` (`lex_until`, `LexCursor`/
`lexcur_new`/`lexcur_tok`/`lexcur_tok_slow`/`lexcur_free`), `src/c/
parser.c`/`parser.h` (`Parser.lc` replacing `Parser.toks`/`.count`,
`cur`/`peek2`/`find_matching_rbrace` routed through `lexcur_tok`,
`asnix_parse`'s signature), `src/c/eval_file.c`, `src/c/irdump.c`,
`tests/ir/test_m45_codegen.c`, `bench/microbench_m45.c` (all 7
lex+parse call sites collapsed to one `asnix_parse(src)` call each).

## M136: compile-time constant folding for int-literal `AST_BINOP`, unified with thunk avoidance

`/subtask` follow-up to the `research-what-the` fork's survey of what
would make an evaluator genuinely fast (item #4: "thunk avoidance as a
first-class target... eagerly folds n-1/forced-int arithmetic"). Checked
first, not assumed: `src/c/irpass_cfold.c` already folds int-literal
arithmetic/comparison triples, but strictly at the bytecode level, and
only when `ASNIX_IR_OPT=1` is set -- a real default-build gap, since an
ordinary `./asnix file.nix` run (no env var set) performs ZERO
constant folding of int arithmetic today: `1 + 2` compiles straight to
`push 1; push 2; add`, executed at runtime on every evaluation.

**Fix**: `src/c/compiler.c` gained `try_fold_const_binop` (next to
`is_thunk_free_literal`, which it's now a case of), checked at the top
of `compile_expr`'s `AST_BINOP` case. It folds `+`/`-`/`*`/`/` and all
six comparisons when both operands are `AST_INT` literals, mirroring
`op_arith.S`'s own checked semantics exactly: the true int64-overflow
check (via `__builtin_add_overflow`/`__builtin_sub_overflow`/
`__builtin_mul_overflow`, not plain C `+`/`-`/`*`, which would wrap
silently) AND the narrower `ASNIX_INT_MIN`/`ASNIX_INT_MAX` tagged-value
window `+`/`-`/`*` are additionally bounded to (per `op_arith.S`'s own
M56 comment). Division by zero and the `ASNIX_INT_MIN / -1` edge are
also left unfolded. Any case that would abort at runtime is
deliberately NOT folded, so the ordinary runtime op still reaches the
exact same abort with the exact same message -- verified directly:
`1152921504606846975 + 1` (one past `ASNIX_INT_MAX`) and `5 / 0` both
still abort with their original messages, not a silently wrong folded
result.

**Unified with thunk avoidance, not bolted on separately**: `is_thunk_
free_literal`'s `AST_BINOP` case calls the same `try_fold_const_binop`
function, so a foldable binop (e.g. `let x = 1 + 2; in ...`) is now ALSO
recognized as thunk-free at every one of the ten `ib_mk_thunk` call
sites (M92's own `maybeThunk` mechanism) -- it collapses to a single
zero-cost push with no `Thunk` heap allocation and no later `OP_CALL`/
force-machinery round trip, exactly like any other literal. Verified via
`ASNIX_SHOW_STATS=1` on a synthetic `let a = 1+2; b = 3-4; c = 5*6; in
a+b+c`: `thunks: 0` (previously each binding would have allocated one).

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green.
`make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (exact baseline
match). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. Output hash on
`d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.
`compiler.c` itself compiles with zero new warnings.

**Not attempted, flagged for follow-on**: `AST_FLOAT` operands, and
constant-folding `builtins.x` (`builtins.currentSystem` etc.) at
compile time when `builtins` resolves lexically to the genuine root
frame -- the fork's own directive's third example, scoped out here to
keep this a single, narrowly-verified change rather than widening the
surface being audited for correctness in one pass.

Files: `src/c/compiler.c` (`try_fold_const_binop`, `is_thunk_free_
literal`'s `AST_BINOP` case, `compile_expr`'s `AST_BINOP` case).

## M137: zero-copy mmap for the bytecode-cache READ path, plus exact ops-array presizing on deserialize

Directed follow-up to the M94/M98/M107 bytecode cache and a research
pass (not a separate milestone) that found `asnix_bytecode_deserialize`/
`read_program_into`/`read_one_tagged_op` accounted for 17-19% of samples
on a warm-cache eval, recursing once per nested sub-program. Scoped
narrowly to "make a cache HIT avoid copying the entry's bytes," not a
full on-disk format redesign -- see the honest scope note below for why
a true parse-free mmap format isn't viable without much larger,
unrelated changes.

**What changed, `src/c/bytecode_cache.c`.** Both `asnix_bytecode_cache_
lookup_fast` and `asnix_bytecode_cache_lookup_verify` used to `fopen`,
`fseek`/`ftell` to find the body's length, `malloc` a buffer sized to
exactly that length, and `fread` the whole body into it before handing
that heap copy to `asnix_bytecode_deserialize`. Replaced with
`mmap_whole_file` (`open`+`fstat`+`mmap(..., PROT_READ, MAP_PRIVATE,
fd, 0)`, mapping from offset 0 -- always page-aligned, unlike the
header-relative body offset mmap's own `offset` parameter requires to
be page-aligned -- then `close(fd)`, since a successful mapping keeps
the pages resident independent of the fd that created it) plus
`parse_header_from_buf` (reads the fixed 72-byte header directly out of
the mapped bytes via `memcpy`, not a pointer-cast, to stay correct on
any platform where the header's own field offsets might not be
naturally aligned for that field's type -- they happen to be 8-byte-
aligned today, but the code doesn't rely on that). The deserializer
itself is handed `map + CACHE_HEADER_LEN` directly -- the only copy left
anywhere in the HIT path is the deserializer's own construction of the
OUTPUT `IrProgram` (ops/pool arrays), which this milestone does not
touch; what's eliminated is the separate, redundant copy of the INPUT
bytes the old code made on top of that. `lookup_verify`'s self-heal
rewrite (`write_entry_atomic`) now reads directly from the still-valid
mapped `body` pointer instead of the old malloc'd copy, since
`write_entry_atomic` only ever reads via `fwrite`, never retains the
pointer past its own return.

**What changed, `src/c/bytecode.c`.** `read_program_into` already reads
`n_ops` as its very first field, and -- verified directly against
`write_program`'s own counting (`program_op_count`, over the ORIGINAL
uncollapsed op array before `OP_MK_ATTRS`'s grouped pairs fold into one
`PTAG_OP_ATTRS` entry) and against this same function's own loop, which
advances `i` by however many ops a single tagged entry actually emits
(`PTAG_OP_ATTRS` emits `count+1` for one group entry, every other tag
emits exactly 1) -- `n_ops` is always this level's EXACT final `d->len`,
never more or less. Every `DBuilder` reaching `read_program_into` is
freshly `{0}`-initialized by its one call site (the top-level call in
`asnix_bytecode_deserialize`, or `PTAG_OP_THUNK`/`PTAG_OP_LAMBDA`'s own
fresh `child = {0}`), so `d->cap == 0` reliably means "first and only
time this level's own `ops` array is sized." Presizing `d->ops` to
exactly `n_ops` up front replaces `db_emit`'s usual start-at-16-and-
double growth with ONE allocation and ZERO growth-reallocs for `ops` at
every level -- mirroring M123's lexer `TokVec` precedent (presize when
the final count is already known, rather than discover it by doubling).
`pool` has no equivalent exact count (`OP_CHECK_FORMALS`/`OP_REC_
OVERRIDES_MERGE` can add many pool entries for a single op), so its
presize to `n_ops` is only a heuristic starting guess -- still correctly
grows via the ordinary doubling path in `db_pool_add` if exceeded, same
safety as before, just a smaller or zero chance of ever needing to.

**Measured** (`perf stat`, `taskset -c 0` pinned to a confirmed quiet
P-core, warm `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE=1` on a real `d.nix`/ffmpeg eval,
1056 cached imports; two binaries built from the otherwise-identical
tree with only `bytecode.c`/`bytecode_cache.c` swapped, 3 interleaved
before/after pairs to rule out host-load confounds rather than trusting
one measurement):
- Instructions: 7,072.4M -> 6,918.8M, **-2.17%** (<0.02% noise on every
  single run -- a hard, repetition-independent fact, not a noisy
  average: this is exactly the `ops`-array-presizing fix's own effect,
  since eliminating growth-reallocs removes a fixed, countable number of
  `realloc`/copy operations regardless of run-to-run timing variance).
- Cycles: 3,996.7M -> 3,806.7M, **-4.75%** (consistent direction across
  all 3 pairs: -0.68%/-3.43%/+-noise, -3.71%/+-noise, -5.80%/+-noise --
  individual-pair deltas vary with host load, but every pair moved the
  same direction).
- Wall-clock: 1.185s -> 1.111s, **-6.24%** across the same 3 pairs.
- Cycles' reduction (4.75%) exceeding instructions' (2.17%) is the same
  signature M129's `CHAR_CLASS` table found: removing the `malloc`+
  `fread` copy doesn't just remove instructions, it removes whatever
  page faults/cache-line touches that copy itself caused, on top of
  the instructions a disassembly count alone would show.

**Correctness, verified three ways beyond the full suite below**: (1)
cold-then-warm run on `d.nix` with `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE_STATS=1` --
identical output hash both runs, 1038/1039 fast-path hits on the warm
run; (2) `touch`ed every cached source file's mtime without changing
content, confirming the content-verify + self-heal path (20 content-
verified hits, then back to 1038 fast-path hits on the NEXT run,
confirming self-heal actually re-stamps the entry); (3) two full passes
of `test-nix-conformance` (`NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`,
806-file corpus) with `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE=1` -- cold and warm, both
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`, same 3 pre-existing pos-tracking failures --
plus two passes of `test-nixpkgs-hash` the same way, both `pass=148
fail=0`.

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green (no
`ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE` set, the default path, confirming this change is
a true no-op when the cache is disabled). `make test-nix-conformance`:
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (exact baseline, cache disabled). `make
test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. Output hash on `d.nix` unchanged
across every configuration tested above.

**Honest scope note -- why this is "zero-copy I/O," not "zero-copy
format"**: the deeper vision implied by "mmap+fixup bytecode cache" --
mapping the cache file and using its `ops`/`pool` arrays almost as-is,
with only a cheap relocation pass instead of any real parsing -- is NOT
what this milestone does, and isn't viable without a much larger,
separate redesign. The current on-disk format (`bytecode.c`'s varint-
encoded, per-op-tagged stream) re-interns every symbol name into THIS
process's own id space on every load (`asnix_intern`, ids are assigned
by first-seen order and differ run to run), re-sorts `OP_MK_ATTRS`/
`OP_CHECK_FORMALS`'s symbol lists against those freshly-assigned ids,
and resolves every op's `handler` field to an actual function pointer
via `ir_link` (a process's own `.text` addresses, not stable across
runs) -- none of that work can be skipped by a smarter memory-mapping
scheme alone; it would need a new wire format that defers symbol
identity to runtime (storing names, not ids, at every op site, with a
level of indirection the current ops-execute-directly design doesn't
have) and a stable index scheme for handler identity, which is a
materially larger, correctness-sensitive change out of scope here. What
this milestone removes is strictly the cache LAYER's own copy of the
file's bytes before handing them to that existing parser -- a real,
measured, bounded win, not the full "no deserialization at all" vision.

Files: `src/c/bytecode_cache.c` (`mmap_whole_file`, `parse_header_from_
buf`, both `asnix_bytecode_cache_lookup_fast`/`_verify`), `src/c/
bytecode.c` (`read_program_into`'s presizing only).

## M138: `asnix_lex`'s own flagged follow-on -- guarding `try_scan_path`/`try_scan_uri` on identifier-leading tokens instead of running them unconditionally

M129's own "Follow-on, NOT attempted here" paragraph named this exactly:
`asnix_lex`'s main dispatch loop unconditionally ran `try_scan_path` (and,
for alpha leads, `try_scan_uri`) on the leading character of EVERY
identifier/number/operator token, before falling through to ordinary
`ident_cont`-based identifier scanning -- meaning every plain identifier
(by far the most common token in real Nix source) paid for a full
`path_char`-run-plus-group scan that was guaranteed to fail, immediately
followed by a second, separate scan over almost the same bytes via
`ident_cont` to actually produce the `TOK_IDENT`. Checked directly against
iets (`~/gnix/iets/src/syntax/lexer.rs`, `next_token`'s
`b'a'..=b'z' | b'A'..=b'Z' | b'_'` match arm): it avoids exactly this
double-scan, but only for identifier-leading tokens -- its own digit/`.`/
`-`/`+` match arms (`or_float_or_path`, and the direct `scan_path_token`
calls in the `-`/`+` arms) still call the full path scan unconditionally,
with no guard at all. This milestone mirrors that scope precisely: only
the identifier-leading case changed, since a digit/operator run is
typically only 1-4 bytes before failing `path_char` (a number literal,
or a lone `-`/`+` next to whitespace), unlike an identifier's potentially
much longer run -- not worth the complexity for a near-zero win there,
and not a difference iets itself bothers to optimize either.

**The guard, reusing M129's own `CHAR_CLASS` table (no new predicates)**:
inside the `ident_start(c)` branch, scan the ordinary `ident_cont` run
once (needed anyway to produce a plain `TOK_IDENT`/keyword), then peek at
the single byte `nb` immediately after that run. The full (expensive)
`try_scan_path`/`try_scan_uri` rescan -- from the token's own start, not
from the `ident_cont` run's end -- only fires when `nb` is `/` (direct
path-group signal), `:` (direct URI-colon signal), or `.`/`+` (the
`ident_cont` run stopped short of where `path_char`/`uri_scheme_char`
would keep going -- ambiguous without the real rescan). Whenever `nb` is
none of those four, both scans are skipped entirely and the already-
computed `ident_cont` run becomes the `TOK_IDENT`/keyword directly.

**The correctness edge case, worked through and landed, not declined**:
`ident_cont` and `path_char`/`uri_scheme_char` are NOT the same character
set -- `CC_IDENT_CONT` includes `'` but excludes `.`/`+`; `CC_PATH_CHAR`/
`CC_URI_SCHEME` include `.`/`+` but exclude `'` (and `CC_URI_SCHEME`
further excludes `_`, which `CC_PATH_CHAR` includes). A token shaped like
`a.b+c:foo` (a URI whose scheme contains `.` and `+`, both legal RFC 3986
scheme characters) or `foo.bar/baz` (a path literal with `.` in its
prefix) needs the real `path_char`/`uri_scheme_char` run checked, not
just where the `ident_cont` run happens to end. The guard's four-character
peek (`/`, `:`, `.`, `+`) is exactly why this stays correct: whenever none
of those four follow the `ident_cont` run, skipping is PROVABLY
equivalent to running both scans and having them fail, not an
approximation --
  - Neither `/` nor `:` can occur strictly before the peeked byte: both
    already stop an `ident_cont` run outright (neither bit is set in
    `CC_IDENT_CONT`), so if either had appeared earlier the run would
    never have reached this far.
  - If the `ident_cont` run contains no `'` (the overwhelmingly common
    case), the `path_char`/`uri_scheme_char` run from the token's start
    tracks the `ident_cont` run exactly on their shared subset (alnum/
    `_`/`-`) and can only diverge AT the peeked byte itself, via `.`/`+`
    -- already covered by the guard's own trigger condition.
  - If the `ident_cont` run DOES contain a `'` before the peeked byte
    (rare -- a primed identifier like `lib'`), the real `path_char`/
    `uri_scheme_char` run stops AT that `'` instead, long before the
    peeked byte -- but `scan_path_groups`/the URI-colon check both
    require that exact stopping byte to be `/`/`:` respectively, and `'`
    is neither, so both scans are guaranteed to fail there regardless of
    what the peeked byte is. Skipping stays safe.
Verified directly, not just argued: built two full binaries from the
otherwise-identical tree (only `lexer.c` swapped, same manual-swap
mechanism M129 used after this session's own live `refs/stash` collision
precedent, avoiding the stash entirely this time), fed both every
adversarial case this reasoning identifies --
`a.b+c:foo`/`x+.y-z:tail`/`a+.b:x`/`a.b.c:x` (dotted/`+`-laden URI
schemes), `foo.bar/baz`/`./a.b${toString x}c/d` (dotted path prefixes,
including through an interpolation boundary), `lib'`/`a'b` (primed
identifiers), `a'.b:x`/`a'/b` (primed identifiers immediately followed by
what could be a path/URI continuation), `a_b:foo`/`x:x+1` (the real-Nix
`uri_scheme_char`-excludes-`_` and longest-match-over-lambda footguns
M129's `try_scan_uri` comment already documents) -- and confirmed
byte-identical output between the two binaries on every single case,
plus on the full `d.nix` eval (ffmpeg's closure). Landed a dedicated e2e
fixture for the headline case (`tests/e2e/m138_uri_scheme_dot_plus.nix`),
itself independently confirmed to already pass identically on the
PRE-this-milestone binary too (it exercises pre-existing, correct
behavior, not something this change newly makes pass).

**Measured** (`perf stat`, `taskset -c 0` pinned to one performance core,
two binaries built from the otherwise-identical tree with only `lexer.c`
swapped, explicit `cpu_core/.../` event selection throughout -- this
session's own host was under real concurrent load from several other
agents for the whole measurement window, `uptime` load average 3-6.8 on
a 22-thread host, so cycles/wall-clock at the FULL-eval scale below are
reported with that caveat; the lex-only microbenchmark's own numbers were
reproducible to +-0.00% on instructions and a tight single-digit percent
on cycles/task-clock across repeated `perf stat -r 9` runs, so they're
trusted at face value):
- **Lex-only microbenchmark** (a from-scratch standalone harness, not
  shipped, linking `lexer.o` directly and looping `asnix_lex` over
  `all-packages.nix`, the same real 326KB nixpkgs file M129 used, 300
  iterations, token count cross-checked identical -- 11,193,300 tokens --
  between both binaries before trusting any timing number): instructions
  4,652,301,103 -> 4,151,206,675 (**-10.8%**), cycles 1,806,131,261 ->
  1,664,679,012 (**-7.8%**), task-clock 519.68ms -> 477.59ms (**-8.1%**).
- **Full real eval** (`d.nix`, ffmpeg's closure, bytecode cache OFF by
  default so every one of the 1057 imported files genuinely re-lexes):
  instructions 9,023,293,940 -> 8,911,672,653 (**-1.24%**), reproducible
  to +-0.00%/+-0.01% across every `perf stat -r 5`/`-r 9` trial run (5
  separate trials, both orders tried to rule out filesystem-cache-
  warming bias). Cycles and task-clock at this whole-process scale swung
  both directions across repeated trials under the concurrent host load
  noted above (one trial pair: cycles +1.9%/task-clock -6.0%; another:
  cycles -1.0%/task-clock +7.1%) -- not trusted as a directional claim on
  their own. The instruction-count win cross-checks cleanly against
  M123's own cycle breakdown, though: lex is ~10.6% of total cycles in a
  real eval, and a ~10.8% instruction cut confined to lexing predicts
  roughly a 1.1% whole-program instruction cut, matching the observed
  -1.24% closely.

**Declined, deliberately, same reasoning iets itself uses**: extending
this same guard to digit-leading or `.`/`-`/`+`-leading tokens. Those
runs are short (1-4 bytes typically) before `path_char` already fails,
so the unconditional `try_scan_path` call there is already cheap --
adding a peek-and-guard there would add real branching complexity for a
win too small to measure reliably against this host's own noise floor,
and iets's own lexer doesn't bother either (`or_float_or_path` and the
`-`/`+` match arms call `scan_path_token` unconditionally, no guard).

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green
(including the new `m138_uri_scheme_dot_plus` fixture). `make
test-nix-conformance NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`:
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3 pre-existing pos-tracking failures).
`make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0` on a clean run (hit this
session's own documented transient-contention flakiness under the
concurrent host load noted above across several earlier attempts --
`(crash)`-tagged failures on a different, random package each time,
e.g. `nano.outPath`/`diffutils.drvPath`/`gnutar.outPath`, then
`less.drvPath`/`zsh.drvPath`, then `diffutils.outPath`, then
`nodejs.drvPath`, then `zstd.drvPath` -- every single one of those
individually reproduced correctly standalone in well under the harness's
own 120s timeout, consistent with the timeout firing on CPU starvation
under concurrent load rather than any real crash; a subsequent clean run
came back `pass=148 fail=0`). Output hash on `d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure)
unchanged: `/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.

Files: `src/c/lexer.c` (`lex_until`'s main dispatch loop -- the
`ident_start(c)` branch now owns its own guarded path/URI check and the
plain-identifier/keyword emission that used to live in a separate,
later `ident_start(c)` block further down, now removed as dead code;
the non-identifier-leading `try_scan_path` call keeps its old,
unconditional behavior, just relocated next to the branch that now
excludes identifier leads from it). `tests/e2e/
m138_uri_scheme_dot_plus.nix`/`.expected` (new fixture).

## M139: compile-time constant folding for `AST_BINOP` extended to `AST_FLOAT` operands -- M136's first explicitly-scoped-out follow-on, landed; the second (`builtins.X` folding) investigated and declined

Directed follow-up to M136, which folded `AST_BINOP` at compile time
only when both operands were `AST_INT` literals and explicitly scoped
out two follow-ons: float-literal operands, and compile-time folding of
`builtins.X` references when `builtins` is provably unshadowed. This
milestone lands the first and declines the second, after checking a
separate research pass's "does asnix already do iets's `maybeThunk`
forced-value-caching trick" question first, per this task's own
directive.

**Checked first, as directed, before changing anything**: grepped
every `ASNIX_THUNK_STATE_FORCED` site in `src/asm/` --
`op_var_ref.S`/`op_select.S`/`op_select_or.S`/`op_with.S`/`force.S`
all compare a Thunk's state word against `ASNIX_THUNK_STATE_FORCED`
and return the already-cached `Value` directly on a hit, never re-
running the Thunk's body or re-wrapping it. This is exactly the
"return already-forced values directly instead of re-wrapping them"
behavior the research pass flagged as possibly missing -- it already
exists, confirming (like M93/M111's bounded `//` sharing and M130's
symtab hash finalizer before it) that this was a research false
positive, not a real gap. No code changed for this part; cited here so
the next pass doesn't re-raise it.

**What changed, `src/c/compiler.c`'s `try_fold_const_binop`**: the
int/int path (both operands `AST_INT`) is byte-for-byte unchanged --
same `__builtin_*_overflow` checks, same `ASNIX_INT_MIN`/`MAX` re-
check, same unfolded-on-overflow/div-by-zero behavior as M136 landed.
A new branch handles any `AST_BINOP` where at least one operand is
`AST_FLOAT` (the other may be `AST_INT` or `AST_FLOAT`): both operands
promote to `double` via the identical cast `value_util.c`'s own
`as_double()` helper uses for an int operand (`(double)int_val`), so a
folded result is bit-for-bit what the corresponding *unfolded* runtime
op (`asnix_add_values`/`asnix_sub_values`/`asnix_mul_values`/
`asnix_div_values`, or `asnix_cmp_{lt,gt,le,ge}_values`/
`asnix_bshared_value_eq`'s own Float branch) would have computed from
the same two literals, not merely numerically close to it. `+`/`-`/`*`
always fold once this branch is reached: unlike checked int arithmetic,
IEEE-754 double arithmetic has no overflow-abort case at all -- a
too-large result is `inf`, the exact same `inf` the unfolded op would
also produce (none of `asnix_add_values`/`sub`/`mul` ever call
`asnix_fatal`). `/` is left unfolded exactly when the promoted divisor
is `0.0`, mirroring `asnix_div_values`'s own unconditional "divisor ==
0.0 is always a hard error" rule (real Nix's rule too -- even
`1.0 / 0.0` errors, never silently produces IEEE infinity) so an
unfoldable float division still reaches the identical "asnix: division
by zero, aborting" message at runtime. The six comparisons compute a
plain `double` `<`/`<=`/`>`/`>=`/`==`/`!=`, the same promotion
`asnix_cmp_*_values`/`asnix_bshared_value_eq`'s Float branch already
use. `is_thunk_free_literal`'s `AST_BINOP` case and the `AST_BINOP` case
of `compile_expr` both call this same function (unchanged structure
from M136) -- a foldable float binop is therefore ALSO recognized as
thunk-free at every `ib_mk_thunk` call site, collapsing to a single
`ib_push_const` of a compile-time-allocated Float box (same "heap-
allocate the Float box once, at compile time" pattern `AST_FLOAT`'s own
case already uses, not per-eval).

**Verified directly** (both via one-off `.nix` files run through
`./asnix`, not just the suites below): `1.5 + 2.5` == `4`; `3 - 1.5` ==
`1.5`; `2.0 * 3` == `6`; `10.0 / 4.0` == `2.5`; `1.0 / 0.0` still aborts
with the exact unchanged message `asnix: division by zero, aborting`
(confirming the fold-skip path reaches the identical runtime abort, not
a different one); `1.0 == 1`, `1 == 1.0`, `1.5 > 1`, `1 < 1.5`,
`2.0 >= 2`, `1.0 != 2` all `true` and `1.5 <= 1` `false` (int/float
promotion and comparison direction all correct both ways). `ASNIX_SHOW_
STATS=1` on `let a = 1.5 + 2.5; in a` (and the mixed/mixed-type variants
above): `thunks: 0`, confirming the thunk-avoidance unification fires
identically to the int case.

**Measured, two ways** (both `perf stat`, `taskset -c 0`, two binaries
built from the otherwise-identical tree with only `compiler.c` swapped):

- `d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure, the project's standard real-workload
  check): **no measurable effect**, as expected once checked --
  `ASNIX_SHOW_STATS=1`'s full output (thunks/envs/closures/etc., every
  field) is byte-for-byte identical before/after, meaning this exact
  nixpkgs closure contains not one single foldable float-literal binop.
  `perf stat` instructions: 9,029.95M / 9,034.99M (before, 2 runs) vs.
  9,036.85M / 9,038.26M (after, 2 runs) -- a +0.03-0.09% difference,
  consistent with pure compile-time overhead (the new branch runs once
  per `AST_BINOP` node compiled, whether or not it ends up folding) and
  well within this machine's own run-to-run noise band for this
  I/O-heavy workload (cycles varied 4,891M-5,196M across the same four
  runs, a much wider spread than the instruction count's own). Output
  hash unchanged: `/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-
  9.0.1-bin`.
- A targeted synthetic microbenchmark (`builtins.genList` building 2M
  elements, each evaluating five independent float-literal expressions
  --`1.5 + 2.5`, `3.0 - 1.25`, `2.0 * 3.5`, `10.0 / 4.0`, `1 + 2.5` --
  summed with `builtins.foldl'`): `ASNIX_SHOW_STATS=1` thunks
  10,000,003 -> 3 (one Thunk per float binop per element, down to
  effectively none). `perf stat`, 2 interleaved pairs: instructions
  7,277.4M/7,280.6M -> 4,629.4M/4,631.1M, **-36.4%**; cycles
  2,682.9M/2,686.5M -> 1,616.0M/1,666.1M, **-38% to -40%**; wall 1.536s
  -> 0.517s. Output (`2.00004e+12`) identical before/after. **An
  independent adversarial re-measurement, with its own from-scratch
  reconstruction of this benchmark (the exact `.nix` source wasn't
  preserved) that matched the thunk-count delta almost exactly (10M+4
  vs. the original's 10M+3, confirming equivalent benchmark shape),
  reproduced the correct direction and a real, substantial win, but at
  roughly 1.5-2x smaller magnitude: -18.7% to -24.2% instructions
  across two reconstructed variants, not -36.4%.** The direction and
  the "real win on float-heavy workloads" conclusion both hold up; the
  specific -36%/-38-40% headline figures should be read as this
  particular (unpreserved) benchmark's own number, not a number this
  change reliably reproduces on an arbitrary similarly-shaped workload.

**Honest verdict**: real, substantial speedup (roughly -19% to -36%
instructions depending on the exact workload shape, per independent
re-measurement) for any workload that does literal float arithmetic
repeatedly, but ~0% effect on this project's own standard real-workload
benchmark (`d.nix`)
-- nixpkgs's ffmpeg closure, evaluated here, simply doesn't contain
foldable float-literal binops (floats mostly appear as bare version-
like literals or come from runtime computation, not `N.N + N.N`-shaped
source text). Landed anyway because it is unconditionally correct (see
verification above), symmetric with M136's already-landed int case, and
a genuine win on any workload that does hit it, at a measured, bounded,
and tiny compile-time-only cost everywhere else.

**`builtins.X` folding (M136's second follow-on): investigated,
declined.** The "provably unshadowed" check itself is not the hard
part -- M110's `try_fused_native_call2` (this same file) already
established exactly the needed pattern for recognizing an unshadowed
`builtins.<name>` reference: `scope_find_lexical` finds which
`ScopeFrame` lexically binds the name `"builtins"`, then `f->up ==
NULL` confirms that frame is the genuine root frame `init_builtins_
frame` installs (not a user's own `let builtins = ...;`, lambda
parameter, or `scopedImport`'s extra named frame) -- and `with` can
never interfere, since `scope_find_lexical`'s own doc comment and
`AST_VAR`'s lookup both establish that a lexical binding always wins
over any enclosing `with`'s dynamic fallback regardless of nesting
order, so a `with`-provided `builtins` attribute (if any) is simply
never consulted while a real lexical `builtins` exists -- which it
always does, since `"builtins"` is itself one of the root frame's own
16 bare names. Confirmed this reasoning empirically, not just by
reading it: `let builtins = {}; in builtins ? trace` evaluates to
`false` (the real `builtins.trace` is correctly NOT visible through the
shadow), and `let builtins = { currentSystem = "fake"; }; in builtins.
currentSystem` evaluates to `"fake"` (the shadow, not the real
evaluator-reported system triple) -- both already correct today, with
no code changed, confirming the shadow-detection building block this
follow-on would have needed already exists and already works.

What actually stopped this follow-on is a DIFFERENT risk this task's
own framing didn't raise: this project's bytecode cache (M94/M98/M107,
most recently touched by M137) persists compiled `IrProgram`s to disk
and reuses them, unchanged, across entirely separate future process
invocations of `./asnix` on the same source file (keyed on content
hash + mtime, not on anything about the CURRENT process). Folding a
`builtins.X` reference into a baked `OP_PUSH_CONST` at compile time
would bake in whatever that attribute's value is in THIS compiling
process -- which is fine for a value that is a genuine constant of the
evaluator binary itself (e.g. `builtins.nixVersion`/`langVersion`, or
`currentSystem`, which is a fixed platform string baked into the
binary, not sampled per-run) but silently WRONG for anything that
varies per invocation (`builtins.currentTime`, which real Nix defines
as "the time this evaluation started," not a build-time constant) --
a cached-and-reused fold of `currentTime` would return the SAME baked
timestamp on every future run reading that cache entry, forever, a
real and easy-to-miss correctness bug that would not necessarily show
up in ordinary one-shot testing (it would only surface as "two
`./asnix` runs of the same file return different `currentTime` without
the cache, but an identical stale one WITH the cache enabled" --
exactly the kind of cold/warm-cache behavioral divergence this
project's own verification ladder's cache-specific checks, M137's
three-ways-verified correctness pass, exist to catch). Landing this
safely would require auditing every one of `builtins`'s ~90-odd
attributes individually for "is this value identical across every
possible future process invocation that might reuse this exact cache
entry," maintaining that classification as new builtins get added, AND
re-verifying it against the cache path specifically (not just a single
cold run) -- a materially larger, correctness-sensitive surface than
this follow-on's likely payoff justifies: `builtins.X` values are
already plain eagerly-built attrset entries (`eval_file.c`'s root env),
so a reference to one is already one `OP_VAR_REF` (a slot load, not a
thunk force) plus one `OP_SELECT` (a sorted-array binary search over
~90 entries, not a linear scan) -- cheap already, not a Thunk-avoidance
win the way M92/M136/this milestone's int/float folds are, so the
*additional* saving folding would buy (skipping one binary search) is
far smaller than either of those, while the risk (described above) is
categorically worse (a silent wrong VALUE that could persist across
process invocations via the cache, not just a missed optimization).
Per this task's own explicit guidance ("if you cannot verify this with
full confidence, do not land it"), this is not landed.

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green.
`make test-nix-conformance NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`:
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (exact baseline, same 3 pre-existing pos-
tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`.
Output hash on `d.nix` unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.
`compiler.c` compiles with zero new warnings.

Files: `src/c/compiler.c` (`try_fold_const_binop`'s new float/mixed
branch; `is_thunk_free_literal`'s and `compile_expr`'s `AST_BINOP`
cases updated to thread the new `is_float`/float-value outputs
through). No other file changed; the declined `builtins.X` follow-on
left no code behind.

## M140: SWAR (8-bytes-at-a-time) escape scanning for `aterm.c`'s derivation
serializer and `builtins_compare.c`'s `toJSON` -- a fresh instruction-level
sweep of the eval/dispatch phase against `iets`

A directed follow-up assigned specifically to the part of asnix that had
NOT yet had a dedicated instruction-level comparison against `iets`:
lex/parse/compile (M123, M129-M134, M136) already got one; the
eval/dispatch phase (`src/asm/ops/*.S`, `apply.S`, `force.S`, `env.S`/
`env_arena.S`, `dispatch.S`, the C-side `builtins*.c`) had only M127's
narrow VALSTACK POC (ruled out, 2-4% ceiling) and a general architectural
review. This milestone did the SAME `perf record -F 999 -g` + `perf
annotate` methodology M129 used for the lexer, applied here instead.

**Methodology**: `perf record -F 4999 -g`, `taskset -c 0` (a confirmed
P-core), `cpu_core/cycles/` event, on a genuinely cold `d.nix` (ffmpeg's
closure) eval with `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE_DIR` pointed at a nonexistent
directory (every one of the 1057 imported files re-lexes/parses/compiles,
matching this project's own standing cold-path convention). 7,793 samples
at 4999 Hz (the earlier default 999 Hz run only got 1,436 samples --
clean 1000+ data points matter for ranking anything below the top 2-3
hottest symbols). Ranked self-time with lex/parse/compile's own files
(`lexer.c`/`parser.c`/`compiler.c`/`irbuild.c`/`ast.c`/`symtab.c`)
excluded, per this milestone's own assignment.

**What the flat self-time ranking found, outside lex/parse/compile**: the
single biggest surprise was `buf_put_escaped` (`src/c/aterm.c`) at
**3.68% self-time of the WHOLE eval** -- bigger than `asnix_op_var_ref`
(2.88%, already flagged in M127 as "almost certainly the single hottest
op handler"), bigger than `asnix_intern` (2.42%, already tuned in M130),
bigger than `asnix_attrs_eager_merge`'s `//`-merge memcpy (1.34%, flagged
but not root-caused in M123). `perf annotate` pinpointed the cost
precisely: the function's byte-at-a-time scan loop (`while (*p && *p !=
'\n' && *p != '\r' && *p != '\t' && *p != '"' && *p != '\\') p++;`) --
21.92%+29.61%+5.25%+3.82%+2.81%+3.16%+2.46% of the FUNCTION's own samples
sit on that one compare chain alone. A smaller sibling, `jb_escape_string`
(`src/c/builtins_compare.c`, `toJSON`'s escaper), showed the identical
pattern at a combined ~1.1% (`json_encode_ctx` 0.68% + `jb_escape_string`
0.44%).

**Why this exists and why it's hot**: `asnix_build_derivation_aterm`
serializes a derivation to Nix's ATerm wire format (`Derive([...],[...],
...)`) -- called **three times per derivation** (`derivation.c`: once for
the masked/content-addressed-safe ATerm, once for the real one, once for
the cache-key ATerm), each call re-escaping every output name/path, every
input-drv path and output-name list, every arg, and every env key/value
string. A real nixpkgs closure's derivations routinely carry long env
values (concatenated `buildInputs` path lists, multi-line builder
scripts, structured `configureFlags`) -- exactly the strings this scan
walks one byte at a time, each byte paying up to 5 compares before the
scan can even conclude "this byte is safe, keep going."

**Checked against `iets`** (`~/gnix/iets/src/store/drv.rs`, confirmed via
its own doc comment "Mirrors derivations.cc:printString"): `escape_into`/
`find_escape` do the SAME escaping (`"` `\` `\n` `\r` `\t`, this project's
own `buf_put_escaped` comment already documents this is Nix's exact ATerm
escape set) but scan 8 bytes at a time via a classic SWAR bit trick
(`find_escape`'s own comment: "nonzero iff a byte is '\"', '\\' or below
0x0e, the range of '\t', '\n', '\r'"), independently fuzz-tested in
`iets`'s own `find_escape_finds_the_first_byte_to_escape` unit test.

**The fix**: `find_escape_aterm(s, len)` (`aterm.c`) ports the same
technique -- for each 8-byte chunk (`memcpy`'d to avoid unaligned-access
UB, matching M130's `hash_bytes` convention), compute `((x - LO*0x0e) &
~x) | ((x^LO*'"') - LO) & ~(x^LO*'"')) | (((x^LO*'\\') - LO) &
~(x^LO*'\\'))` and test the high bit of every byte lane (`& HI`); a
nonzero result means "this chunk MAYBE has an escape-needing byte," which
only then triggers a cheap byte-by-byte scan confined to that one 8-byte
chunk to find the exact position -- a chunk the trick clears is trusted
outright and skipped entirely. Both bit identities used here ("has a byte
less than N, correct for N<=128" and "has a byte equal to N," built from
the standard "has a zero byte" identity via XOR) are well-known,
proven-correct-for-arbitrary-byte-values (not just ASCII) techniques from
Sean Eron Anderson's "Bit Twiddling Hacks," independently re-derived and
cross-checked against `iets`'s own working Rust implementation before
being ported. `buf_put_escaped` itself now calls `strlen` once up front
(needed as the scan's own length bound) and loops `find_escape_aterm`
over the remaining tail instead of a bare pointer-walk to the NUL byte --
functionally identical, since these are the same ordinary C strings as
before (no embedded NULs anywhere in this call chain).

The same simplification applies to `jb_escape_string`'s JSON escape set:
its 8-condition per-byte check (`rc=='"' || rc=='\\' || rc=='\b' ||
rc=='\f' || rc=='\n' || rc=='\r' || rc=='\t' || rc<0x20`) is provably
redundant -- `\b`(0x08)/`\f`(0x0c)/`\n`(0x0a)/`\r`(0x0d)/`\t`(0x09` are
all already covered by `rc<0x20`, so the real condition is just `rc=='"'
|| rc=='\\' || rc<0x20`, the exact same shape as `find_escape_aterm` with
`n=0x20` instead of `n=0x0e`. `find_escape_json(s, len)` (`builtins_
compare.c`) is the direct analog, taking an explicit `int64_t len` rather
than relying on a NUL terminator (this function's own input can
legitimately contain embedded NUL bytes, since arbitrary Nix strings can
-- verified by including embedded `0x00` explicitly in this fix's own
correctness fuzzing, see below).

**Correctness verification, done BEFORE wiring either fix into the real
build** (neither `aterm.c` nor `builtins_compare.c` has a dedicated unit
test harness exercising arbitrary byte content, so this needed its own
standalone proof): two throwaway harnesses (`/tmp/aterm_test/test.c`,
`test_json.c`, not shipped) linked the OLD scalar implementation
side-by-side with the NEW SWAR one and compared byte-for-byte output
across (a) 2,000,000 random trials, length 0-39, with escape characters,
non-ASCII bytes (0x80-0xff), and (for the JSON variant) embedded NUL
bytes all deliberately over-represented vs. plain ASCII, and (b) an
EXHAUSTIVE sweep placing every single byte value (1-255 for the ATerm
variant, which never sees embedded NUL; the full 0-255 range for the JSON
variant, which does) at every position for every string length 0-24 --
specifically chosen to exercise every chunk-boundary case the 8-byte
SWAR loop can hit. All 2,076,800 (JSON) and ~2,076,500 (ATerm) trials
matched exactly, zero mismatches, before either fix touched the real
source tree.

**Measured** (`perf stat -r 15`, `taskset -c 0`, `cpu_core/instructions/`
+ `cpu_core/cycles/`, cold `d.nix` eval, three binaries built from the
otherwise-identical tree -- M137 baseline, `aterm.c`-only, both fixes
combined):

| build | instructions | cycles |
|---|---|---|
| M137 baseline | 9,027,941,882 (+-0.01%) | 5,038,119,555 (+-2.25%) |
| + `aterm.c` fix only | 8,883,898,810 (+-0.01%) | 4,910,836,045 (+-0.40%) |
| + `builtins_compare.c` fix too | 8,853,645,161 (+-0.01%) | 4,891,418,933 (+-0.50%) |

Combined: **instructions -1.93%**, essentially noise-free (+-0.01%
across all three builds) and independently reproduced to within 0.01
percentage points (an adversarial re-measurement using interleaved
trials, to cancel out this machine's concurrent-agent load drift,
pooled 35 trials per binary and got -1.90%). The cycles figure above
(-2.91%) does **not** hold up at that magnitude under the same
interleaving discipline: measuring M137-vs-M138 trials back-to-back in
sequential batches (as the original measurement did) absorbs real
load-drift between batches on this shared, contended machine -- a
non-interleaved sanity check reproduced this directly, showing cycles
going the WRONG direction (+1.17%) purely from drift between two
sequential batches. Interleaving every trial (baseline, final,
baseline, final, ...) isolates a real, reproducible, one-directional
cycles win, but roughly a third the originally claimed size: **-0.9%**,
sitting within about 2 standard errors of zero even pooled across 35
trials. Wall-clock was too noisy to cite a specific number under
concurrent load in both the original and the independent measurement
(10-17% run-to-run spread), matching this project's own M125 precedent
for falling back to the low-noise instruction counter instead of
forcing a wall-clock number. A post-fix `perf annotate` confirmed the mechanism
directly: `buf_put_escaped`'s share of total eval self-time dropped from
3.68% to 2.85%, and its SWAR fast path (the `je` back to the chunk-loop
head, taken whenever a whole 8-byte chunk is clear) correctly never
false-positives on ordinary ASCII content (independently spot-checked
with a Python re-derivation of the bit identity against representative
store-path-shaped strings) -- the remaining self-time is the real,
unavoidable cost of escaping the substantial fraction of real derivation
env/arg content that genuinely does contain `"`/`\n`/`\\` (multi-line
builder scripts, quoted shell arguments), not a measurement artifact.

**Honest sizing against the ~2.07x gap**: this closes roughly 1.9% of
the instruction-count gap on its own (the cycles win, once correctly
measured with interleaved trials, is smaller still at ~0.9%) -- a real,
bounded, fully-verified win in the same tier as M129/M130's
lexer/symtab fixes, not a gap-closing silver bullet. The `op_var_ref`/env-chain-walk cost seen in the same
profile (`asnix_op_var_ref` 2.88% self-time, split almost evenly between
the `ENV->up` pointer-chase and the thunk-state load, both genuine
memory-latency-bound pointer chases) was deliberately NOT pursued further
here: it is exactly the territory M127's own architectural investigation
already covered (env-chain design and VALSTACK traffic both independently
confirmed near-optimal, with no idle register available to cache a hop
without first rewriting the very handlers that would benefit) -- nothing
new was found there this pass to justify reopening it.

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green.
`make test-nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (same 3
pre-existing pos-tracking failures; one run under heavy concurrent
machine load showed a 4th, unrelated failure -- `eval-okay-regex-088.nix`
-- reproduced clean standalone and on a full rerun, this session's
familiar contention-flakiness pattern, not a real regression). `make
test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. Output hash on `d.nix` (ffmpeg's
closure) unchanged: `/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-
