ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`, byte-identical before and after.

Files: `src/c/aterm.c` (`find_escape_aterm`, `buf_put_escaped`), `src/c/
builtins_compare.c` (`find_escape_json`, `jb_escape_string`).

## M141: `Token` shrunk from 56 to 12 bytes, with deferred literal decode -- a from-scratch lexer/parser rewrite, honestly scoped after two prior full attempts at adjacent pieces both regressed

Directed as a genuine, from-scratch rewrite of the lexer and parser,
targeting iets's own `Token` design (`~/gnix/iets/src/syntax/lexer.rs`:
`kind` + `start: u32` + `end: u32`, 12 bytes, no eager int/float decode)
as the single biggest remaining, not-yet-attempted lever M133/M134 flagged
in this area. Two prior full attempts at ADJACENT pieces of this same
design -- "intern identifiers at parse time, carry the `Sym` on the AST
node, replace the compiler's linear-scan scope lookup with a hashmap" and
"fuse lex+parse into one pull-based pass" -- were each built, fully
verified, and measured as real regressions (the first: +1.36% instructions
even after fixing its own two root causes; the second, M135: +3.3%
instructions, landed anyway and still the production path today). Read
both writeups in full before starting this milestone, per this task's own
explicit directive, and designed around both findings rather than
re-attempting either blindly -- see the "what was declined" section below
for exactly how.

**What changed.** `lexer.h`'s `Token` is now exactly:
```c
typedef struct {
    TokKind kind;
    uint32_t start;
    uint32_t end;
} Token;
```
-- `sizeof(Token)` 56 -> 12 (confirmed via a throwaway `sizeof` probe,
matching `~/gnix/iets`'s own `Token` exactly). `start`/`end` are byte
offsets into the one source buffer every token is lexed from, for EVERY
token kind uniformly -- `int_val`/`float_val`/the decoded-buffer `start`
pointer/`len`/`pos`/`istr_has_indentation`/`is_home` are all gone. Every
literal's real value is now computed exactly once, on demand, by whichever
`parser.c` call site builds the `Ast` node that actually needs it, never
eagerly at lex time -- the "defer literal decoding" half of iets's design,
done for every literal kind this lexer produces:

- **Int/float literals**: the lexer still scans to find where the literal
  ends (unchanged grammar, unchanged `scan_float_tail`), but no longer
  calls `strtoll`/`strtod` or mallocs a NUL-terminated copy. `parser.c`'s
  `parse_atom` calls `strtoll(src+start, NULL, 10)` directly for `TOK_INT`
  (already safe unbounded, exactly as the pre-M141 lexer itself already
  did) and a new `asnix_decode_float_literal(src, start, end)` for
  `TOK_FLOAT`, which calls `strtod(src+start, NULL)` UNBOUNDED (no length
  cap, no malloc) -- provably safe because the lexer's own scan already
  found the maximal span the identical float grammar matches at that
  position, so `strtod`, parsing the same grammar, cannot consume anything
  past `end` either (verified directly against the `ERANGE` overflow/
  underflow fixtures this project's own `scan_float_tail_and_parse`
  comment already documented testing against: `1.0e400`, `1.0/0.0`, both
  still abort with their exact original messages).
- **Double-quoted string parts (`TOK_STR_PART`)**: the lexer now scans
  PAST escapes (skipping `\<c>` by 2 bytes) without decoding them, to find
  where the raw span ends -- the whole `ByteBuf` accumulator (`bb_push`/
  `bb_take_copy`) is gone from `lex_dquote_run` entirely. `parser.c`'s
  `parse_dquote_string` calls a new `asnix_decode_dquote_span(src, start,
  end, &out_len)` exactly once per part, mallocing the provable upper
  bound (`end-start`, since every escape only ever shrinks the decoded
  length) and applying the identical `decode_escape_char` rules the old
  eager lexer used -- same total decode work, same bytes out, just
  relocated to the point the `AstStringPart` is actually built.
- **Indented-string parts**: `lex_indented_run` is restructured around the
  same raw-span principle, but needed one real new design decision: the
  pre-M141 lexer's `istr_has_indentation` flag (whether a chunk is real
  content, for `stripIndentation`'s own indentation-counting pass, vs. an
  escape unit, which never counts) was a separate `Token` field with
  nowhere left to live on a 12-byte `Token`. Folded into the KIND tag
  instead -- two new token kinds, `TOK_ISTR_PART` (a raw run of plain
  content, no escapes in it by construction) and `TOK_ISTR_ESC` (exactly
  one `''$`/`'''`/`''\<c>` escape unit's raw 3-4-byte span) -- needing no
  extra `Token` field at all. `TOK_ISTR_PART` needs no decode step
  whatsoever (it's already plain source text -- `parser.c` points
  `RawIndPart.text` straight at `src+start`, a real, additional win over
  the pre-M141 lexer, which malloc'd and copied even this plain-content
  case); `TOK_ISTR_ESC` is decoded by a new `asnix_decode_istr_esc(src,
  start, out, &out_len)`, a direct port of the old `istr_append_escape`'s
  three-way switch, evaluated later instead of eagerly.
- **Paths/URIs/search-paths**: were already raw spans into source (no
  escapes exist in this grammar) -- a trivial pointer-pair-to-offset-pair
  conversion, no behavior change. `TOK_PATH`'s `is_home` flag is gone too;
  the parser derives it with `src[t->start] == '~'` instead (spot-checked
  directly: `let a = ./foo; b = ~/bar; in ...` still resolves `b` through
  the home-path expansion path, confirming the derivation fires correctly).

**A real, documented, narrow behavioral-equivalence edge case, found and
accepted rather than engineered around.** The pre-M141 lexer's indented-
string escape handling MERGED two or more back-to-back escape units
(`''$`/`'''`/`''\<c>`) into one accumulated token (an artifact of its
`ByteBuf`'s "only flush on a category change" logic); M141's rewrite emits
one `TOK_ISTR_ESC` per escape unit, never merged -- deliberately not
replicated, after working through exactly what it would cost
(`stripIndentation`'s own indentation-counting pass never inspects a
non-indentation chunk's text at all, so merging-vs-not never changes
indentation; the final `AstStringPart` list's concatenated VALUE is
likewise unaffected by how many pieces it's split into -- Nix has no way
to observe a string's own internal part count). The ONE place this can
matter: `stripIndentation`'s "drop a trailing line that's empty-or-
spaces-only" check looks only at the literal's OVERALL LAST part, and
splitting shifts which chunk that is for the specific case of two or more
escape units back-to-back at the very end of a literal with no plain
content after them. Checked directly against this project's own full
corpus (806 nix-conformance fixtures, all `tests/e2e/str_indented_*.nix`
fixtures, the `test-nixpkgs-hash` 148-package corpus) for any case shaped
like this -- none found; documented in `lexer.h`'s own `TOK_ISTR_ESC`
comment rather than silently accepted, in case a future real-world file
ever hits it.

**What was declined, and why -- reading, not re-deriving, the two prior
negative findings.**

1. **Symbol-carrying (`Sym` on `Ast` nodes, replacing `compiler.c`'s
   per-occurrence `asnix_intern` calls) -- NOT attempted.** The task's own
   brief flagged this as the natural next step once a fresh `Token`/lexer
   design exists to build it on. Declined anyway, for two independent
   reasons, both already on the record: M133's own ranked-causes table
   (item 6) measured the scope-resolution linear scan this would also
   speed up at only 0.40% self-time on this workload -- a small ceiling
   even before any implementation risk is counted. More importantly, the
   one FULL prior attempt at exactly this (identical scope: intern at
   parse time, carry `Sym` on the AST node, hashmap scope lookup) was
   built, fully correct, fully tested, and STILL measured a net +1.36%
   instruction-count regression on `d.nix` even after finding and fixing
   both of its own named root causes (the `Ast` union's largest-arm growth
   from 80 to 96 bytes, and `BTNode`'s double-interning bug) -- "a smaller
   but still real regression remained, diffuse across the many small
   struct-field-write/malloc-pattern changes spread across a dozen-plus
   call sites, not attributable to any single further-fixable hotspot."
   That diffuse, never-fully-explained residual regression is a load-
   bearing fact this milestone takes seriously rather than assumes away:
   it means the prior attempt's failure was not reducible to "two
   specific bugs," and a second attempt -- even one starting from a
   cleaner `ast.h` built together with the `Sym` design from scratch,
   exactly as this task's own brief suggests -- has no guarantee of
   avoiding the same diffuse cost. Given a sub-1%-of-cycles ceiling and a
   documented history of a correct, careful implementation still losing,
   this stays explicitly flagged as future work, not attempted here.
2. **True single-token-lookahead, no-backing-array fused lexing (iets's
   actual architecture) -- NOT attempted, and not newly blocked by
   anything this milestone did.** `asnix_parse` already lexes on demand
   through a `LexCursor` (M135, landed as the live production path despite
   its own measured regression) -- but that `LexCursor` still owns a
   persistent, lazily-filled backing array (`TokVec`), not iets's "no
   array at all, just the current and next token" design, because
   `find_matching_rbrace`'s `{...}:`-pattern-vs-attrset disambiguation
   needs genuine unbounded forward random access, a hard architectural
   fact M135 already found while implementing it, unchanged by this
   milestone. This matters for HOW to read this milestone's own numbers
   below: shrinking `Token` was applied ON TOP OF the already-fused M135
   `LexCursor`, not as a fresh combination of fusion-plus-shrink from a
   clean two-phase baseline -- the comparison below is "fused-with-56-byte-
   Token" vs. "fused-with-12-byte-Token," the one half of M134's own
   "two things both need to be true for fusion to pay off" framing that
   had never actually been measured in isolation before (M135 only tested
   fusion with the OLD large Token). Worth noting explicitly: M135's own
   root-cause reasoning for its regression (the bounds-check/function-call
   boundary cost is paid once per token ACCESS, independent of `Token`'s
   size, while the array-write-elision benefit scales WITH `Token`'s size)
   predicts that shrinking `Token` should make a hypothetical "add fusion
   on top of a small Token" experiment pay off even LESS than M135's own
   now-smaller-upside attempt, not more -- consistent with leaving fusion
   exactly as M135 left it rather than revisiting that decision here.

**Measured.** Two methodologies, both `perf stat -r 10`, `taskset -c 0`
(the same confirmed P-core every recent milestone pins to), `cpu_core/
instructions/,cpu_core/cycles/` explicit event selection, two full
binaries built from `git archive HEAD` (pre-M141) vs. the working tree
(post-M141) so the ONLY difference is this milestone's own 2-file diff
(`lexer.c`/`lexer.h`) plus `parser.c`'s call-site updates.

*Compile-only harness* (a from-scratch, not-shipped `timeit_compile.c`
linking `libasnix.a` directly, matching M131's own precedent methodology:
loops `asnix_parse`+`asnix_compile`+`asnix_ast_arena_reset` with NO
evaluation at all over the exact 1057 real `.nix` files `d.nix`'s ffmpeg
closure imports, collected fresh via `strace -e trace=openat` -- confirmed

| pair 1: after | 3,738,071,235 (**-5.46%**) | 1,650,221,452 (**-12.80%**) | 0.5152s (**-11.30%**) |
| pair 2: before | 3,954,197,182 | 1,834,471,160 | 0.6800s |
| pair 2: after | 3,737,785,357 (**-5.47%**) | 1,623,304,996 (**-11.51%**) | 0.5883s (**-13.48%**) |

across runs, same as every prior milestone's own lex/parse/compile
numbers) -- a real, repeatable ~5.5% instruction cut and a LARGER ~12%

whenever a change reduces memory TRAFFIC (here: the `TokVec` backing
array shrinks 4.67x, directly cutting cache pressure) rather than just

**Honest reading**: instructions are a hard, reproducible fact -- a

## M142: profiling iets directly (not just reading its source) found AST_ATTRSET's own compile-time binding sort was O(n^2) -- real for pkgs/top-level/all-packages.nix's ~4,280-binding literal

Directed follow-up after a user asked why asnix was still slower than iets
"for the same work," having already ruled out redundant computation (file-
level compile dedup exactly 1:1, identifier interning unchanged at its own
long-established baseline, attrset-union materialization correctly cached).
This milestone took a different, previously-unused approach: profiling
`iets`'s own binary directly with `perf record`/`perf report` (cold,
`--impure --no-cache --workers 1`, same `d.nix` workload), not just reading
its Rust source and inferring. Nobody had done this yet this session --
every prior comparison either profiled asnix alone or compared against
iets's source code.

**What direct profiling of both sides, call-graph-categorized, found**:
asnix's lex+parse+compile subtree is 35.65% of its own total cycles (down
from M123's 43.9% after M129-M141); iets's equivalent (lexer + parser +
`Compiler::expr` + `Interner::intern`/hashmap scope lookup) is only 23.3%
of ITS own total cycles. Converting both to absolute cycles (using each
side's own measured total) shows the front end alone accounts for roughly
55% of the ENTIRE absolute cycle gap between the two evaluators, despite
being only about a third of either evaluator's own total work -- a far
more concentrated, more actionable finding than "lex/parse/compile is
~40% of cycles on both sides," which undersells how disproportionate this
slice of the gap actually is.

**Two specific pieces turned out NOT to explain the disproportion, measured
directly rather than assumed**: identifier interning + scope resolution
costs almost identical RELATIVE shares on both sides (asnix: `asnix_intern`
+ `hash_bytes` + `scope_find_lexical` = 4.08% of its own total cycles;
iets: `Interner::intern` + `HashMap::get_key_value` = 4.16% of its own) --
directly explaining, with hard data for the first time, why the two
separate full attempts at Sym-carrying-AST-plus-hashmap-scope (M133 item
6+7's original flag, and the just-declined M141-adjacent re-attempt) both
regressed: that mechanism was never actually where iets's advantage lived,
on this workload. Raw lexing is also now close to proportionate post-M141
(asnix's `lex_until`: 4.48% of its own total; iets's `next_token`: 4.27%).

**What DID turn out disproportionate, isolated after ruling out the above**:
asnix's `compile_expr` costs 5.44% of its own total cycles; iets's
`Compiler::expr` costs only 2.60% of its own -- more than 2x the relative
share, over 3x in absolute terms. `perf annotate` on `compile_expr`
(address-level, not just function-level) found the reason: two insertion-
sort blocks (`AST_ATTRSET`'s own binding-key sort, by interned symbol id)
account for 47.88% of `compile_expr`'s OWN sampled self-time -- roughly
2.6% of asnix's total process cycles, on this one data structure's compile-
time preparation alone. The code's own comment claimed "n is a source-level
binding count, always tiny" -- false for real nixpkgs:
`pkgs/top-level/all-packages.nix` is confirmed (directly, `grep -c`) to be
a single `rec {}` literal with roughly 4,280 top-level bindings.

**The fix, and an honest account of two failed attempts before landing the
right one** -- all three measured directly on the real `d.nix` eval, not
assumed:
1. First attempt: replace the O(n^2) insertion-sort-by-index with
   `qsort` unconditionally, for every attrset literal regardless of size.
   REGRESSED (+0.65% instructions, interleaved-verified): `qsort`'s per-
   comparison indirect function-pointer call costs more than insertion
   sort's own O(n^2) saves across the overwhelming majority of small
   literals (most attrset literals in real code have a handful of keys,
   where insertion sort's low constant factor wins outright).
2. Second attempt: keep insertion sort for all sizes, but make its own
   comparisons branch-direct (a contiguous `{sym,idx}` pairs array instead
   of the original's `order[]`-then-`syms[]` double indirection), falling
   back to `qsort` only above a size threshold. STILL regressed (+0.24%):
   this version paid an extra `malloc`/`free` pair building the pairs array
   on EVERY call regardless of size, even though insertion sort ran on the
   common small-n path -- the extra allocation alone outweighed the direct-
   comparison saving.
3. Third attempt, landed: a true hybrid -- below `ASNIX_ATTRSET_SORT_
   INSERTION_MAX` (32, chosen as a reasonable threshold matching this
   project's own precedent for small-vs-large thresholds elsewhere, e.g.
   `SCRATCH_VEC`'s cap tuning), run the ORIGINAL insertion-sort algorithm
   on `order[]`/`syms[]` completely unchanged -- byte-for-byte the pre-
   existing code, zero extra allocation, zero extra cost on the common
   path. Above the threshold, call a newly-factored-out `static` helper,
   `sort_attrset_bindings_large`, which builds a `{sym,idx}` pairs array
   and calls `qsort` -- isolated into its own function specifically so the
   rare branch's extra code doesn't grow `compile_expr`'s own size/layout
   (an EARLIER version of this same hybrid, inlined directly into the
   switch statement, measured a small but real regression purely from
   `compile_expr` becoming a larger function -- factoring the rare branch
   into a separate function recovered it).

**A measurement trap hit and corrected during this work, worth recording**:
an early measurement of attempt 3 against a `baseline` number from several
steps earlier in this same session appeared to show a regression. Rebuilding
and re-measuring the TRUE baseline fresh, at the same moment, under the
SAME (contended, multi-agent) machine load, showed the baseline itself had
drifted upward by over 2% since that earlier number was taken -- the
"regression" was comparing against a stale reference point measured under
different load, not a real effect. Properly interleaved (alternating
before/after binaries every single trial, 8 pairs) resolved this cleanly:
a real, consistent, reproducible win. This is the exact load-drift trap
M138's own verification pass already documented and warned about;
repeating it here anyway, and correctly diagnosing it via interleaving
rather than trusting a sequential before/after number, is recorded as its
own lesson.

**Correctness, verified three ways**: (1) a 50-binding literal with
shuffled key order, output compared byte-for-byte against `nix-instantiate
--eval --strict` -- identical. (2) The exact threshold boundary, n=31/32/33
(straddling `ASNIX_ATTRSET_SORT_INSERTION_MAX`), each compared against
`nix-instantiate` -- identical in all three. (3) A genuinely adversarial
worst-case construction (4,280 names first interned in ascending order via
a throwaway literal, then declared in a SEPARATE attrset in fully-reversed
order, forcing insertion sort's true O(n^2) worst case) -- output identical
to `nix-instantiate` both before and after, confirming the fix changes
performance, not behavior.

**Measured, interleaved (8 alternating before/after trials on the real
`d.nix` eval, to cancel load drift)**: instructions -1.99% (8,730.3M ->
8,556.6M, tight variance across all 8 pairs); cycles roughly -3.9% (noisier,
as always on this metric, but one-directional in 3 of 4 pairs and flat,
not reversed, on the fourth). On the isolated adversarial worst-case
construction specifically: instructions 132,250,811 -> 43,590,543, a 67%
reduction -- confirming the complexity fix delivers exactly the kind of
win the diagnosis predicted when the pathological shape is actually hit,
not just in the diffuse real-workload average.

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green.
`make test-nix-conformance NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`:
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (exact baseline, same 3 pre-existing pos-
tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. Output
hash on `d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.
`compiler.c` compiles with zero new warnings.

Files: `src/c/compiler.c` only (`sort_syms`'s own call sites, lambda
formals, were already genuinely tiny and left untouched; only
`AST_ATTRSET`'s separate, previously-undiagnosed binding-key sort changed).

## M143: a pattern-string-keyed cache for `builtins.match`/`builtins.split`'s compiled regexes -- both glibc's `regex_t` and the custom ERE engine's own compiled form, ported directly from iets's own design

Investigated a specific candidate from a cross-evaluator profiling pass:
`src/c/builtins_regex.c` called glibc's `regcomp` (`REG_EXTENDED`)
unconditionally on every `match`/`split` call, with no pattern-keyed cache
anywhere in this file or `regex_engine.c` (confirmed via a targeted grep,
zero hits for `cache`/`CACHE`) -- `iets/src/builtins/text/mod.rs`, by
contrast, has a thread-local `REGEX_CACHE: RefCell<HashMap<Vec<u8>,
Rc<CompiledRegex>>>`, so a repeated pattern string is compiled exactly
once per process there. The profiling pass's own estimate (`perf record
-F 4999 -g`, cold `d.nix`): asnix's regex-family self-time summed to
1.39% of its own total cycles vs. iets's 0.30% of its own, a ceiling
estimate of ~57.7M cycles / ~2.78% of the total inter-evaluator cycle gap.

**Confirmed the mechanism by reading both sides' actual source** (not
just trusting the profiling pass's numbers): `builtins_regex.c`'s
`compile_or_fatal` (glibc path) and the two direct `asnix_regex_compile`
call sites (the bracket-extension "needs custom engine" bypass, and
`groups_to_list_recomputed`'s per-match capture-group recompute) all ran
unconditionally, every call, with no memoization. One thing the
profiling pass's own framing underweighted, found only by reading the
actual call sites: `groups_to_list_recomputed` is called once per MATCH
inside `split`'s loop, not once per `split` CALL -- so an N-match
`split` on a capturing pattern was previously recompiling the custom
engine's own hand-rolled parser N times for the exact same pattern
string, not just once. `split2_impl`'s own capture-recompute decision
(the `nsub > 0 && slen <= ASNIX_REGEX_CUSTOM_MAX_SPAN` branch) ALSO
separately called `asnix_regex_compile` a second time even within a
single call that had already compiled the identical pattern once via
`compile_or_fatal`'s glibc path moments earlier.

**The fix**: a pattern-string-keyed cache, `RegexCacheEntry`, holding
both compiled forms per distinct pattern -- glibc's `regex_t` (`have_
glibc`/`glibc_re`, plus `glibc_bad`/`glibc_err` if `regcomp` itself
rejected the pattern) and the custom engine's `AsnixCustomRegex`
(`custom_attempted`/`custom_re`/`custom_nsub`), plus the two pattern-text
pre-scans (`pattern_rejected_by_real_nix`, `asnix_regex_needs_custom_
engine`) computed once at insert time instead of on every call/branch.
Looked up via the same open-addressed, linear-probe hash-index technique
`eval_file.c`'s `import_cache_find`/`import_cache_insert` already uses
(a parallel `size_t` index array over a separate `RegexCacheEntry*`
array, grown/rehashed at 75% load factor before each insert, same word-
at-a-time hash mixing as `import_cache_hash`/`symtab.c`'s `hash_bytes`,
M130). `asnix_prim_match2_impl`/`split2_impl` resolve (or create) the
pattern's cache entry once, up front, via `regex_cache_get`, and pass it
down into `groups_to_list_recomputed` so the per-match recompute path
reuses the SAME compiled custom-engine form across every match in one
`split` call, not just across separate calls. Entries are never evicted
or freed for the life of the process -- the same unbounded-per-process
tradeoff iets's own `REGEX_CACHE` already makes; real nixpkgs calls
`match`/`split` with a small, heavily-repeated set of literal patterns
(`lib.versions`-style version-parsing helpers) across thousands of
packages in one closure, so the number of DISTINCT patterns is small
relative to how many times each is called.

**Correctness around the fatal-on-bad-pattern path**: a pattern
`pattern_rejected_by_real_nix` or `regcomp` itself rejects still goes
fatal on the FIRST call, exactly as before (both checks are pure,
deterministic functions of the pattern bytes, so computing them once at
insert time instead of per-call/per-branch changes nothing observable).
The cache entry also stores the rejection/failure so a REPEATED lookup of
an already-known-bad entry would replay the identical fatal reason
without re-running `regcomp` -- in practice this branch is unreachable
within a single process today, since `asnix_bshared_fatal` calls `exit(1)`
unconditionally and immediately, so there is never a second lookup of a
bad entry before the process has already terminated; kept anyway as
cheap, correctly-inert defensive symmetry with the valid-pattern path,
documented as such in `regex_cache_ensure_glibc`'s own comment rather than
left as an unexplained dead branch.

**Correctness, verified three ways**: (1) the full verification ladder,
unchanged baselines (below). (2) Four new targeted e2e fixtures added to
`tests/e2e/` specifically exercising cache-reuse correctness, not just
performance: `m143_regex_cache_repeated_pattern` (same pattern, three
different subjects via `map`, checking the glibc `regex_t`/`nsub` cached
from the FIRST call still produces correct per-call results for later,
different subjects); `m143_regex_cache_split_many_matches` (one `split`
call, pattern `"([a-c])"` against a 12-character subject producing SIX
matches, stressing `groups_to_list_recomputed`'s now-shared custom-engine
form across repeated matches within a single call); `m143_regex_cache_
match_then_split_shared_entry` (the SAME pattern string used first via
`match`, then via `split`, confirming the two different primops correctly
share one cache entry); `m143_regex_cache_custom_engine_route` (a bracket-
extension pattern, `"[[:alpha:]]+"`, forcing the needs-custom-engine
bypass route, reused across three subjects via `map`). (3) Output on all
four cross-checked by hand against POSIX ERE semantics before trusting
the binary's own answer, then additionally diffed byte-for-byte against
the UNMODIFIED pre-M143 binary on the identical five probe expressions
(including the three above) -- identical in every case, confirming the
cache changes performance, not behavior.

**Measured, interleaved (7 alternating before/after trials on the real
`d.nix` eval, `taskset -c 0`, `cpu_core/instructions/`+`cpu_core/cycles/`,
to cancel this shared machine's load drift)**: instructions -3.63%
(8,365.4M -> 8,061.7M average across all 7 pairs, B consistently lower
than A in all 7); cycles -5.9% to -6.6% depending on which subset of
pairs is averaged (noisier, as always on this metric, but B was lower
than A in all 7/7 pairs, never reversed). This is notably larger than
the profiling pass's own ~2.78%-of-gap ceiling estimate -- expected, since
that estimate only measured the top-level `compile_or_fatal`/`asnix_regex_
compile` call sites' own aggregate self-time, not the specific fact that
`groups_to_list_recomputed`'s per-match recompile inside `split` was
paying the SAME cost multiple times within a single call on any
capturing, multi-match pattern (confirmed directly via `perf report` on
both before/after `perf record` captures: `build_trtable` collapsed from
0.60% to 0.02% of total self-time, `re_compile_internal` 0.31% -> 0.02%,
`re_compile_fastmap_iter`/`free_dfa_content`/`re_dfa_add_node`/`asnix_
regex_needs_custom_engine` all present before and absent after; the new
`regex_cache_find`/`regex_cache_get`/`regex_cache_hash` lookup machinery
itself costs at most 0.05% of total self-time, confirming the cache
lookup is cheap relative to what it replaces).

**Verified**: `make test`/`test-e2e` (including the 4 new fixtures)/
`test-nix-conformance NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance` all green
-- `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`, exact baseline, same 3 pre-existing pos-
tracking failures. `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. Output on
`d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged: `/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-
ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`. `builtins_regex.c` compiles with zero new warnings
(the one pre-existing `/*`-within-comment warning in `regex_engine.h` is
unrelated and unchanged).

Files: `src/c/builtins_regex.c` only (`regex_engine.c`/`.h` untouched --
`asnix_regex_compile`/`asnix_regex_needs_custom_engine`'s own signatures
and behavior are unchanged, just called at most once per distinct
pattern instead of once per call/match); four new fixtures under
`tests/e2e/`.

## M144: `asnix_prim_derivation`'s own fixed-size scratch arrays pooled by recursion depth instead of malloc'd/free'd on every single derivation

A profiling pass against iets's mimalloc hypothesized that glibc's
ptmalloc (`_int_malloc`/`_int_realloc`/`unlink_chunk`/`cfree`) costs asnix
roughly 2x the relative self-time share, and ~3.6x the absolute cycles,
that mimalloc costs iets -- estimated (via `perf record`'s own
self-time-plus-whole-call-stack accounting, since `kptr_restrict=1` on
this shared machine hides the actual kernel routines underneath) at
~13.66% of asnix's own cycles vs. iets's ~6.85%, a ~463.5M-cycle (~22.4%
of the whole asnix-vs-iets gap) contribution if true. The hypothesis
named several call sites spanning the whole C tree (`string_context.c`'s
`dup_cstr`, `aterm.c`'s `buf_grow`, `derivation.c`'s many `malloc`'d
per-derivation tables, `builtins_compare.c`'s growable `Buf`/order
arrays) as the likely sources, but -- because `kptr_restrict=1` also
defeats call-graph attribution past the syscall boundary -- could not
rank which one actually drove the volume. This milestone reads
`derivation.c` directly to find out.

**What's actually there.** `asnix_prim_derivation` (the `derivation {}`
builtin -- called once per derivation forced, and a real nixpkgs eval
forces thousands) used to `malloc` SEVEN fixed-size scratch arrays on
every single call and `free` all seven again before returning:
`group_paths`/`group_outs`/`group_nouts` (grouping referenced input
derivations by `drv_path`), `group_order` (a sort-index array over the
same), `masked_input_drvs`/`real_input_drvs`/`masked_hash_hex` (the
masked- and real-ATerm-pass input-derivation lists), all sized
`ASNIX_DRV_MAX_INPUT_DRVS` (1024) -- plus `drv_refs`, sized dynamically
per call. `group_outs` alone is `1024 * ASNIX_DRV_MAX_OUTPUTS *
sizeof(char *)` = 131,072 bytes -- exactly glibc's default
`mmap_threshold` (128 KiB) -- so that ONE same-sized allocation went
through a real `mmap`/`munmap` syscall round-trip, not just ptmalloc's
ordinary bin machinery, on every derivation. This exactly matches the
profiling pass's own suspicion that hidden kernel-side time (page
faults, `mmap`/`munmap`) was being charged to malloc's name.

Why heap-, not stack-allocated in the first place (M74): forcing one
derivation's own attribute values can recursively force a nested
`derivation {}` call several levels deep in nixpkgs's own dependency
graph -- stack-allocating 1024-entry arrays per level overflowed the
real stack chasing `d.nix` once already. But the recursion is a plain,
synchronous call stack: a call at depth D always fully returns before
another call at the SAME depth D starts. That makes a small pool of
these buffer sets, indexed by recursion depth and allocated once (the
FIRST time each depth is ever reached) instead of once per call, safe
and correct -- real nixpkgs dependency chains are shallow, so this
allocates these buffers a handful of times total for the whole eval
instead of once per derivation. Implemented as `DrvScratchFrame` / a
`g_drv_scratch_frames` array indexed by `g_drv_scratch_depth`
(incremented/decremented across `drv_scratch_acquire`/`_release`, which
bracket the single return path), following this file's own established
"grow a cache, never shrink it" convention (`g_masked_hash_cache`/
`g_drv_outputs_cache`/`g_drv_closure_cache`, all above this in the same
file). `drv_refs` (whose size varies per call, since `refs.nsrcs` isn't
bounded by `ASNIX_DRV_MAX_INPUT_DRVS`) is pooled the same way with a
grow-never-shrink capacity per frame.

**Correctness of the pooling itself**: no call in `asnix_prim_derivation`
between the acquire point and the single return path forces/coerces any
`Value` (confirmed by reading that whole span -- only cache lookups,
`sha256_or_die`, `snprintf`, `qsort`), so recursion genuinely cannot
happen while a frame is held, which is the one invariant the whole
scheme depends on.

**Verified correctness**: added `tests/e2e/m143_derivation_scratch_reuse.nix`
-- a 3-level derivation chain (`top` -> `mid1`/`mid2`, each with TWO
distinct input derivations -> `x1`/`x2`/`x3`) specifically shaped to
exercise (a) real recursion depth 0/1/2, (b) SIBLING reuse of the SAME
depth-1 pool frame across two sequential, non-nested calls (`mid1`
fully returns before `mid2` is forced) with different-but-overlapping
(`x2` shared) group contents each time, and (c) `ngroups > 1` so
`group_paths`/`group_outs`/`group_order` are exercised past index 0 --
output confirmed byte-identical to real `nix-instantiate --eval
--strict` on the same expression. `make test`/`test-e2e`/
`test-conformance` all green. `make test-nix-conformance
NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`
(exact baseline). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. `./asnix
d.nix` unchanged: `/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.

**Measured, interleaved (16 alternating before/after trials total, two
separate batches of 6 and 10, on the real `d.nix` eval, `taskset -c 0`
pinned, `cpu_core/instructions/,cpu_core/cycles/`, to cancel this shared
machine's load drift)**: instructions -0.22% (8,362.4M -> 8,343.8M,
consistent in direction across EVERY SINGLE one of the 16 trials,
~18-25M fewer every time -- the cleanest possible signal that the
fix removes real, fixed per-call work); cycles -1.15% on average
(4,882.5M -> 4,826.5M), directionally consistent across both batches
but noisier trial-to-trial than instructions (as this session's own
established measurement discipline predicts for cycles on a shared,
contended machine) -- real and positive, but modest.

**Honest verdict on the hypothesis**: confirmed real, but only a SMALL
slice of the ~22.4%/463.5M-cycle figure the profiling pass estimated
for the whole ptmalloc-vs-mimalloc gap. This milestone's fix removes
exactly the fixed-size, same-shape-every-time malloc/free churn for ONE
named call site (`derivation.c`'s own `ASNIX_DRV_MAX_INPUT_DRVS`-sized
scratch arrays) -- real, measured (~0.22% instructions / ~1.15% cycles
on the whole eval), but far short of even half the hypothesized total.
The other named call sites in the original hypothesis were deliberately
NOT touched this session and remain open:
- `derivation.c`'s own `InputRefSet` (`input_ref_add_built`/
  `input_ref_add_src`) -- an UNBOUNDED, per-referenced-(drv,output)-pair
  `dup_cstr` (one `malloc` per entry, never freed -- a genuine, if
  small, per-call leak, not just transient churn) plus two independently
  growable open-addressing index tables, scaling with the total number
  of references across the WHOLE eval (likely far larger in aggregate
  than the sum of the fixed 1024-sized arrays this milestone pooled,
  since a real nixpkgs closure's total (drv,output) reference count is
  easily in the hundreds of thousands). The most promising next
  candidate by raw volume, not attempted here for lack of session time
  to design and verify a pooling/arena scheme for it specifically.
- `string_context.c`'s `dup_cstr`, `aterm.c`'s `buf_grow` (realloc-
  doubling from a 256-byte start), and `builtins_compare.c`'s growable
  `Buf`/order arrays -- all named in the original hypothesis, all still
  unexamined.

Files: `src/c/derivation.c` only. Tests:
`tests/e2e/m143_derivation_scratch_reuse.nix` /
`tests/e2e/m143_derivation_scratch_reuse.expected` (new).

## M145: `asnix_attrs_eager_merge`'s `//`-merge inner loop recomputed each entry's address from an index instead of walking a pointer -- a small, real, confirmed fix

A cross-evaluator profiling pass flagged `src/c/attrs_update.c`'s
`asnix_attrs_eager_merge` (the two-pointer sorted-array merge behind `//`,
already named back in M123 as 17.11% of a page-fault profile but never
root-caused) as a candidate: self-time 1.22% of asnix's own total cycles
on `d.nix` vs. iets's `update_attrs` at 0.64% of iets's own total cycles
-- roughly 2x the relative cost, ~3.4x the absolute cost using this
campaign's running totals (~57.6M asnix cycles vs. ~17.0M iets cycles,
~1.96% of the total cycle gap). The task's own hypothesis (batch the
per-entry `memcpy` calls into fewer `memmove`s) did NOT hold up on
inspection: `objdump -d src/c/attrs_update.o` showed GCC already inlines
every 12-byte (`ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE`) `memcpy` into two plain `mov`s (8 bytes
+ 4 bytes) at `-O2` -- there was never a real `call memcpy` in this
function to begin with, so "fewer, larger calls" was not a real lever.

Reading iets's own `update_attrs` (`iets/src/eval/mod.rs:2444`) found it
does the *same* two-pointer merge shape (even an extra first pass just to
count the common-key overlap, which asnix's single-pass-plus-slack-
allocation approach skips), copying each entry via `AttrsObj::init_from`
-> `init` -- a `#[inline]` field-by-field struct write of a 16-byte
`Attr` (bigger than asnix's 12-byte entry). So the algorithm wasn't the
gap; the per-element *codegen* was. Disassembling asnix's own compiled
loop found the real, bounded culprit: the merge's main `while` loop reads
`aentries + i * ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE` and `bentries + j * ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE`
computed fresh from the loop-carried indices `i`/`j`/`k` every iteration
-- GCC could not prove it could turn that into simple pointer increments
(12 isn't a power of 2), so it emitted two extra `lea`s per side, every
iteration, to redo `base + idx*12` from scratch (confirmed directly in
`objdump -d -M intel --disassemble=asnix_attrs_eager_merge`). The two
*tail* loops right below it (the ones copying whatever's left once one
side is exhausted) happened to already compile to plain incrementing
pointers, just not the hottest, fully-interleaved main loop.

**Fix**: rewrote the function to walk explicit `const char *pa`/`pb` and
`char *pout` byte pointers advanced by `ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE` each step
(`pa`/`pb`/`aend`/`bend` replacing `i`/`j`/`acount`/`bcount`), instead of
indices multiplied by the entry stride on every access. Re-disassembling
confirmed the fix: the main loop's address computation for both sides
collapses to the same "plain pointer, no `lea` recompute" shape the tail
loops already had. Entry count for the header write (`k`) is now derived
once at the end from `(pout - out_entries) / ASNIX_ATTR_SIZE` (a single
magic-number division, done once per call, not per entry -- negligible).
Semantics are untouched: same sorted-merge order, same right-biased
duplicate-key handling (`b` wins), same single worst-case allocation.

**Correctness**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green.
`make test-nix-conformance NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`:
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (exact baseline, same 3 pre-existing pos-
tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. Output
hash on `d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`. Added a
new targeted e2e fixture, `tests/e2e/ops_update_large_merge.nix` (two
~28-30-entry attrsets, built so the merge exercises a long a-only run, a
long b-only run, an interleaved run, AND a duplicate-key run, all forcing
the eager-merge path directly since both sides exceed
`ASNIX_UNION_RHS_MAX`/`ASNIX_UNION_LHS_MIN`=16) -- verified both against
hand-computed expected output and that the result's `builtins.attrNames`
count is exactly `acount + bcount - overlap` (90, before trimming the
fixture to fit under `main.c`'s own pre-existing, unrelated 64-entry
top-level-print display cap, which the first version of this fixture
tripped over and which is noted here only so a future session doesn't
mistake that printer limit for a merge bug again).

**Measured, interleaved (10 alternating before/after trials on the real
`d.nix` eval, `taskset -c 2`, `cpu_core/instructions/,cpu_core/cycles/`)**:
instructions dropped in all 10/10 paired trials, mean -13.0M (8,362.8M ->
8,349.8M, -0.156%), a small but completely consistent, deterministic win
(the function's control flow doesn't depend on timing, so this result
doesn't need statistics to trust, just confirmation it's not a fluke --
it isn't). Cycles were, as this whole session has repeatedly found on
this shared contended machine, too noisy to read cleanly even with
interleaving: paired cycle deltas ranged from -370M to +245M trial-to-
trial (dwarfing this function's own ~57.6M-cycle total estimated
contribution), AFTER only "won" 4/10 paired trials on raw cycles. Four
separate `perf record -F 4999 -g` samples (2 before, 2 after,
interleaved) of `asnix_attrs_eager_merge`'s own self-time percentage are
directionally consistent with a real, modest win: before 1.45%/1.34%/
1.59% (mean 1.46%), after 1.28%/1.35%/1.13% (mean 1.25%) -- roughly a
14% relative reduction in this one function's own self-time, consistent
with, but noisier than, the clean instruction-count signal.

**Honest sizing**: this is a genuinely small fix. The task's own
baseline-contribution estimate for this whole function (~1.96% of the
total cycle gap) bounds how much there was to win here even in the best
case, and the measured instruction-count win (-0.156% of the *whole
program's* instructions) is consistent with having captured a real
fraction of that -- a legitimate, low-risk, surgical win, not a
headline one. The bigger items this same profiling pass's sibling
candidates were assigned (lex/parse/compile, symtab/AST representation)
remain the larger levers; this just closes out M123's one still-open
thread on `asnix_attrs_eager_merge` with an actual root cause and fix
instead of leaving it flagged.

Files: `src/c/attrs_update.c` (`asnix_attrs_eager_merge` only --
`make_union_header`, `asnix_attrs_update`, `asnix_attrs_insert_dynamic`
untouched), plus the new `tests/e2e/ops_update_large_merge.nix`/
`.expected` fixture pair.

## M146: mimalloc as a static-link-time process-wide allocator override -- tested for real (not assumed), then adopted

A fresh `perf record -e cpu_core/instructions/,-c 10000,-g` instruction-
sampled profile (NOT the usual `-F`-based time sampling, specifically to
rank where INSTRUCTIONS, not cycles, are spent) categorized asnix's full
~2.97B-instruction gap against `iets` (cold, `--impure --no-cache
--workers 1`, real `d.nix`/ffmpeg eval) and found the allocator family
(glibc's `_int_malloc`/`_int_realloc`/`cfree`/`unlink_chunk`/`calloc`,
charged against `iets`'s own mimalloc) as the single largest named
category: asnix 1,055,398,725 instructions (13.14% of its own total) vs.
`iets`'s 292,372,016 (5.78% of its own) -- a 763,026,709-instruction gap,
~9.5% of asnix's whole-program instruction count if mimalloc eliminated
100% of it (the theoretical ceiling, not expected in practice). This is
the user's own direct, explicit suggestion -- adopt mimalloc as asnix's
allocator -- tested for real before committing to anything, per this
milestone's own explicit two-step mandate.

**Step 1: LD_PRELOAD ceiling check, no code change.** mimalloc was
already present in the local Nix store at two versions (3.1.5, 3.5.1)
plus a 3.5.3 resolved later via the flake's own pinned nixpkgs -- found
via a scoped `find /nix/store -maxdepth 1 -iname "*mimalloc*"`, not an
unscoped filesystem search. `nm -D libmimalloc.so` confirmed it exports
standard-named `malloc`/`free`/`calloc`/`realloc`/`aligned_alloc`/
`posix_memalign` directly (mimalloc's Unix build has override baked in
by default -- confirmed directly, not assumed from documentation alone),
so the plain (non-"-override"-suffixed) shared library intercepts the
full malloc family with no special variant needed. A real gotcha hit and
solved along the way: `LD_PRELOAD=<mimalloc.so> taskset -c 0 perf stat
... ./asnix d.nix` initially FAILED -- `taskset`/`perf` themselves are
dynamically linked against the system's own (older) glibc, and
inheriting `LD_PRELOAD` through the `taskset -> perf -> asnix` exec chain
preloaded mimalloc into `taskset`/`perf` too, which then pulled in the
nix-store-pinned `libpthread.so.0`'s newer glibc-ABI symbol versions
(`GLIBC_ABI_DT_X86_64_PLT`/`GLIBC_ABI_DT_RELR`) that the system loader
resolving `taskset` itself doesn't provide -- a real cross-glibc-version
collision, not a mimalloc bug. Fixed by scoping `LD_PRELOAD` to just the
measured process via `taskset -c 0 perf stat ... env LD_PRELOAD=<path>
./asnix d.nix` (`env`'s own child process is the only one that inherits
the preload; `taskset`/`perf` never see it).

**Measured, interleaved (10 alternating plain/LD_PRELOAD trials, `taskset
-c 0`, `cpu_core/instructions/`+`cpu_core/cycles/`, real `d.nix`/ffmpeg
eval, output hash cross-checked byte-identical on every single trial)**:
instructions 8,032,677,523 (avg) -> 7,311,069,127 (avg), **-8.98%**,
B lower than A in all 10/10 trials, tight variance (every PLAIN trial
within 8,029.7M-8,040.2M, every MIMALLOC trial within 7,309.1M-7,313.3M
-- essentially noise-free, the same "hard, repetition-independent fact"
character this project's measurement culture already established for
instruction counts). Cycles: 4,346,104,737 -> 3,960,946,861 average,
**-8.86%**, noisier trial-to-trial (as always on this shared, contended
machine) but one-directional in every pair. This clears the bar by a
wide margin against the 9.5%-of-total-instructions theoretical ceiling
computed above -- mimalloc captures essentially the ENTIRE allocator-
category gap, not just a fraction of it.

**Step 2: full build integration**, per mimalloc's own documented Unix
override mechanism (checked directly via `nm`, not improvised): on Unix,
simply linking a program against mimalloc's own library (static or
dynamic) is sufficient for a full process-wide override, since its
default build already exports the standard `malloc`/`free`/`calloc`/
`realloc` names rather than only `mi_malloc`-prefixed ones. Chose the
STATIC path (`libmimalloc.a`, not `LD_PRELOAD`/dynamic linking) for the
shipped build: confirmed via `nm libmimalloc.a` that the same standard
names are defined there too, then verified directly that linking it into
`asnix`'s own executable makes `malloc`/`free`/`calloc`/`realloc` resolve
to DEFINED symbols inside `asnix`'s own symbol table (`nm asnix | grep -E
" [tT] (malloc|free|calloc|realloc)$"` -- all 4 present, `T` not `U`) --
this is the real override, happening at normal dynamic-symbol-resolution
time with zero `LD_PRELOAD`/runtime environment-variable dependency, and
zero new dependency on a nix-store path surviving into the running
process (unlike `LD_PRELOAD`, which would need the exact store path kept
alive and re-specified by whoever runs the binary later). Needed no
`mimalloc.h` include, no `mi_malloc` call site, no source change
anywhere in this tree -- the override is 100% a link-step change.

**What changed, concretely**:
- `flake.nix`: added `mimalloc` to the devShell's `packages`, and the
  shellHook now exports `ASNIX_MIMALLOC_LIB="${pkgs.mimalloc}/lib/
  libmimalloc.a"` -- an absolute nix-store path baked in at flake-eval
  time (same convention this file already uses for `ASNIX_LIBCRYPTO_LIB`,
  except that one's a runtime `dlopen` target resolved by `getenv`, while
  this one is a build-time linker input).
- `nix/asnix.nix`: added `mimalloc` to the derivation's inputs and sets
  the same `ASNIX_MIMALLOC_LIB` env var directly on the derivation, so
  `nix build`'s own packaged binary gets the identical override, not just
  interactive `nix develop` sessions.
- `Makefile`: a new `MIMALLOC_LDLIBS` variable, populated only `ifdef
  ASNIX_MIMALLOC_LIB` (so a plain `cc`/`make` run outside the flake's
  devShell -- no env var set -- degrades gracefully to the exact
  pre-existing link command, not a build failure), appended ONLY to the
  final `asnix` executable's own link rule (`$(CC) $(LDFLAGS) -o $@
  $(MAIN_OBJ) -L. -lasnix $(MIMALLOC_LDLIBS)`) -- deliberately NOT
  applied to `irdump` or any `tests/{asm,ir,c}/*` unit-test binary, since
  this is a real-eval-workload speed change, not something the
  correctness-focused test binaries need, keeping the blast radius to
  exactly the one binary real users actually run. `-lpthread` is linked
  alongside (mimalloc's own `pkg-config` metadata lists `-lpthread -lrt
  -latomic` as `Libs.private`; linking confirmed `-lrt`/`-latomic` are
  NOT actually needed on this glibc version -- modern glibc merges
  `librt`'s/`libpthread`'s symbols into `libc` itself -- so only
  `-lpthread` was kept, verified by a clean link with zero undefined-
  symbol errors). The existing `OPT_STAMP` stale-build guard (previously
  keyed on `$(OPT)` alone, to catch switching between `make`/`make
  debug`/`make release` without an explicit `make clean`) now keys on
  `$(EFFECTIVE_OPT)|$(MIMALLOC_LDLIBS)` instead, so switching in or out of
  a devShell that sets `ASNIX_MIMALLOC_LIB` also correctly forces a full
  rebuild+relink rather than silently keeping a stale `asnix` binary built
  under the other configuration.

**Verified, both configurations**:
- WITH `ASNIX_MIMALLOC_LIB` set (`nix develop --command make`): link
  command confirmed to include `.../libmimalloc.a -lpthread`;
  `./asnix d.nix` output byte-identical:
  `/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`; `nm
  asnix` confirms `malloc`/`free`/`calloc`/`realloc` all defined (`T`)
  inside the executable itself.
- WITHOUT it set (plain `make` in an ambient shell that merely happens to
  have `cc` on `PATH`, no nix devShell): link command confirmed to
  `MIMALLOC_LDLIBS` empty, identical to the pre-this-milestone command;
  `./asnix d.nix` output byte-identical; `nm asnix` confirms ZERO locally-
  defined `malloc`/`free`/`calloc`/`realloc` symbols (correctly falling
  back to ordinary dynamic resolution against libc).
- Full ladder (WITH mimalloc linked in, the shipped configuration): `make
  test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green. `make test-nix-
  conformance NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3
  skip=148` (exact baseline, same 3 pre-existing pos-tracking failures).
  `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`, clean on the first attempt.

**Final measured win, on the actual integrated build** (10 interleaved
trials, `taskset -c 0`, `cpu_core/instructions/`+`cpu_core/cycles/`, the
real nix-devShell-built mimalloc-linked `asnix` vs. the same tree built
with `ASNIX_MIMALLOC_LIB` unset): instructions 8,032,677,523 (avg) ->
7,407,413,639 (avg), **-7.79%**, B lower than A in all 10/10 trials
(tightest band: every NO-MIMALLOC trial 8,029.7M-8,040.2M, every MIMALLOC
trial 7,403.6M-7,410.0M); cycles 4,504,481,076 -> 4,221,017,404 average,
**-6.3%**, directionally consistent in 9/10 pairs (the one reversal,
pair 3, sits inside this shared machine's familiar load-drift noise band
-- a single NO-MIMALLOC outlier elsewhere in the same run, pair 4,
5,609M cycles vs. a typical ~4,350M, shows the same contention this
project's whole measurement culture already documents and discounts).
The ~7.8% final figure (vs. step 1's own ~8.98% LD_PRELOAD ceiling check)
is close to, not identical to, the earlier number -- expected, since step
1 used mimalloc 3.5.1 from an ad-hoc store path and this integrated
build resolves the flake's own pinned nixpkgs mimalloc (3.5.3) instead;
both are real, both clear the bar by a wide margin over the 9.5%
theoretical ceiling's own ~82-94% capture rate.

**Honest sizing against the full asnix-vs-iets gap**: this closes
roughly 7.8% of asnix's OWN total instruction count, and (cross-
referencing this session's running gap-accounting convention) a
proportionally similar slice of the full inter-evaluator instruction
gap -- not a silver bullet for the ~1.59x-and-shrinking overall ratio,
but the single largest one-change win landed this campaign, larger than
any individual lex/parse/compile fix (M129-M141) or any other allocator-
adjacent fix (M144's derivation-scratch pooling, ~0.22%). This also
RETIRES M144's own still-open "other named call sites... remain open"
list (`InputRefSet`'s unbounded `dup_cstr`, `string_context.c`'s
`dup_cstr`, `aterm.c`'s `buf_grow`, `builtins_compare.c`'s growable
`Buf`/order arrays) as individually-worth-root-causing follow-ons --
every one of those still goes through `malloc`/`free`/`realloc`, so this
milestone's process-wide override already captures their aggregate cost
too, without needing to find and fix each call site by hand.

**What this does NOT change**: asnix's own hand-written `Value`/`Env`/
`Thunk`/`Closure` arena (`asnix_arena_alloc`, `src/asm/arena.S`) was
already, and remains, entirely separate from `malloc`/`free` -- this
milestone affects only the C-side bookkeeping paths that already went
through the malloc family (parser/AST vectors, derivation/regex/JSON
scratch buffers, the symtab/import-cache/bytecode-cache/regex-cache hash
tables), exactly as scoped in this milestone's own brief.

Files: `flake.nix` (devShell `packages`/`shellHook`), `nix/asnix.nix`
(`mimalloc` input, `ASNIX_MIMALLOC_LIB`), `Makefile` (`MIMALLOC_LDLIBS`,
`asnix`'s link rule, the `OPT_STAMP` key). No `src/` file touched.

## M147: the lexer's keyword lookup called `strlen()` on all 13 `KEYWORDS` entries for every single identifier-shaped token in the source -- fixed by carrying each keyword's length as a compile-time constant

This campaign's instruction-event-sampled profile (`perf record -g -e
cpu_core/instructions/ -c 10000`, `taskset -c 0`, pinned to a confirmed
P-core) had flagged `libc_misc` (`memcmp`/`memmove`/`memset`/`strlen`/
`strcmp`/`memchr`) as a 448,510,508-instruction gap vs. iets, not yet
investigated this campaign. Re-running that same profile on `d.nix` and
walking ordinary userspace call-graphs (`perf report -g graph,...,caller
--symbol-filter=__strlen_avx2`) found `__strlen_avx2` itself at 2.63%
self-time, with the single largest identified call site:

```
asnix_eval_file -> asnix_parse -> parse_expr (x3) ->
  find_matching_rbrace (inlined) -> lexcur_tok_slow -> __strlen_avx2   (0.83%)
```

Chasing that down through `lexcur_tok_slow` -> `lex_until` landed on
`src/c/lexer.c`'s identifier/keyword-classification block (the `ident_start`
case in `lex_until`, immediately below the M138 path/URI-scan guard): for
every identifier-shaped token -- the single most common token shape in any
real Nix file, and nixpkgs has an enormous number of them -- the lookup
loop ran

```c
for (size_t k = 0; k < sizeof(KEYWORDS) / sizeof(KEYWORDS[0]); k++) {
    size_t kwlen = strlen(KEYWORDS[k].kw);
    if (kwlen == len && memcmp(KEYWORDS[k].kw, src + start, len) == 0) { ... }
}
```

`KEYWORDS` is a fixed, compile-time-known 13-entry table of C string
literals (`"let"`, `"in"`, `"if"`, ... `"or"`) -- its lengths never change
at runtime, yet this call re-derived `strlen(KEYWORDS[k].kw)` from the NUL
terminator on *every one of those 13 entries, for every single identifier
token in the whole program*. The exact same class of waste M141's `Token`
shrink and M143's regex cache fixed elsewhere (a runtime length re-derived
from a NUL-terminated string when the real length was knowable up front),
just on a literal table instead of a parsed string.

**Fix**: added a `kwlen` field (`uint8_t`, 13 keywords all fit) to the
`Keyword` struct, populated via a small `KW(lit, kind)` macro that computes
`sizeof(lit) - 1` at compile time (the string literal's own length minus
its NUL), and dropped the runtime `strlen()` call from the lookup loop
entirely -- it now just compares `KEYWORDS[k].kwlen == len`. No change to
`memcmp`'s own cost (unchanged, still does the real byte comparison when
lengths match); this only removes the now-redundant length computation.

**Measured** (interleaved `taskset -c 0 perf stat -e
cpu_core/instructions/,cpu_core/cycles/`, before/after/before/after/
before/after, same `d.nix`, byte-identical output
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin` confirmed
on both binaries before measuring):

| trial | before instructions | after instructions |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8,037,857,775 | 7,832,706,335 |
| 2 | 8,034,579,393 | 7,831,919,845 |
| 3 | 8,032,592,655 | 7,829,700,827 |

Mean before: 8,034,676,608. Mean after: 7,831,442,336. A consistent
-203,234,272 instruction reduction (-2.53% of the whole program's
instructions), reproduced identically on all 3 interleaved pairs (this
workload is deterministic, so trial-to-trial variance here reflects
measurement noise, not real run-to-run variation) -- closing roughly 45%
of this profiling pass's named 448,510,508-instruction `libc_misc` gap
with one bounded, mechanical change. Cycle counts moved in the same
direction but, as usual on this shared machine, noisier
(4,327M/4,418M/4,238M before vs. 4,251M/4,077M/4,243M after).

**Other `libc_misc` leads found but not fixed this milestone** (left for
a follow-on, since each needs a broader signature change to thread a
known length through, not a single bounded edit):
- `asnix_build_derivation_aterm`'s `buf_put_escaped`/`buf_puts` (aterm.c)
  take plain `const char *` and `strlen()` internally, even though every
  caller (`derivation.c`) already holds these strings as length-carrying
  `Value`s before coercing them down to C strings for this function --
  measured at ~0.50% self-time (`__strlen_avx2`) plus a further
  `__memmove_avx_unaligned_erms`/`__strcmp_avx2` share from the same
  function and its neighbor `asnix_collect_input_refs`'s dedup-by-strcmp
  walk (derivation.c). Fixing this means changing
  `AtermOutput`/`AtermInputDrv`/`AtermEnvVar`'s field shapes (or adding a
  parallel `_len` field to each), a wider-blast-radius change than this
  milestone's scope.
- A further `__memmove_avx_unaligned_erms` share (~1.03%) attributes to
  kernel addresses as the immediate "child" of the userspace `memmove`
  frame -- this is page-fault service cost for newly-touched heap pages
  (COW/zero-fill faults during `realloc`/arena growth), misleadingly
  nested under `memmove` in the call graph because the fault happened on
  the very instruction that touched the new page, not an actual callee;
  not actionable at the C-call-site level, and outside what ordinary
  userspace call-graph profiling can attribute further (kptr_restrict
  hides the kernel-internal symbols, as expected -- see this campaign's
  own clarification that this does NOT block userspace-side attribution,
  which is all that was needed here).

**Verification**: `make test`, `make test-e2e`, `make test-conformance`
all pass; `make test-nix-conformance NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`
reproduces the documented baseline exactly (pass=655 fail=3 skip=148);
`make test-nixpkgs-hash` passes (pass=148 fail=0). `./asnix d.nix` output
unchanged byte-for-byte before and after.

Files: `src/c/lexer.c` (`Keyword` struct, `KEYWORDS` table, and the
keyword-lookup loop in `lex_until`'s `ident_start` case only).

## M148: fixing the fresh profile's "0.00% SHA256" symbol-resolution blind spot -- real, confirmed, and a small genuine fix found along the way

A fresh `perf record -e cpu_core/instructions/ -c 10000 -g` profile (the
one behind this campaign's current ranked instruction-gap breakdown:
allocator 763M, libc_misc 448.5M, string_ops 483M) showed asnix's own
SHA256/crypto hashing at exactly 0.00% -- flagged as almost certainly a
symbol-resolution artifact, not a real one-sided gap, since an earlier
profiling pass had found asnix's hashing cost (3.56% of its own cycles)
comparable to iets's (4.40%), both confirmed via `objdump` to already use
hardware SHA-NI (`sha256rnds2`/`sha256msg1`/`sha256msg2`). This session
re-confirms that properly and finds one small, real, previously-invisible
gap along the way.

**Root cause of the blind spot**: `src/c/hash_shim.c` `dlopen`s
`/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcrypto.so.3` (this machine's system
OpenSSL, reached via Tier 2's bare-soname fallback when `ASNIX_LIBCRYPTO_
LIB` isn't set, i.e. whenever asnix isn't run inside `nix develop`) --
and that specific file is `strip`ped (confirmed: `readelf -S` shows no
`.symtab`; no matching entry for its build-id,
`50bbae5166dbdbc281f876ad8e0cc56f362e2954`, exists under `/usr/lib/debug/
.build-id/50/`, and no `-dbgsym` package is installable without root/a
dbgsym apt source on this machine). Critically, `nm -D` shows its
*dynamic* symbol table is intact (5,505 exported symbols, including
`SHA256`/`SHA256_Init`/`SHA256_Update`/`SHA256_Final`) -- so `perf
record --buildid-all` + `perf report` DOES correctly attribute time to
`libcrypto.so.3` as a DSO (2.94%-3.36% self/children of the whole `d.nix`
run, confirmed directly, not 0.00% at the DSO level) and DOES resolve
every *exported* function by name (`OPENSSL_LH_retrieve`, `EVP_MD_free`,
`SHA256_Final`, `CRYPTO_THREAD_read_lock`, etc., all show up correctly).
The actual hot SHA-NI compression routine, though, sits in a large
~0x15E0E-byte stretch of `.text` *past the last exported symbol address*
(`RC4_options` at `0x2f11b0` is the last dynsym entry; the hot region is
`0x306fbe`-`0x30724a`) with zero dynsym coverage at all -- a genuinely
un-exported local/hidden-visibility function, not merely missing debug
info, so `perf` has no symbol to attach those samples to and shows raw
hex addresses instead. This explains the earlier run's "0.00%": the
original profile likely didn't even register the DSO's buildid (no
`--buildid-all`, or a stale `perf buildid-cache`), compounding the local-
symbol gap into a total miss. Confirmed by reproducing: a run with plain
`perf record -g` (no `--buildid-all`) against the same workload shows
the same raw-hex-cluster pattern, and whether the DSO rolls up to "0.00%"
vs. "~3%" in a report is sensitive to exactly this registration step --
consistent with the earlier profile's 0.00% being an artifact of that,
not a real zero.

**Fix for the blind spot**: pointed `ASNIX_LIBCRYPTO_LIB` at the
nixpkgs-resolved, *unstripped* `openssl-3.6.3` build already present in
the local `/nix/store` (`not stripped`, confirmed via `file`) and re-
profiled the identical `d.nix` workload. This fully resolves the hot
region: `sha256_block_data_order_shaext` -- the SHA-NI hardware-
accelerated compression function -- is the single hottest symbol inside
`libcrypto.so.3` at 1.72% of the whole program's instructions, reached
via `SHA256 -> EVP_Q_digest -> EVP_Digest -> sha256_block_data_order_
shaext`, called from `asnix_hash_one -> SHA256() -> ... <- asnix_prim_
derivation`. **This confirms the earlier finding stands**: asnix's
hashing is real SHA-NI-accelerated work, not a hidden gap, and the
"0.00%" was purely the symbol-resolution artifact it was suspected to be.

**The one real thing found along the way**: profiling with the unstripped
library surfaced a cluster of OpenSSL-internal symbols around the
SHA-NI call (`EVP_MD_free`, `EVP_MD_up_ref`, `evp_generic_fetch`,
`evp_md_init_internal`, `ossl_namemap_name2num`, `ossl_lib_ctx_get_data`,
`ossl_ht_get`, `CRYPTO_THREAD_run_once`, `OPENSSL_cleanse`, `ossl_fnv1a_
hash`) that don't belong to actual digest computation -- they're OpenSSL
3.x's EVP provider-fetch machinery. `hash_shim.c`'s header comment
already notes it deliberately uses OpenSSL's *legacy* one-shot wrappers
(`SHA256()` etc., the same API upstream real Nix's own `libutil/hash.cc`
uses) specifically to avoid `EVP_MD_CTX` plumbing -- but OpenSSL 3.x
silently reimplemented those legacy one-shot wrappers as full
`EVP_Digest()` calls under the hood, meaning every single call now pays a
provider-registry fetch/init/free round-trip that doesn't exist in the
older (pre-3.0) implementation `hash_shim.c`'s comment was written
against. This is a real, call-count-proportional (not byte-proportional)
tax, and iets's `sha2` Rust crate (no provider abstraction at all) never
pays anything equivalent.

**Isolated microbenchmark** (`tools/bench_hash_shim.c`, kept in-tree;
also two throwaway `/tmp` harnesses used only for the dlsym-cost and
instruction-count variants, not kept): calls `hash_shim.c`'s own
`asnix_hash_sha256` entry point directly, buffer sizes chosen from real
data, not guessed -- a one-off debug counter temporarily added to
`asnix_hash_sha256` (reverted before this commit, confirmed via `git
diff` showing no residual change to `hash_shim.c`'s old behavior at that
point) found the real `d.nix`/ffmpeg eval makes exactly 34,988 calls to
`asnix_hash_sha256`, averaging 1,649.5 bytes each -- i.e. almost entirely
`derivation.c`'s masked-ATerm hashing (matches real `.drv` text sizes
sampled directly from `/nix/store`, ~2-4KB). `taskset -c 0`-pinned,
interleaved trials at that exact average size (1,000,000 iters/trial, 2
trials each, `cpu_core/instructions/`): one-shot `SHA256()` averaged
7,906.97 instructions/call; the low-level `SHA256_Init`/`_Update`/
`_Final` triplet averaged 4,784.67 instructions/call -- a **3,122.3-
instruction fixed tax per call**, confirmed size-independent (same ~3,100-
instruction gap measured at 2,048 and 4,096 bytes too; at 64 bytes the
same fixed tax is 266.9% of the low-level cost in wall-time terms,
confirming it doesn't scale with input size). A separate isolated check
found `dlsym()`'s own per-call cost (~49-54ns) is not a meaningful
contributor by comparison (hash_shim.c re-`dlsym`s its symbol on every
call, old and new code both; ruled out as the cause).

**Fix landed** (small, bounded, same digest family, verified correctness-
preserving): `src/c/hash_shim.c`'s `asnix_hash_one` now resolves and
calls the classic streaming triplet (`MD5_Init`/`_Update`/`_Final` and
its SHA1/SHA256/SHA512 siblings) instead of the one-shot wrappers,
bypassing the EVP provider-fetch path entirely while computing the exact
same digest. All four streaming-API symbol families confirmed present
via `nm -D` against both this machine's system libcrypto and the
nixpkgs-resolved `openssl-3.6.3`, same discipline M8 used for the
original one-shot symbols. `tests/c/test_hash_shim.c`'s existing oracle
values (independently generated via `md5sum`/`sha1sum`/`sha256sum`/
`openssl dgst -sha512`, covering empty input, embedded-NUL input, and
three ordinary strings per algorithm) all still pass unchanged.

**Correctness**: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green
(including `test_hash_shim`). `make test-nix-conformance
NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`
(exact baseline). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. `d.nix`
output byte-identical before and after:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.

**Measured, interleaved** (5 alternating before/after trials, full real
`d.nix`/ffmpeg eval, `taskset -c 0`, `cpu_core/instructions/,cpu_core/
cycles/`): instructions dropped in all 5/5 paired trials, tight variance
on both sides (<0.1% spread within each side across all 5 runs --
expected, since this code path's control flow doesn't depend on timing).
Mean before 8,028,544,549 instructions, mean after 7,968,271,697 --
**-60,272,852 instructions, -0.751% of the whole program's total**.
Cycles were, as repeatedly found this campaign on this shared contended
machine, too noisy to read cleanly even interleaved (one "after" trial
spiked to 4.94B cycles against a ~4.1-4.3B baseline on both sides);
excluding that one outlier trial, cycles point the same direction
(~0.6% reduction) but this metric needs more trials than time allowed
here to trust on its own -- instructions are the clean, trustworthy
signal, consistent with this whole campaign's stated reason for using
instruction-sampled profiling in the first place.

**Honest sizing**: this is a small, bounded fix (-0.75% of the whole
program's instructions), well below the campaign's three named top-
ranked gaps (allocator 763M/9.5%, libc_misc 448.5M/5.6%, string_ops
483M/6.0%, all as a fraction of the 2,973.6M-instruction gap). It does
NOT change the answer to this task's central question: asnix's hashing,
properly measured, is still fundamentally comparable to iets's (both
genuinely SHA-NI-accelerated), and the "0.00%" was correctly suspected to
be a measurement artifact, not a real one-sided gap -- but about half of
asnix's own total hashing-category instruction budget (extrapolating the
per-call tax across the real workload's 34,988 calls, ~109M of a DSO-
level-estimated ~211M self-instructions) was, until this session,
entirely invisible to every prior profiling pass this campaign ran,
simply because it lived in library-internal provider machinery with a
name nobody had reason to go looking for before the blind spot itself
was investigated.

Files: `src/c/hash_shim.c` (`asnix_hash_one` and the four public
`asnix_hash_{md5,sha1,sha256,sha512}` wrappers -- `asnix_load_libcrypto`,
`asnix_hash_to_hex`, and `hash_shim.h`'s public signatures untouched),
plus the new `tools/bench_hash_shim.c` isolated microbenchmark.

## M149: `compiler.c`'s own `compile_expr` -- the real source of the remaining 763M-instruction allocator gap, not any single runtime call site

A prior task handed off a precise, categorized instruction-gap figure:
glibc's malloc family (`_int_malloc`/`_int_realloc`/`cfree`/`unlink_chunk`/
`calloc`) cost asnix 1,055,398,725 instructions (13.14% of its own total)
vs. iets's mimalloc at 292,372,016 (5.78%) -- a 763,026,709-instruction
gap, the single largest named category in a fresh instruction-sampled
profile, measured AFTER M144 (derivation.c's scratch arrays) and M145
(attrs_update.c's merge loop) had already landed. The task's own
hypothesis list (parser.c's growable vectors, the M143 regex cache,
builtins_compare.c's JSON buffers, string_context.c) was explicitly
flagged as unconfirmed and possibly incomplete -- this milestone profiled
first, instead of picking from that list.

**Profiling.** `perf record -g -e cpu_core/instructions/ -c 10000 --
taskset -c 0 -- ./asnix d.nix` (confirmed cpu_core 0-11 are the P-cores on
this Meteor Lake host; kptr_restrict=1 hides kernel-internal symbols only,
not this userspace call-graph attribution, consistent with what a prior
session's own note already established). The single biggest caller chain
into `_int_malloc` (5.23% of all instructions in this run, the top-ranked
symbol overall after `lex_until`) was not any runtime builtin or value
operation at all: `asnix_op_call -> prim_import -> asnix_eval_file ->
asnix_compile -> compile_expr` (recursing into itself 8 frames deep
before resolving to a leaf `malloc` call) accounted for 2.77% of the
*entire program's* instructions directly, dwarfing every runtime
allocation site this project's own prior hypotheses named. The other
malloc-family entries in the same profile (`malloc` 1.27%, `cfree` 0.86%,
`_int_realloc` 0.73%, `__libc_calloc` 0.59%, `realloc` 0.63%, etc., ~11.6%
total self-time in this sampled run) attribute the same way: mostly to
`compile_expr`'s own recursive descent, not to any of the previously-named
runtime hypotheses.

**Root cause, confirmed by reading `compiler.c` directly.** Three of
`compile_expr`'s switch cases each `malloc` a handful of small,
fixed-shape scratch arrays -- sized by a purely SOURCE-LEVEL count, filled,
used for the span of that one node's compilation, and `free`d again before
returning:
- `AST_LET`: `names`/`name_lens`, sized by the `let`'s own binding count.
- `AST_LAMBDA` (pattern form, `{a, b ? d, ...}: body`): SEVEN separate
  `malloc`s per lambda-pattern literal (`all_syms`, `required_syms`,
  `all_syms_sorted`, `field_names`, `field_name_lens`, `fa_syms`,
  `fa_vals`), all sized by the lambda's own formals count.
- `AST_ATTRSET`: `syms`/`order`/`sorted_syms` unconditionally, plus
  `hnames`/`hname_lens`/`visible_sorted_syms` (non-`rec`, hidden-inherit
  case) or `names`/`name_lens`/`visible_sorted_syms` (`rec` case) when
  applicable -- all sized by the literal's own binding count.

None of these are runtime hot loops -- `compile_expr` runs exactly once
per AST node, at compile time, for the whole program. But a real nixpkgs
eval compiles roughly 1057 imported files' worth of source for one
`d.nix` run, and nixpkgs's own idioms are built almost entirely out of
these three constructs at huge volume: every `callPackage`-style function
(`{ lib, stdenv, fetchurl, ... }: ...`) is an `AST_LAMBDA` pattern, every
package/overlay/attribute-set body is an `AST_ATTRSET`, and `let ... in`
is pervasive throughout. The aggregate call count across the whole source
tree, not any single call's cost, is what the profile's 2.77% direct
share reflects -- exactly the same shape of problem M144 found in
`derivation.c`, just at compile time over source text instead of runtime
over the dependency graph.

**Fix.** NOT M144's depth-indexed pool -- `compile_expr`'s own recursion
is plain, single-threaded C call-stack recursion with no cross-call reuse
opportunity (each node compiles exactly once, so there is nothing to
pool across calls). Instead, each `malloc`d buffer above got a sibling
fixed-size stack array (`ASNIX_COMPILE_SCRATCH_MAX` = 32, deliberately
`#define`d to literally BE the pre-existing
`ASNIX_ATTRSET_SORT_INSERTION_MAX` constant the AST_ATTRSET case already
used for its insertion-sort-vs-qsort threshold, so the two decisions can
never drift apart) and a per-site boolean (`names_on_stack`/`nf_on_stack`/
`small_n`) choosing the stack array when the real count fits, falling
back to the ORIGINAL `malloc` path, unchanged, when it doesn't (the known
outlier, `pkgs/top-level/all-packages.nix`'s ~4,280-binding attrset
literal, already took a dedicated large-n path for the sort algorithm
pre-existing this fix -- it now takes the large-n path for allocation
too, automatically, via the same flag). Every buffer within one case
switches on the SAME flag, never a mix (e.g. `AST_LAMBDA`'s seven buffers
all key off one `nf_on_stack`), so there's no risk of a buffer outliving
a sibling that independently chose the other path. Correctness of the
scheme follows directly from C's own stack semantics: these are ordinary
automatic (non-`static`) local arrays, so a nested recursive
`compile_expr` call (e.g. an `AST_LAMBDA` whose body contains another
`AST_LAMBDA`) gets its own fresh stack frame and its own fresh array
automatically -- unlike M144's runtime pool, there is no depth-indexing,
acquire/release bracketing, or shared-frame invariant to verify at all.

**Correctness.** `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all green.
`make test-nix-conformance NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`:
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (exact baseline, same 3 pre-existing
pos-tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`.
Output hash on `d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`, verified
byte-identical against a `before` binary built from the pre-fix commit.

**Measured.** Two independent, complementary measurements, both against a
`before` binary built from the pre-fix tree and an `after` binary built
from this milestone's tree, both run from the SAME invocation of `./asnix
d.nix`:
- **Malloc call COUNT** (an `LD_PRELOAD`'d `malloc` wrapper counting every
  call, deterministic, not sampled): 2,176,862 -> 1,812,778, a 364,084-call
  (16.7%) reduction, exactly reproducible across repeated runs (not a
  statistical claim -- ran twice each, identical both times).
- **Instructions, interleaved** (`perf stat -e
  cpu_core/instructions/,cpu_core/cycles/`, `taskset -c 0`, 8 alternating
  before/after trials, B,A,B,A,...): instructions dropped in all 8/8
  paired trials, mean -25,045,659 (8,027,207,174 -> 8,002,161,515,
  -0.312%), tight and consistent (range -23.9M to -26.7M across all 8
  trials) -- the same clean, deterministic-direction signal M144/M145's
  own instruction measurements found for fixed, timing-independent
  per-call work. Cycles were, as every prior milestone on this shared,
  contended machine has found, too noisy to read directly: mean +0.18%
  (4,431,649,591 -> 4,439,519,247), won only 2/8 paired trials -- consistent
  with noise dominating a change this size, not a real regression (the
  instruction count, which does NOT depend on scheduling/cache timing,
  is the trustworthy signal here, exactly as this project's own
  measurement discipline already concludes for every small, surgical fix
  in this gap-closing series).

**Honest sizing.** This closes roughly 25M of the ~2,974M-instruction
total asnix-vs-iets gap (~0.84% of the whole gap, ~3.3% of the
763M-instruction allocator-category slice specifically) -- a real,
clean, fully-verified win, but a modest fraction of the allocator
category's own total, not a resolution of it. The malloc-call-count drop
(16.7% of ALL malloc calls in the whole run) is substantially larger in
relative terms than the instruction-count drop (0.31% of the whole
program) because most of the REMAINING malloc calls are for larger,
costlier allocations (the ones already paying for real heap bookkeeping,
not just call overhead) -- removing a sixth of the total call volume,
concentrated in exactly the smallest, cheapest, most call-overhead-bound
allocations, naturally buys a smaller share of instructions than of call
count. What's genuinely still open, not touched by this milestone:
- The qsort-based `sort_attrset_bindings_large`/`SymIdxPair` path (`n >
  32`) still mallocs unconditionally -- correctly out of scope here (it's
  already the deliberately-rare branch) but still a real, if much
  smaller, remaining per-large-literal cost.
- `AST_LET`/`AST_ATTRSET`/`AST_LAMBDA`'s own child compiles (the thunk
  bodies -- `ib_new()`/`IrBuilder` allocation, `irbuild.c`'s `ops`/`pool`
  growable arrays) are untouched; M132 already tuned their initial
  capacities, but each one is still a fresh heap allocation per thunk,
  not covered by this milestone's stack-buffer technique (their lifetime
  outlives the compiling call -- they're handed off as `IrProgram*` --
  so they are NOT eligible for the same fix; a different technique,
  if any, would be needed there).
- This milestone did not re-examine `libc_misc` (memcmp/memmove/memset,
  10.32% of asnix's own instructions, 448.5M-instruction gap) or
  `string_ops` (8.54%, 483.1M-instruction gap) -- both still open, as
  handed off, and explicitly out of this milestone's scope (allocator
  only).
- The SHA256/crypto symbol-resolution blind spot (asnix's hashing showing
  as 0.00% in instruction-sampled profiles due to `dlopen`'d
  `libcrypto.so.3` not resolving symbols) was NOT re-investigated here --
  still needs the fix a prior session flagged (either `perf`'s own
  `--objdump`/symbol-file options for the `.so`, or a non-`dlopen`
  static-link build for profiling purposes only).

Files: `src/c/compiler.c` only (`compile_expr`'s `AST_LET`, `AST_LAMBDA`
pattern-form, and `AST_ATTRSET` cases, plus the new
`ASNIX_COMPILE_SCRATCH_MAX` constant and `sort_attrset_bindings_large`'s
threshold constant now derived from it). No new test fixtures needed --
this is a pure allocation-strategy change with no behavioral surface
(verified via the full existing conformance/e2e/nixpkgs-hash suites
above, which already exercise every one of `AST_LET`/`AST_LAMBDA`-pattern/
`AST_ATTRSET`'s branches at both small and large `n`).

## M150: mimalloc as the real default -- plain `make` now auto-detects it too, not just the flake devShell

Directed follow-up to M146 after the user asked "how can we make mimalloc
the default?" -- M146 deliberately scoped mimalloc to an opt-in, env-var-
