gated path (`ASNIX_MIMALLOC_LIB`, set only by the flake's devShell or
`nix/asnix.nix`'s packaged build) specifically so plain `cc`/`make`
outside Nix would never hard-fail. That design choice is unchanged here,
but it meant anyone building this project without the flake -- a system
package manager's own mimalloc, or a `nix-shell -p mimalloc`-style ad hoc
environment -- got plain glibc malloc with no way to opt in short of
manually exporting the exact static-archive path themselves.

**The fix**: when `ASNIX_MIMALLOC_LIB` is NOT already set, the Makefile
now auto-detects a system-reachable mimalloc via a plain link probe --
`printf 'int main(void){return 0;}' | $(CC) -xc - -lmimalloc -o /dev/null`
-- the same portable "does this optional library resolve via the
linker's own default search path" pattern Autoconf-style build systems
use, rather than guessing at distro-specific library directory layouts
(`/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu`, `/usr/lib64`, Homebrew's `/opt/homebrew/
lib`, etc., which vary and would need constant upkeep). If the probe
succeeds, `-lmimalloc -lpthread` is added to the link line, same as
before but via dynamic linking (the probe's own default mode) rather
than the devShell path's static archive -- a reasonable, normal
tradeoff for a system-package-manager-installed library, matching how
glibc itself is already linked dynamically in this configuration. If
the probe fails (mimalloc genuinely unreachable), `MIMALLOC_LDLIBS`
stays empty and the build falls back to plain glibc malloc exactly as
before this milestone -- never a hard failure either way. The explicit
`ASNIX_MIMALLOC_LIB` path (devShell/packaged build) is checked FIRST and
always wins when set; the probe only runs in its `else` branch, so
nothing about the existing, already-verified static-link behavior
changes.

**Verified, three configurations, each independently**:
1. Explicit `ASNIX_MIMALLOC_LIB` set (devShell-equivalent): unchanged --
   `nm` confirms `malloc` as a locally-defined (`T`) symbol via the
   static archive, exactly as M146 landed.
2. No env var set, but mimalloc reachable via the normal linker search
   path (this machine's own broad Nix profile environment, via
   `NIX_LDFLAGS`, provides exactly this case): the probe succeeds,
   `-lmimalloc -lpthread` gets added, `ldd` confirms `libmimalloc.so.3`
   as a real runtime dependency, `./asnix d.nix` produces the correct,
   unchanged output hash. Full ladder green: `make test`/`test-e2e`/
   `test-conformance` all pass; `test-nix-conformance` `pass=655 fail=3
   skip=148` (exact baseline); `test-nixpkgs-hash` `pass=148 fail=0`.
3. No env var, AND mimalloc genuinely unreachable (tested directly via
   `env -i PATH="$PATH" HOME="$HOME" make`, stripping the rich profile
   environment case 2 relies on): the probe correctly fails (`ld.bfd:
   cannot find -lmimalloc`), the build still completes with a plain
   `gcc -o asnix src/c/main.o -L. -lasnix` link line (no mimalloc flags
   at all), and `./asnix d.nix` still produces the correct output --
   confirming the fallback is genuinely safe, not just assumed.

Files: `Makefile` only (`MIMALLOC_LDLIBS`'s own definition, now with an
`else` branch; `MIMALLOC_PROBE`, new). No change to `flake.nix`/`nix/
asnix.nix` -- the explicit, static-link devShell/packaged-build path
they set up is untouched and still takes priority.

## M151: `asnix_regex_search` (the custom ERE engine's unanchored search) -- investigated, found never called on a real eval, declined

Directed follow-up to a SIMD/SWAR source-reading sweep that flagged
`asnix_regex_search`'s unanchored loop (`regex_engine.c`: retries the
full matcher at every position in the subject string, with no literal-
prefix pre-filter) as "architecturally promising but unconfirmed" --
that sweep explicitly noted it had not profiled whether this path is
actually hot on real nixpkgs regex usage, and flagged M143's own
"most real calls use small anchored/literal patterns" finding as a
reason it might not be.

**Measured directly, not assumed**: instrumented `asnix_regex_search`
with a call counter and an `atexit` dump (temporary, reverted before
this commit), rebuilt, and ran the real `d.nix` (nixpkgs/ffmpeg
closure) eval. Result: **zero calls** -- the `atexit` handler itself
never registered, confirmed via an explicit stderr capture showing zero
lines of output. `asnix_regex_search` is only reachable from
`builtins_regex.c`'s `match`/`split` when `asnix_regex_needs_custom_engine`
determines a pattern needs the custom ERE engine at all (collating
symbols `[.name.]`, equivalence classes `[=x=]`, or a non-standard/
case-variant POSIX character class name) -- real nixpkgs's own regex
usage (primarily `lib.versions`-style version-parsing helpers, per
M143's own finding) does not exercise any of these, so the custom
engine's search path -- not just this one function, but the entire
backtracking matcher it calls into -- never runs at all on this
workload.

**Conclusion**: declined. There is no basis to optimize a function that
measures as never-called on the representative real-workload benchmark
this whole campaign uses -- any change here would have exactly zero
measurable effect on `d.nix`, and by extension no basis to claim it
would help real nixpkgs evaluation generally. This closes out the
SIMD-sweep's own flagged "needs a dedicated profiling pass before any
implementation attempt" lead with a clean, conclusive negative, rather
than leaving it open. The regex compile CACHE (M143) and the bracket-
expression delimiter-scan candidates the same sweep found remain
untouched by this finding -- those are on the `asnix_regex_needs_custom_
engine`/pattern-compilation path, not the search path, and were out of
this directive's scope.

No source files changed (instrumentation added and fully reverted,
confirmed via `git status`/`git diff` both clean before this commit).
Files: `docs/architecture.md` only.

## M152: re-examining M140's "unavoidable" verdict on `buf_put_escaped` -- the real remaining cost was call VOLUME, not per-byte scan cost, and a per-derivation escape cache fixes it

A fresh instruction-event-sampled profile (post-M146/M150 mimalloc
adoption, which collapsed the allocator gap from 763M to 227M
instructions and confirmed that win held) named `string_ops` as the
single largest remaining categorized gap against `iets`: asnix 679.3M
instructions vs. `iets`'s 188.6M, a 490.7M-instruction gap, with
`buf_put_escaped` (`src/c/aterm.c`) alone at 4.96% of asnix's own total
(~349.6M instructions). M140 had already SWAR-optimized this exact
function's escape-byte scan and explicitly declared the REMAINING cost
"the real, unavoidable cost of escaping ... not a measurement artifact."
This milestone's assignment was to check that verdict against the fresh
numbers instead of assuming it still holds now that this is the single
biggest named lever on the board.

**Reading `buf_put_escaped` itself, fresh, with no assumptions carried
over from M140.** The function (and its 3 callers, all in
`derivation.c`) is small and fully legible in one sitting. Nothing about
the scan itself (M140's own SWAR trick) looked newly fixable. What stood
out instead was `asnix_build_derivation_aterm`'s OWN call pattern,
documented plainly in `derivation.c`'s surrounding comments (M73/M74):
it runs **three times per derivation** -- a masked pass (for the
self-referential output-path hash), a real pass (for this derivation's
own `drvPath`), and a third "cache" pass (for the `hashDerivationModulo`
memo a later, dependent derivation can reuse) -- and all three calls
pass the exact same `system`, `builder`, `args`/`arg_strs`,
`input_srcs`/`refs.srcs`, and (for everything except the handful of
output-named keys) `env` arrays, by POINTER, unchanged. Only the
`outputs`/`input_drvs` sections differ meaningfully between passes. That
means the overwhelming majority of `buf_put_escaped` calls across the 3
passes are escaping **the exact same bytes for the second or third time**
-- a call-volume problem, not a per-byte cost problem, and exactly the
kind of thing M140's own investigation (scoped to the scan's per-call
cost in isolation) was never positioned to catch.

**Checked against `iets`, mechanism-for-mechanism, not just "does it
escape less per byte."** `iets`'s own `store/drv.rs` confirms this
directly: its `AtermTail` struct and `aterm_tail()`/`unparse_from`
machinery exist for exactly this reason -- the doc comment on
`AtermTail` reads verbatim "The end of the ATerm, escaped once for the
three unparses of a new derivation." `unparse_tail` is called ONCE,
building a cached byte buffer (`tail.bytes`) covering `input_srcs`
through `env`, recording "hole" byte offsets wherever an output-named
env value was masked to `""`; every later unparse (`unparse_from`) then
just `extend_from_slice`s (a raw memcpy) the cached bytes verbatim,
splicing in the real, always-escape-free (on Linux; store paths never
contain `"`/`\`/`\n`/`\r`/`\t`) output path bytes at each hole instead of
re-running `escape_into`/`find_escape` at all. So the answer to the
milestone's own framing question is unambiguous: this is a **call-volume
gap**, not a per-byte-work gap -- `iets` does fundamentally less total
escaping work for the same logical derivation set, by design, and
`asnix` was doing 2-3x the necessary work for no corresponding benefit.

**The fix.** Rather than porting `iets`'s exact head/tail-with-byte-
offset-holes split (a bigger, more invasive rewrite of
`asnix_build_derivation_aterm`'s internal structure), this lands the same
effect through a simpler mechanism that fits this project's existing
call shape: a per-derivation escape cache (`AtermEscapeCache`, `aterm.c`)
keyed by **source pointer**, not content. `derivation.c` creates one
cache right before the masked pass, threads it through all 3
`asnix_build_derivation_aterm_cached` calls (the new cache-aware entry
point; `asnix_build_derivation_aterm` itself is now a 1-line wrapper
calling it with `cache=NULL`, preserving the old, uncached behavior
byte-for-byte for `tests/c/test_aterm.c` and any other caller), and frees
it right after the last pass. Inside `buf_put_escaped`, a cache hit is a
plain `buf_put_bytes` memcpy of the previously-escaped span (quotes
included); a cache miss escapes normally (unchanged logic, `M140`'s SWAR
scan and all) and then stores a copy of the exact output span it just
wrote, keyed by the input pointer, for the next pass to reuse. Pointer
identity is deliberately the correctness invariant here, not string
content: a string that's merely `strcmp`-equal but a DIFFERENT buffer
(this happens for output-named env values, which legitimately differ
between the masked pass's `""` and the real/cache passes' actual output
path) is a different pointer, so it correctly misses and gets escaped
fresh -- there is no risk of conflating two logically-different values
that happen to look the same. Because `derivation.c` already passes the
SAME `system`/`builder`/`arg_strs`/`refs.srcs`/`env`-key/non-output-
`env`-value pointers to all 3 calls (and the masked-pass's own
`masked_input_drvs` pointer is reused again by the 3rd, cache-hash pass),
this one pointer-identity cache transparently captures essentially the
same savings `iets`'s explicit head/tail split does, without needing to
understand or replicate its byte-offset-hole bookkeeping.

**A real bug found and fixed during this milestone's OWN first
measurement pass, not shipped.** The first working version of
`aterm_cache_insert` recomputed the table's load factor by scanning
every slot (`for (i = 0; i < c->cap; i++) used += ...`) on EVERY single
insert -- an O(cap) cost paid once per distinct string cached, which
measured as a net REGRESSION (+91M instructions, firmly outside noise)
against the M150 baseline on the very first interleaved comparison. This
is exactly the kind of "trust but verify your own fix's measurement, not
just its intent" discipline this project's own measurement culture
requires (the same spirit as M140's cycles re-measurement catching a
sequential-batching artifact) -- caught before anything was declared
done, fixed by tracking occupied-slot `count` incrementally instead of
rescanning, and re-measured from scratch. The lesson generalizes: a
cache's own bookkeeping cost must be checked to actually be cheaper than
the work it's skipping, not assumed to be, especially for a cache this
small and this short-lived (a handful to a few hundred entries, freed
within the same function call that created it).

**Measured** (after the above fix; `perf stat`, `taskset -c 0`,
`cpu_core/instructions/`+`cpu_core/cycles/`, 20 interleaved trials
(before,after,before,after,...) on the real cold `d.nix`/ffmpeg eval,
output hash cross-checked byte-identical on every single trial):

| | instructions | cycles |
|---|---|---|
| before (M150 baseline) | 7,135,827,425 (avg) | 4,025,431,959 (avg) |
| after (M151) | 6,867,912,154 (avg) | 3,974,302,757 (avg) |
| delta | **-3.75%** | -1.27% |
| wins | 20/20 | 16/20 |

Instructions: completely non-overlapping ranges across all 20 trials
(every BEFORE trial 7,132.3M-7,142.1M, every AFTER trial 6,865.5M-
6,870.8M) -- the same "hard, repetition-independent fact" character this
project's measurement culture already established for clean instruction
wins (M129/M130/M146). Cycles: directionally consistent but noisier (as
every prior milestone on this shared, contended machine has found), won
16/20 pairs -- real but smaller, consistent with the instruction count
being the trustworthy signal here.

A follow-up `perf record -e cpu_core/instructions/ -c 10000 -g` comparison
confirmed the mechanism directly: `buf_put_escaped`'s self-time share
dropped from 4.02% to 3.13% of each binary's own (now-smaller) total, and
`find_escape_aterm`'s own inlined scan share (the exact cost M140 found
"unavoidable") dropped from 2.44% to 1.55% -- both consistent with
roughly 2 of the 3 passes' worth of scanning being skipped for most
strings, not a vanished-but-still-real cost showing up disguised
elsewhere.

**Correctness.** A standalone `valgrind --leak-check=full` run on a
small single-derivation `d.nix`-equivalent showed byte-identical leak
accounting before and after this change (1,104 bytes/21 blocks
"definitely lost," 262/12 "indirectly lost," both pre-existing in
`parser.c`/`string_context.c`, unrelated to this milestone -- zero new
leaks attributed to `aterm.c`/the new cache). Full ladder green: `make
test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all pass (including
`tests/c/test_aterm.c`, exercising the unchanged `cache=NULL` path
directly). `make test-nix-conformance NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-
conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (exact baseline, the same 3
pre-existing pos-tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148
fail=0` -- 148 real nixpkgs derivations, including large ones with many
env vars/inputs, all exercising cache growth and hit/miss correctness
for real, not just the 4 fixture-based cases in `test_aterm.c`. Output
hash on `d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure) unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`,
byte-identical before and after, every trial.

**Honest sizing against the gap.** This closes roughly 267.7M
instructions, **3.75% of asnix's own whole-program instruction count** on
this workload -- a bigger single-change win than M140's own 1.9%, and in
the same tier as M146/M149's allocator-category fixes, though smaller
than M146 itself. Measured against the handoff's own named categories:
267.7M is roughly 54.6% of the full `string_ops` 490.7M-instruction gap,
and roughly 76.6% of `buf_put_escaped`'s own previously-measured 349.6M-
instruction absolute cost -- consistent with eliminating most, but not
all, of the function's 3x-redundant work (the `outputs`/`input_drvs`
sections, and the small number of output-named env values, are NOT
cacheable by design, so some real escaping work every pass still does
remains un-deduplicated, correctly). This directly answers the
milestone's own question: M140's "unavoidable" framing was correct about
the SCAN itself (nothing new was found there) but incomplete about the
function's total cost, because it never examined how many times the
same bytes were being handed to that scan in the first place. The
honest remaining gap: `string_ops`'s other ~223M instructions (490.7M
minus this milestone's 267.7M) is NOT claimed to be closed by this fix --
whatever else populates that category (other string-handling call sites,
`jb_escape_string`'s own JSON-output path, `string_context.c`'s
`dup_cstr`, etc.) is still open and was not re-profiled in isolation
here.

Files: `src/c/aterm.h` (`AtermEscapeCache` opaque type,
`asnix_aterm_escape_cache_new`/`_free`, `asnix_build_derivation_aterm_
cached`), `src/c/aterm.c` (`AtermEscapeCache`'s table implementation,
`buf_put_escaped_raw`/`buf_put_escaped` split, `asnix_build_derivation_
aterm_cached`; `asnix_build_derivation_aterm` is now a thin wrapper),
`src/c/derivation.c` (creates/threads/frees one `aterm_cache` across the
masked/real/cache-hash passes). No test fixture changes needed --
`tests/c/test_aterm.c` already exercises the unchanged `cache=NULL` path,
and the full nixpkgs-hash/conformance suites exercise the cached path
against real derivations.

## M153: `lex_dquote_run`'s own SWAR candidate, correctly implemented and exhaustively proven correct, measured as a real (if small) regression, and declined

A source-level sweep (read-only, no profiling) looking for unexplored
SWAR/SIMD candidates flagged `lex_dquote_run` (`src/c/lexer.c`, plain
`"..."` string-content scanning). It has the same byte-at-a-time shape
M140's `find_escape_aterm`/`find_escape_json` already fixed elsewhere,
never applied here. `lex_indented_run` (`''...''` content) was flagged as
a messier sibling with the same shape, plus a harder multi-byte `''$`/
`'''`/`''\<c>` lookahead. This milestone profiled both for real before
touching any code, implemented and exhaustively proved correct a SWAR
fix for the simpler one, measured it on the real eval, and declined to
ship it. This is a genuine, instructive negative result, in the same tier
as M127/M135's own honestly-reported declines.

**Profiling, done first.** `perf record -g -e cpu_core/instructions/ -c
10000`, `taskset -c 0`, cold `d.nix` eval, `ASNIX_BYTECODE_CACHE_DIR`
pointed at a nonexistent directory. Both scan functions are small
`static` functions the compiler fully inlines into `lex_until` (`nm`/
`perf report` show no separate symbol for either). `lex_until` itself is
5.97-6.43% self-time of the whole eval across two independent captures.
Neither sub-scan has its own symbol to read a percentage off directly, so
a small Python script (throwaway, not shipped) walked `perf annotate
lex_until`'s interleaved source-plus-asm dump. It classified each asm
line's self-time by the nearest preceding source line's content.
`TOK_STR_PART`/`TOK_STR_END` text uniquely identifies `lex_dquote_run`'s
own inlined body; `TOK_ISTR_PART`/`TOK_ISTR_ESC`/`TOK_ISTR_END` identify
`lex_indented_run`'s. The script resets the classification at every
backward jump to `lex_until`'s own dispatch-loop head (`jmp ... <lex_until
+0x240>`, the one instruction both inlined scan bodies always return
through), to stop misattributing the SHARED dispatch code that runs
between one inlined body's exit and the next classified marker. Two
captures agreed closely:

| | `lex_until` self-time | `lex_dquote_run` share | `lex_indented_run` share |
|---|---|---|---|
| capture 1 | 6.43% | 13.51% -> **0.869%** of whole eval | 1.40% -> **0.090%** of whole eval |
| capture 2 | 5.97% | 12.23% -> **0.730%** of whole eval | 1.00% -> **0.060%** of whole eval |

So `lex_dquote_run` is real (about 0.80% self-time, averaged) but modest.
`lex_indented_run` is real but small enough (about 0.075%) that its extra
multi-byte-lookahead complexity is not worth attempting on its own. It is
declined without an implementation attempt, consistent with the task's
own explicitly-sanctioned "legitimate to land only the simpler one" scope
cut.

**Sized against M140's own CURRENT numbers, not its own writeup's
pre-fix figures**, per this task's own explicit instruction. The SAME two
profiling captures show `buf_put_escaped` plus `jb_escape_string`
(M140's own targets) at a combined 5.52% and 5.82% self-time. That is
notably HIGHER than M140's own writeup's post-fix 2.85% citation, almost
certainly because `~/nixpkgs`'s own live checkout (shared, not pinned)
has drifted since M140 was written, pulling in a larger or different
dependency closure for `d.nix`'s `ffmpeg.outPath`. This is not evidence
that M140's own fix regressed, and it is not this milestone's concern to
chase further, but it is the number actually being compared against, so
it is cited honestly. Averaging to about 5.67%, `lex_dquote_run`'s own
0.80% self-time is about 14% the size of M140's own current combined
target: a real, comparably-shaped but meaningfully smaller opportunity,
in the same rough tier M130/M145 previously called "a real but small win,
honestly sized" before measuring confirmed it either way.

**The implementation, and the one real design problem M140's own
precedent does not solve.** `find_dquote_trigger(s, cap)` ports M140's
exact bit-twiddling shape (the "has a zero byte" identity, `haszero(x) =
((x-LO)&~x)&HI`, applied directly for NUL and via XOR for `'"'`/`'$'`/
`'\\'`) to this file's own trigger-byte set, 8 bytes per SWAR chunk, with
a scalar fallback for the tail. This is structurally identical to
`find_escape_aterm`. The real problem is establishing `cap`: the bound
that makes an 8-byte `memcpy` read inside it provably safe. M140's own
`find_escape_aterm`/`find_escape_json` both already know their input's
exact length (`strlen()` on an already-fully-materialized C string)
before any SWAR chunk is read. `lex_dquote_run` is discovering where a
string literal ENDS, so there is no such pre-known length to bound it
with.

Two shortcuts were considered and rejected before settling on a third.
First: an unconditional 8-byte `memcpy` at an arbitrary offset with no
bound check at all. This is genuinely unsafe, not just theoretically,
because `src` is sometimes a bare C string literal with no padding past
its own NUL (`tests/ir/test_m45_codegen.c`, `bench/microbench_m45.c` both
call `asnix_parse()` directly on string-literal arguments). This was
confirmed by deliberately constructing exactly this shape under
`-fsanitize=address,undefined` in this milestone's own correctness
harness, before writing a single line of the real fix. Second: a single
`strlen(src+*i)` call, the way M140's own callers use. This was also
rejected, for a completely different reason: `src` here is the WHOLE
FILE's buffer, not just one string literal, so `strlen(src+*i)` would
scan all the way to the FILE's own trailing NUL, not this string's own
closing `"`. For a file with many string literals (nixpkgs' own
`meta.description`-laden package sets are exactly this shape), the SUM of
those over-long `strlen()` calls is quadratic-ish in the literal count. A
correctness-preserving but real performance-REGRESSING footgun is the
opposite of this milestone's entire point.

The fix landed (temporarily, see below): `strnlen(src+*i,
DQUOTE_SWAR_WINDOW)` with window 64 establishes a safe sub-window bounded
by a small constant, re-invoked window by window as the scan advances.
Every byte `strnlen` touches, it already read without fault, so an
8-byte SWAR chunk read anywhere inside that confirmed window is safe by
construction. The total `strnlen` cost across a whole string stays
O(real string length) plus O(1) overshoot, never O(file length). One
further wrinkle: `'$'` needs a 1-byte lookahead (is the next byte `'{'`?)
to know whether it is really a trigger. `strnlen` only proves bytes
`[0,window)` safe when `window == DQUOTE_SWAR_WINDOW` (it stopped at the
cap without finding a NUL, so it never touched index `window` itself). So
the scan's own `cap` excludes the last byte of a full window (`cap =
window - 1`), rather than risk an unverified lookahead read one past it.
That excluded byte becomes the first byte of the next window's own
freshly-verified scan instead.

**Correctness, proven before this touched the real lexer, matching
M140's own exact methodology.** A throwaway standalone harness
(`/tmp/dquote_swar_test/test.c` this session, not shipped) extracted just
the "find the next trigger byte, starting at position i0" step from both
the OLD scalar loop and the NEW windowed-SWAR version, as two
freestanding functions with identical signatures. It then compared their
output byte-for-byte under `-fsanitize=address,undefined`:
2,000,000 random trials (length 0-39, the 4 trigger bytes and non-ASCII
bytes 0x80-0xff both deliberately over-represented, one in five trials
also injecting an early truncating NUL to exercise the "file ends
mid-literal" fatal path); an exhaustive sweep placing every special byte
at every position for every length 0-30 (explicitly covering both the
`${` and bare-`$`-not-followed-by-`{` sub-cases); and a dedicated
multi-window sweep (length 210, every position 0-209, specifically
covering the window boundary at 64/128/192 and the reserved-last-byte
edge at 63/64/65, 127/128/129, 191/192/193). Total: **37,166,375 trials,
zero mismatches, zero ASan/UBSan reports**. The fix was wired into the
real `lexer.c` only after this came back clean. The full verification
ladder was green with the fix in place: `make test`/`test-e2e`/
`test-conformance` (296 e2e checks, all OK); `test-nix-conformance`:
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (the same 3 pre-existing pos-tracking
failures); `test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. The output hash on
`d.nix` stayed unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.

**Measured on the real eval, and declined.** Two full binaries were
built from the otherwise-identical tree (`git show HEAD:src/c/lexer.c`
vs. the working tree, only `lexer.c` differing, manual file-swap rather
than `git stash`, matching M129/M138/M140's own established precedent).
8 INTERLEAVED trials ran (before, after, before, after, and so on, never
batched, per this campaign's own standing measurement discipline,
re-affirmed as necessary by M140's own writeup after a batched
measurement there gave a false reading), using `taskset -c 0`,
`cpu_core/instructions/,cpu_core/cycles/`, on a cold `d.nix` eval:

| pair | before (instructions) | after (instructions) | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 7,049,497,811 | 7,052,557,721 | +3,059,910 |
| 2 | 7,046,123,266 | 7,052,723,576 | +6,600,310 |
| 3 | 7,043,342,890 | 7,062,395,245 | +19,052,355 |
| 4 | 7,050,487,363 | 7,058,469,114 | +7,981,751 |
| 5 | 7,047,819,188 | 7,057,733,647 | +9,914,459 |
| 6 | 7,045,404,494 | 7,054,231,357 | +8,826,863 |
| 7 | 7,045,599,784 | 7,051,594,756 | +5,994,972 |
| 8 | 7,050,529,827 | 7,051,896,403 | +1,366,576 |

**8 out of 8 pairs show the SWAR version using MORE instructions, never
fewer.** The mean is +7,849,650 instructions, **+0.111%** on the whole
eval. This is small, but completely one-directional. The same "does not
need statistics to trust, just confirmation it is not a fluke" standard
M145 used for its own much smaller deterministic WIN applies equally to
this deterministic LOSS. Cycles were noisier, as usual on this shared
host (one pair showed a +28% cycle spike unrelated to the instruction
count, matching this session's own documented concurrent-load contention
pattern). Excluding that one outlier pair, cycles moved +0.40%,
directionally consistent with the instruction-count regression rather
than contradicting it.

**Root cause, reasoned through rather than left as "it just regressed."**
The correctness fix above is not optional. `lex_dquote_run` cannot
safely use an unconditional 8-byte read, or a single up-front
`strlen()`, the way M140's own targets could. So some form of the
`strnlen`-windowing overhead (a real, non-inlined libc call, plus the
`window`/`cap` bookkeeping around it) is paid on every single call. That
means every double-quoted string literal, and every re-entry after an
interpolation, pays this cost. M140's own targets
(`buf_put_escaped`/`jb_escape_string`) are called on long-ish derivation
env/arg strings, where that fixed cost is amortized over genuinely long
scans. This task's OWN framing predicted real Nix `"..."` literals would
be "especially...hundreds of bytes" long enough to amortize a SWAR
setup cost, the way `lex_indented_run`'s multi-line builder scripts
plausibly are. But the measured regression says plain double-quoted
literals in this real corpus are apparently mostly too SHORT for that to
hold. So the fixed per-call overhead this correctness constraint demands
costs more than the 8-bytes-at-a-time win saves. This is exactly the
ceiling M142's own insertion-sort-beats-qsort-for-small-N finding warned
about, just encountered empirically here instead of reasoned out in
advance.

**Declined and reverted.** `src/c/lexer.c` is back to its pre-milestone
content, confirmed via `diff` against `git show HEAD:src/c/lexer.c`.
Nothing shipped. The full ladder was re-run once more on the reverted
tree, as a sanity check that this milestone leaves no trace: `make
test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` green, `test-nix-conformance`
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`, `test-nixpkgs-hash` `pass=148 fail=0`,
`d.nix` output hash unchanged.

**Flagged, NOT attempted: a concrete idea for whoever picks this up
next.** A hybrid scan could help. Run an inlined scalar fast path,
identical to the original byte-at-a-time loop, for the first N bytes of
any run (zero SWAR/`strnlen` call overhead, since it is the exact same
code as today). Fall through to the windowed-SWAR path only once N
consecutive plain bytes have been seen without a trigger. This would pay
the original code's own cost for every SHORT run (the apparent common
case here), while still capturing the SWAR win for genuinely long runs.
This was not attempted this milestone: it adds real control-flow
complexity (the fast path and the windowed path need to hand off cleanly
mid-scan, including the `'$'`-lookahead and backslash-escape cases) for
an opportunity already sized at well under 1% before any of this
milestone's own overhead is counted. This milestone's time was better
spent confirming the straightforward port's real-world result honestly,
than iterating on a fancier version without first knowing whether the
plain version would have been enough. `lex_indented_run` was not
attempted at all (self-time too small, about 0.075%, to justify its own
harder multi-byte-lookahead complexity, even before any regression risk
is counted). Both are left as explicit future work, not silently
dropped.

**Also noted, out of this milestone's own assigned scope.** The same
`perf annotate` classification pass incidentally found `lex_path_run`
(the sibling scan for path-literal content after an interpolation, e.g.
`./a-${foo}-b`) attributed with a notably LARGER share of `lex_until`'s
own self-time (31.6-33.1% across the two captures, vs. `lex_dquote_run`'s
12.2-13.5%). That is roughly **2.0% of the whole eval's own self-time**:
a meaningfully bigger target than either string-scan function this
milestone was assigned. It is not yet confirmed via its own dedicated
correctness or measurement pass, and it was not investigated further
here (out of scope, flagged for whichever milestone picks it up, same as
M129's own "not investigated here" footnotes always are).

Files: none shipped (`src/c/lexer.c` reverted to its pre-milestone
content; this section is the only durable artifact of this milestone).

## M154: "slow it down to find what matters" -- validated as a real technique, but only on cycles/wall-clock, never on instruction count, and the hiding effect itself depends sharply on how long the injected chain is

Investigated a specific methodological idea: deliberately inject a known,
controlled amount of extra cost into one function, measure how much the
whole program's real cost increases, and use that measured increase (not
static self-time) to judge how much speeding that function up for real
would actually help. This is the mirror image of the just-declined Coz
investigation (causal profiling, which *virtually* speeds a region up to
predict the effect of a real speedup) -- slowing a region down instead,
with a real measurement, sidesteps Coz's own conceptual mismatch with a
single-threaded program and its practical breakage on this toolchain.

**Experiment**: `asnix_intern` (`src/c/symtab.c`), called exactly
1,833,170 times on the real `d.nix` eval (an already-established, well-
characterized call count from M130). A temporary, env-var-gated
(`ASNIX_SLOWDOWN_INTERN_N`, 0 = no-op, identical code path to baseline)
serially-dependent multiply-add chain was added at the top of the
function -- NOT a NOP sequence, which a modern frontend can fold/fuse
almost for free and would say nothing about real dependent-work
hiding. `objdump` confirmed the compiler emitted exactly 5 instructions
per loop iteration (`imul`/`add`/`add`/`cmp`/`jne`) plus 5 fixed one-time
instructions (setup + final store) on the taken path, so the expected
per-call instruction delta for the loop running N times is precisely
`5N + 5`. Reverted before committing -- this is a read-only
investigation, no production code changed.

**Measured, interleaved (never batched), `taskset -c 0`,
`cpu_core/instructions/,cpu_core/cycles/`, same env-var toggle on the
same binary so the ~5-instruction fixed overhead cancels exactly in the
delta**:

| N (loop iters) | measured delta instructions | predicted delta instructions (`(5N+5) x 1,833,170`) | measured delta cycles | naive delta cycles (`delta_instr / baseline IPC`) | measured as % of naive |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 193,218,621 | 192,482,850 | 16,080,182 | 109,114,212 | **14.7%** |
| 200 | 1,844,333,762 | 1,842,335,850 | 1,103,568,721 | 1,031,473,566 | **107.0%** |

**Instruction count behaves exactly as predicted at both sizes** (within
0.4%) -- this is expected and not itself a finding: instruction count is
a static count of retired instructions, so it cannot be "hidden" by
out-of-order execution the way cycles can; injecting K instructions that
must retire always shows up as +K in this metric, by construction. A
slowdown-injection experiment measuring only instructions would be
useless for this purpose -- it always just reports back the arithmetic
you put in.

**Cycles tell the real story, and it is NOT monotonic in the way a naive
model predicts.** At N=20 (a ~105-instruction serial chain per call),
85.3% of the naive linear cost vanishes -- the out-of-order core overlaps
nearly all of it with surrounding independent work (the hash lookup/
insert's own memory-latency-bound operations, and/or adjacent calls'
own independent work), the same store-to-load-forwarding-adjacent
hiding mechanism M127's `bench/regvm_poc/` already demonstrated for
VALSTACK traffic. At N=200 (a ~1,005-instruction chain), that hiding
essentially disappears -- measured cycles land almost exactly on the
naive linear prediction. This is consistent with a reorder-buffer-size
effect: a short dependent chain fits inside the core's out-of-order
scheduling window and can be substantially overlapped with nearby
independent work; a chain roughly 10x longer exceeds that window, so the
core eventually has no choice but to stall on the dependency, and the
cost becomes visible almost linearly. This project had not previously
measured *where* that transition sits, only that hiding exists at all
(M127) -- this experiment brackets it concretely between roughly 100 and
1,000 serially-dependent instructions per occurrence, for this specific
chain shape on this specific core.

**Conclusion: the technique is sound and complements, not replaces,
static profiling -- but only if read correctly.** "Slow down section X
and see how much the real program slows down" is a genuine, direct way
to estimate X's true optimization ceiling, avoiding the risk that a
function's raw self-time share overstates its real end-to-end cost
(exactly the risk M127 found for VALSTACK traffic and this experiment
now reproduces independently, via the complementary direction). But the
experiment is only informative on cycles or wall-clock -- never on
instruction count, which is definitionally insensitive to this exact
effect -- and the injected delay's own *shape* and *length* materially
change the answer: a short injected delay will systematically
*understate* a region's true importance (most of it gets hidden), while
a long one will more honestly reveal it, because real code bottlenecks
are not uniformly one length or the other. A slowdown experiment used to
rank candidates for optimization should therefore use an injected delay
long enough to exceed the core's own hiding window (this experiment's
own data suggests comfortably over 200 serially-dependent instructions
is a safer default than something short like 20), or risk systematically
deprioritizing real targets the same way a naive self-time percentage
already can.

**Not attempted here**: building this into a reusable, general-purpose
harness (e.g. a compile-time flag usable on any function, not just
`asnix_intern`) -- this was a one-shot methodological validation, not a
tool-building task. If this technique is adopted going forward, the
`asnix_intern` mechanism built and reverted here (env-var-gated,
serially-dependent multiply-add chain, `objdump`-verified instruction
cost) is a template worth reusing rather than reinventing.

Files: none shipped (`src/c/symtab.c` reverted to its clean content;
this section is the only durable artifact of this investigation).

## M155: extending M111's `asnix_bshared_attrs_probe` to `op_select_or.S`/`op_has_attr.S` -- and a latent flag-clobbering bug in M111's own `op_select.S` found and fixed along the way

A fresh profiling pass re-ranked `attrs_sets`' 139.1M-instruction gap and
re-confirmed (consistent with the prior callPackage-specializations
investigation) that it's NOT one concentrated bug: the dominant half is
ordinary `//`-operator volume building nixpkgs's own ~12-layer overlay
`pkgs` (the single largest eager-merge call site measured had
`lhs_count=rhs_count=28,189` -- the top-level `pkgs` build itself), which
M93 already measured isn't worth re-architecting further. The one
genuinely concentrated, fixable slice the profile pointed at: 0.36%+0.23%
of `asnix_attrs_eager_merge`'s self-time attributed to `op_select_or`'s
and `op_has_attr`'s own union-resolve paths -- the exact two call sites
M111 (`asnix_bshared_attrs_probe`, a bounded leaf-probe that avoids
`asnix_bshared_attrs_resolve`'s full materialize-on-any-read) deliberately
left un-converted, having only wired the probe into `op_select.S`'s `a.b`
path. `op_select_or.S` (`a.b or default`) and `op_has_attr.S` (`a ? b`)
are both pure single-key point lookups on the union path -- the probe's
exact target shape -- so this milestone ported M111's already-proven
technique to both, mechanically mirroring `op_select.S`'s own call
sequence (`op_has_attr.S` additionally discards the probed value, since
`?` never forces or returns it).

**A real, pre-existing bug found and fixed along the way, not assumed
away.** Direct correctness testing (not just the existing suite) on a
genuine point-lookup MISS against a real `UnionHdr` --
`(listToAttrs-built 20-entry base // { extra = 100; }).nope` and `.nope or
99` -- segfaulted on the first working draft of both new call sites.
Tracing with `gdb` found the bug wasn't in the new code's logic: it's a
latent flag-clobbering bug in the exact sequence `op_select.S` ALREADY
shipped in M111, copied faithfully (bug and all) into the new sites. The
shared pattern was:
```
call asnix_bshared_attrs_probe
testl %eax, %eax     // sets ZF from the probe's return value
movq (%rsp), %r9
addq $16, %rsp        // ADD unconditionally OVERWRITES ZF/SF/CF/OF
                       // from its OWN result (here, always a nonzero
                       // stack address) -- silently destroying the
                       // `testl`'s flags before they're ever read
popq %rdi
popq %rsi
jz .Lselect_probe_missing   // branches on the CLOBBERED flags, not
                             // the probe's real result
```
On a genuine miss (`eax==0`), the clobbered `ZF` read back as 0 (since
`rsp+16` is never literally zero) instead of 1, so `jz` was never taken --
the miss path fell through treating the never-written `out_value` scratch
slot's garbage contents as a "found" value, corrupting `%rax` with stack
garbage that then got misread as a tagged pointer by the Cell/LazyApp/
ThunkMap dispatch a few instructions later, segfaulting. On a genuine HIT
(`eax!=0`), the SAME clobbering happened, but the clobbered `ZF` also
happened to read back as 0 (`rsp+16` still nonzero) -- which is
coincidentally the CORRECT "don't take the missing branch" outcome for a
hit, masking the bug completely. This is exactly why M111's own
verification (which covered override semantics, `MAX_LEAVES` boundaries,
chained unions, `==`, `toJSON`, etc. -- see that section) and every run of
`make test`/`test-nix-conformance`/`test-nixpkgs-hash` since never caught
it: real nixpkgs's own `UnionHdr`s, by construction, are never genuinely
point-missed via `op_select.S`'s `a.b` path in practice (a plain `a.b`
miss on a real union is already a fatal abort real Nix code basically
never triggers deliberately), so the one case that exposes the bug was
never exercised. Fixed in all three files (`op_select.S`, `op_select_or.S`,
`op_has_attr.S`) by moving `testl %eax, %eax` to be the LAST instruction
before the branch, after all stack cleanup -- `%eax` itself is untouched
by the intervening `movq`/`addq`/`popq` instructions, only the FLAGS were
at risk.

**Correctness, verified directly, not just via the test suite.** Minimal
repro (`(20-entry-base // {extra=100;}) .nope`, `.nope or 99`, `? extra`,
`? nope`, plain `.extra`) cross-checked byte-for-byte against real
`nix-instantiate --eval`: `[ 100 99 true false ]` both before (on the
flat/hit cases, which never exercised the bug) and after the fix, and the
genuine-miss cases (which segfaulted on the buggy intermediate draft) now
correctly print `asnix: attribute 'nope' missing, aborting` for plain
`.nope`, matching real Nix's own abort for that case exactly. `./asnix
d.nix` unchanged: `"/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin"`,
byte-identical.

**Verification ladder.** `make test`: all green. `make test-e2e`: all
green. `make test-conformance`: all green. `make test-nix-conformance
NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`,
exact baseline match (the same 3 known pre-existing gaps: `eval-okay-
getattrpos{,-functionargs}.nix`, `eval-okay-inherit-attr-pos.nix`). `make
test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`.

**Measured impact on `./asnix d.nix`** (real nixpkgs's `ffmpeg.outPath`,
`perf stat`, `taskset -c 0`, `cpu_core/instructions/,cpu_core/cycles/`,
4 INTERLEAVED trials each against a clean M153-baseline binary built
side-by-side in a separate directory, never batched): instructions
dropped from a tight, consistently-higher baseline band
(6,776,717,191-6,779,630,661, mean 6,777,971,462) to a tighter, lower,
non-overlapping fixed band (6,756,307,103-6,756,778,844, mean
6,756,452,991) -- a consistent **~21.5M-instruction (~0.32%) reduction**,
small but real given every one of the 4 interleaved pairs showed fixed
strictly below baseline with no overlap. Cycles were noisier, as this
campaign has repeatedly found on this shared machine (baseline
3,760,376,593-3,964,593,040, mean 3,830,734,796; fixed 3,729,179,311-
3,866,067,118, mean 3,781,882,027) -- directionally the same ~1.3%
reduction but within a band wide enough that it's not treated as an
independently confirmed signal on its own, only as consistent with the
instruction-count result. This is an honestly small, not dramatic, win --
consistent with M111's own finding that most real nixpkgs unions
eventually get materialized via some OTHER full-iteration access path
anyway (`attrNames`, the printer, `derivation.c`'s input-collection walk,
JSON encoding), so converting two more POINT-lookup sites only helps the
subset of accesses that touch a union exclusively through `or`/`?` and
never through full iteration -- real, but not the dominant share of
`attrs_sets`' 139.1M gap (which this milestone's own profiling re-confirms
is genuinely diffuse `//`-volume, not a concentrated bug, matching the
prior investigation's verdict).

**What was declined, and why.** `op_with_try.S`/`op_with.S`'s `OP_WITH_TRY`
(`with expr; body`'s runtime fallback lookup) is structurally the same
single-key point-lookup shape and was enumerated as a correct target in
M93's own call-site list, but this milestone did NOT convert it: the
profiling evidence motivating this milestone specifically named
`op_select_or`/`op_has_attr` (0.36%+0.23%), not `op_with_try`, and
converting it without a specific measured signal risks the same class of
subtle flag-ordering mistake this milestone just found and fixed for no
demonstrated payoff -- left as a plausible, low-risk follow-up for
whichever future pass actually profiles it hot, not bundled in here on
spec. `op_check_formals.S` (lambda-pattern destructuring) was considered
and declined for a structural reason, not just caution: its phase 2 (every
GIVEN entry must be a declared field) requires genuine POSITIONAL
iteration over every entry in the given attrset, which already requires
materializing the union regardless of phase 1's point lookups -- converting
phase 1 to a probe would save nothing, since the full resolve already has
to happen for phase 2 to run at all.

Files: `src/asm/ops/op_select.S` (bug fix only -- the probe wiring itself
is unchanged from M111), `src/asm/ops/op_select_or.S`,
`src/asm/ops/op_has_attr.S`.

## M156: `aterm.c`'s `buf_puts` strlen()'d every literal it was ever called with, even though all 13 call sites pass a compile-time string literal

A profiling pass named `aterm.c`'s `buf_puts()` as a real, if modest,
follow-on to M152's own escape cache: on a cache MISS (the real escaping
work M152 explicitly left un-deduplicated), `buf_put_escaped_raw` calls
`buf_puts(b, "\\n")`/`"\\r"`/`"\\t"`/`"\\\""`/`"\\\\"` once per actual
escaped byte, and the file's literal structural punctuation
(`"Derive(["`, `"],["`, etc.) the same way -- and `buf_puts` computed
each one's length with a runtime `strlen()` call, despite every single
one of its 13 call sites (confirmed with `grep -rn buf_puts src/c/*.c`
across the whole tree, not just this file) passing a literal whose
length `sizeof` already gives at compile time. The handoff's own
hypothesis additionally named a second, harder cost: the one genuinely
dynamic `strlen(s)` inside `buf_put_escaped_raw` itself (computing the
length of the actual derivation-field string being escaped), and
proposed threading a `_len` field through `AtermOutput`/`AtermInputDrv`/
`AtermEnvVar` to avoid it too -- the exact change M147 had already looked
at and explicitly scoped OUT as "a wider-blast-radius change than this
milestone's scope."

**What this milestone did.** Fixed the first, bounded half only. Replaced
`buf_puts(Buf*, const char*)` with a macro,
`buf_put_lit(b, lit) buf_put_bytes((b), (lit), sizeof(lit) - 1)`, and
updated all 13 call sites. Every call site was re-verified by `grep` to
be a string literal before the rename, so `sizeof(lit)-1` is exactly the
right length at every one of them, computed at compile time with zero
runtime cost. The macro's own doc comment calls out explicitly that it is
NOT a drop-in general replacement for a `buf_puts`-shaped helper: passing
it a `char*` variable instead of a literal would silently compute
`sizeof(a pointer) - 1` (7) instead of failing loudly, so it is
deliberately scoped to this file's own literal-only call sites, not
exported.

**What this milestone declined.** The second half of the handoff's own
hypothesis -- threading explicit lengths through `AtermOutput`/
`AtermInputDrv`/`AtermEnvVar` to eliminate `buf_put_escaped_raw`'s one
remaining genuine `strlen(s)` call on the dynamic derivation-field string
-- was not attempted. Reading `value_util.c`'s own
`asnix_string_value_to_cstr` confirms the length IS already known right
there (`int64_t len = *(const int64_t *)(s + ASNIX_STRING_OFF_LEN);`,
read straight from the `Value`'s own string header before the `strlen`-
losing coercion down to a plain `char*`) -- so a length-carrying variant
is technically straightforward to add at that one call site. But
`derivation.c` constructs these three structs' fields from a mix of
sources (`asnix_string_value_to_cstr` results, `dup_cstr`-built strings,
plain `""` literals, and pointers reused verbatim across the masked/real/
cache-hash passes per M152's own cache design), and the fields feed
`strcmp`-based sort/compare calls elsewhere in the same file
(`aterm_envvar_cmp`/`aterm_output_cmp`) that would need auditing too if
the fields' meaning changed. That is the same "wider blast radius"
M147 already weighed and declined, re-confirmed here rather than
re-litigated, and this milestone's own measured gain (below) did not
make revisiting that call look newly justified.

**Measured** (`perf stat`, `taskset -c 0`, `cpu_core/instructions/`+
`cpu_core/cycles/`, 20 interleaved trials (before,after,before,after,...)
on the real cold `d.nix`/ffmpeg eval, output hash cross-checked
byte-identical on every single trial, zero mismatches in the reported
run -- an earlier 20-trial run hit one transient empty-output hiccup on a
`before`-binary's separate verification invocation, re-run standalone and
confirmed correct immediately after, consistent with this project's own
documented occasional flakiness under shared-machine load, not a real
bug, and excluded from the numbers below):

| | instructions | cycles |
|---|---|---|
| before (M153 baseline) | 6,777,522,089 (avg) | 3,865,212,962 (avg) |
| after (M154) | 6,728,233,859 (avg) | 3,872,852,555 (avg) |
| delta | **-0.727%** | +0.198% |
| wins | 20/20 | 11/20 |

Instructions: completely non-overlapping ranges across all 20 trials
(every BEFORE trial 6,772.7M-6,782.7M, every AFTER trial 6,724.4M-
6,731.3M) -- the same "hard, repetition-independent fact" character
this project's measurement culture already established (M129/M130/M146/
M152). Cycles: not a win this time, noisy and roughly flat (11/20,
+0.198% on average) -- consistent with every prior milestone's own
finding that cycles are the noisier signal on this shared, contended
machine, and with this fix's own mechanism being almost entirely about
removing INSTRUCTIONS (call/ret overhead, register spills around the
eliminated calls, and the `strlen` loop itself on 2-byte literals) rather
than anything that would obviously move cycle-level stalls.

A follow-up `perf record -e cpu_core/instructions/ -c 10000 -g`
comparison confirms the mechanism directly: the separate `buf_puts`
symbol (0.17% self-time before) disappears entirely from the `after`
profile (now inlined into `buf_put_escaped` via the macro, confirmed via
`objdump -dr` showing only ONE remaining `strlen` relocation in
`aterm.o`, down from six call sites previously), and `asnix`'s own
`strlen@plt` self-time share drops from 0.07% to 0.04%. `buf_put_escaped`
itself (`__strlen_avx2`'s self-time via the one remaining, genuinely
dynamic `strlen(s)` call this milestone deliberately left alone) stays
essentially flat, 0.90% before vs. 0.93% after -- exactly the expected
signature of removing the literal-strlen cost while leaving the dynamic
one, now a slightly larger share of a smaller total, untouched.

**Honest sizing against the gap.** The handoff's own profiling pass sized
this whole candidate (both the `buf_puts` literal cost AND the dynamic
`strlen(s)` cost it declined to also fix) at roughly 0.5%/34M
instructions. This milestone's measured result, -0.727%/~49.3M
instructions, is bigger than that combined estimate, not smaller --
plausible because inlining `buf_put_lit` at its 13 call sites removes not
just the `strlen` call itself but the surrounding `call`/`ret`/
register-shuffle overhead of a separate `buf_puts` function call, and
lets the compiler fold each case's fixed 2-8 byte `memcpy` into plain
`mov`s instead of a real `memcpy` dispatch -- savings the handoff's own
sampled-profile estimate (self-time attribution across an inlined/
non-inlined boundary is notoriously lossy, as M153's own writeup already
noted for a different pair of functions) did not fully capture. The
genuinely dynamic `strlen(s)` cost (the handoff's own "sibling direct
strlen call," roughly 0.14% by that estimate) is NOT claimed to be closed
here -- it remains open, correctly scoped out, same call as M147's.

**Correctness.** No allocation pattern, struct layout, or byte sequence
written changes -- `buf_put_lit` produces byte-for-byte the same output
as the old `buf_puts` for every one of its 13 literal call sites (the
length was always the true length; only how that length gets computed
changed, compile-time `sizeof` instead of runtime `strlen`). Full ladder
green: `make test`/`test-e2e`/`test-conformance` all pass, including
`tests/c/test_aterm.c` (exercising both the `cache=NULL` path and the
cached path, all through the rewritten literal-append calls). `make
test-nix-conformance NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`:
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (exact baseline, the same 3 pre-existing
pos-tracking failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`.
`d.nix` output hash unchanged on every trial:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.

Files: `src/c/aterm.c` (`buf_puts` replaced by the `buf_put_lit` macro;
all 13 call sites updated; no other file touched -- `buf_puts` was never
called outside this file).

## M157: `json_encode_attrs_ctx`'s insertion sort re-derived `(sym,name,len)` on every pairwise comparison instead of once -- fixed with `iets`'s own collect-then-sort split

A profiling pass flagged `builtins_compare.c`'s `json_encode_attrs_ctx`
(the `__structuredAttrs '__json'` env-var JSON encoder, called from
`asnix_toJSON_cstr` <- `asnix_prim_derivation`, and also reachable from
plain `builtins.toJSON`) as a real, previously-uncounted candidate --
flagged explicitly as open by M152's own closing paragraph ("`jb_escape_
string`'s own JSON-output path" was named there as unexamined). Its
insertion sort called `asnix_sym_name(asnix_bshared_attrs_sym(v, order[j
-1]), ...)` and the same for `order[j]` **again, from scratch, on every
single pairwise comparison**, instead of resolving each entry's name
once -- the exact "re-derive instead of cache" shape M152 just fixed for
`buf_put_escaped`, now found in a second, unrelated call site.

**The fix**, landed verbatim as proposed: a `JsonAttrEntry {const char
*name; size_t len; int64_t idx;}` array, filled in ONE `O(n)` pass before
sorting (`asnix_sym_name`/`asnix_bshared_attrs_sym` called exactly once
per entry), then an insertion sort over that already-materialized array
comparing cached `name`/`len` fields directly -- the same two-step
collect-then-sort split `iets`'s own `lexicographic_order()`
(`src/print.rs:112-120`) uses, ported structurally rather than
line-for-line (iets collects into a `Vec` and calls `sort_unstable_by`;
this keeps the project's existing insertion sort, since the comparison
COUNT was never the problem, only the redundant lookups backing each
comparison). `json_name_cmp` itself (the `memcmp`-based comparator) is
unchanged.

**Correctness.** `make test` (all C/IR unit suites, including
`tests/c/test_builtins_misc.c`'s toJSON cases) and `make test-e2e`
(296/296 OK, including `tests/e2e/m18_tojson.nix`, `m51_float_json.nix`,
`m57d_tojson_unicode_ok.nix`, `m69_structured_attrs_basic.nix`,
`m69_structured_attrs_nested_env.nix`) both green. `make test-nix-
conformance NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`: exact baseline
`pass=655 fail=3 skip=148` (the same 3 pre-existing pos-tracking
failures). `make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. Manual
differential checks against the pre-fix binary on hand-written cases the
instrumented-call-count evidence specifically motivated -- an empty
attrset, an already-sorted attrset, a reverse-sorted attrset, and an
attrset with one name a strict prefix of another plus an empty-string
name (`{ ab=1; a=2; abc=3; ""=4; }`) -- all byte-identical to the old
code's output. A standalone `valgrind --leak-check=full` run on `tests/
e2e/m69_structured_attrs_nested_env.nix` (exercises a nested
`__structuredAttrs` env, so `json_encode_attrs_ctx` runs for real) showed
byte-identical leak accounting before and after this change (1,272 bytes
/24 blocks "definitely lost," 288/12 "indirectly lost," both pre-existing
and unrelated to this milestone, matching the exact pre-existing figures
M152 itself already characterized on a different fixture) -- zero new
leaks, including on the `n==0` (`malloc` returns `NULL`, loop bodies
never run, `free(NULL)` is a no-op) path. `d.nix` (ffmpeg's closure)
output hash unchanged: `/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-
ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`, byte-identical on every single measurement trial
below (dozens of them, both binaries, every run).

**Measured, interleaved, with an honestly-reported mid-investigation
discrepancy.** `perf stat`, `taskset -c 0`, `cpu_core/instructions/` +
`cpu_core/cycles/`, before/after binaries built from the exact same
tree (confirmed via `md5sum` identity with a reproducible `make` rebuild
each time), cold `d.nix`/ffmpeg eval, before/after/before/after
interleaving throughout, output hash checked every trial.

The FIRST interleaved batches, run early in this milestone's own
session (10 trials, then 20 more), gave a materially larger number:
instructions avg 6,776,478,030 (before) -> 6,614,420,461 (after, the
first 17 of 20 trials tight at 6,592.6M-6,596.9M, the last 3 at
6,723-6,727M -- flagged at the time as likely contention, see below),
a **-2.39% to -2.68%** delta depending on which sub-window is averaged,
20/20 instruction wins. Taken at face value this looked like a clean,
M152-tier win.

**Re-measuring later in the same session (the same discipline M152's
own cycles re-check and M153's own regression-catch both used) did NOT
reproduce that number.** A fresh set of interleaved trials run after a
gap, using freshly-copied before/after binaries at new paths (to rule
out any stale-file-handle explanation) and confirmed byte-identical via
`md5sum` to the originals, consistently measured the AFTER binary at
~6,725-6,728M instructions -- the SAME elevated level the earlier run's
last 3 trials had shown, not the earlier run's own first-17 level of
~6,594M. This was reproduced across 59 further trials total (20 + 20 +
20, one of the 60 discarded as a transient single-trial failure --
`insn=4,104,700`, no output, consistent with this project's own
documented "a single failure under heavy concurrent load...rerun
standalone before trusting it as real" flakiness note), at two
different measured system load levels (`loadavg` 1-minute figure 5.5-6.0
for one batch, 2.2-2.4 for a later batch) -- so it is NOT simply "the
machine was busier." The BEFORE binary, by contrast, stayed in an
extremely tight band (6,771.7M-6,783.7M) across literally every trial in
every batch, early or late, busy or idle.

Several explanations were checked and ruled out for this step-shift
specifically landing on the AFTER binary and not the BEFORE binary:
binary identity (ruled out -- `md5sum` matched the originally-built
artifact throughout, both before and after the shift); `~/nixpkgs`
tracked-file drift (ruled out -- `git status`/`git log -1` showed the
checkout at the same commit throughout this milestone's own session,
and `stat` on `pkgs/build-support/fetchurl/default.nix`, `pkgs/top-
level/all-packages.nix`, and `default.nix` all showed modification times
hours-to-weeks older than this session, not mid-session edits); system
load level (ruled out directly above). The root cause of this specific,
discrete, binary-specific step-shift was NOT found within this
milestone's own time budget, and is reported here unresolved rather
than quietly dropped or used to justify picking the more favorable
number -- this is a materially different character of noise than this
campaign's own usual, continuous, cycles-only jitter (see M152's own
"cycles: noisier... won 16/20" framing), and is flagged honestly as a
new, open methodological question for whichever future milestone has
time to chase it, NOT claimed as understood.

**The number reported in this milestone's own original session:** 39
clean interleaved trials (the discarded 60th excluded as above), taken
AFTER the step-shift, at two different load levels, using both the
original and freshly-copied binary files:

| | instructions | cycles |
|---|---|---|
| before | 6,775,042,784 (avg) | 3,763,762,888 (avg) |
| after | 6,725,526,430 (avg) | 3,756,695,266 (avg) |
| delta | -0.73% | -0.19% |
| wins | 39/39 | 24/39 |

Instructions: completely non-overlapping across all 39 pairs (every
BEFORE trial 6,771.7M-6,783.7M, every AFTER trial 6,723.4M-6,728.3M) --
a small but hard, repetition-independent win by this project's own
standard for what counts as real on the instructions side. Cycles:
directionally weak (24/39, -0.19%), consistent with this campaign's
repeated finding that cycles are the noisier signal on this shared
machine and instructions are the one to trust.

**This -0.73% figure turned out to be the anomaly, not the steady
state -- resolved by two further independent measurements after this
milestone's own session ended.** An independent verify pass (55 trials
across 3 separate batches, including an order-swap test to rule out
ordering bias) measured its own AFTER binary at 6,594-6,598M
instructions every single time -- NOT the ~6,725-6,728M regime this
milestone's own "number actually being reported" table above used, but
matching almost exactly the EARLIER regime this milestone's own session
had flagged and excluded (see the first table above, "a materially
larger number"). A separate, fresh 20-trial interleaved measurement
(same protocol: `perf stat`, `taskset -c 0`, `cpu_core/instructions/`+
`cpu_core/cycles/`, before/after/before/after, binaries rebuilt from a
clean checkout at this milestone's own parent/child commits) reproduced
that same larger-win regime a third time:

| | instructions | cycles |
|---|---|---|
| before | 6,707,812,761 (avg) | 3,779,840,536 (avg) |
| after | 6,526,222,702 (avg) | 3,745,400,693 (avg) |
| delta | **-2.71%** | -0.91% |
| wins | 20/20 | n/a |

Non-overlapping across all 20 pairs (every BEFORE trial 6,707.1M-
6,713.3M, every AFTER trial 6,525.2M-6,527.0M). Three of the four total
measurement attempts made on this fix (this follow-up run, the
independent verifier's 55-trial run, and this milestone's own FIRST,
self-excluded 10+20-trial run) now agree tightly in the -2.4% to -2.7%
range; only this milestone's own "officially reported" 39-trial run,
taken later in its own single session, landed in the -0.73% band. The
honest conclusion is the reverse of this milestone's own original
framing: the -0.73% number is most likely the step-shifted outlier
(whatever transient system state caused it was local to that one
session), and **the real win is approximately -2.7% (roughly 180M
instructions on this workload), not -0.73%.** The absolute scale of the
baseline ("before") instruction count itself also differs between
sessions (6,775M vs. 6,708M here) due to unrelated milestones landing
in between (M155/M156 on this later measurement's baseline), which is
expected and does not affect the relative delta comparison within each
session.

A follow-up `perf record --call-graph dwarf,4096 -e cpu_core/
instructions/ -c 10000` comparison (21K/22K samples, 0 lost) confirmed
the mechanism is real and operating as designed, though the SIZE of its
contribution is harder to pin down precisely than the hard instruction-
count delta above: `json_name_cmp`'s own `memcmp` share (filtered to
calls specifically via `json_encode_attrs_ctx`, using `perf report -g
graph,...,callee`) was 1.80% before vs. 1.72% after -- a small, direction-
consistent drop. The `asnix_bshared_attrs_sym`/`asnix_sym_name` shares
filtered the same way did NOT show a comparably clean drop (0.50%->0.53%
and roughly flat respectively) despite the fix cutting their CALL COUNT
from this path by roughly the hypothesized ~24x (2 calls per comparison,
up to `O(n^2)`, down to 1 call per entry, `O(n)`) -- most plausibly
because each call's own self-time is small enough, and the number of
`perf`samples landing specifically on this narrow, caller-filtered
slice is small enough (on the order of 100 samples out of ~21K total),
that sampling noise dominates any true signal at that level of
attribution. This is a case where the exact, non-sampled `perf stat`
instruction count is the trustworthy number and the sampled call-graph
breakdown is not precise enough to corroborate it at this granularity --
noted honestly rather than papered over with a confident-sounding
breakdown the data doesn't actually support.

**Honest sizing.** Taking the two later, independently-reproduced
measurements as the trustworthy estimate (not this milestone's own
single-session "officially reported" -0.73%, now understood to be the
outlier -- see above), this is a real, reproducible, and MODERATE win:
approximately -2.7% of asnix's own total instruction count on this
workload (roughly 180M instructions), close to the ~2-4% this
milestone's own handoff had hypothesized (390M upper bound, 70-200M
likely range) from the instrumented call-count evidence alone -- the
handoff's estimate was essentially correct, and this milestone's own
first self-measurement already landed in that range before an
unexplained, never-fully-diagnosed step-shift made the "officially
reported" figure in its own session look smaller than the true effect.
Shipped (and its sizing corrected here rather than left standing)
because it is unambiguously correct (full ladder green, byte-identical
leak accounting, byte-identical output hash, hand-checked differential
cases), unambiguously in the right direction on the trustworthy
(instructions) signal across every measurement attempt regardless of
which regime it landed in, and a strict simplification of the existing
code (same sort, same comparator, same call shape, zero new data
structures beyond one small stack-adjacent array) -- not a speculative
rewrite that would need a bigger win to justify its own risk.

Files: `src/c/builtins_compare.c` (`JsonAttrEntry`, `json_encode_attrs_
ctx` rewritten to collect once then sort; `json_name_cmp` unchanged).

## M158: `find_matching_rbrace`'s full brace-depth scan to disambiguate `{...}` -- replaced with `iets`'s own bounded 1-2 token lookahead

A fresh instruction-weighted profile (`perf record`, DWARF call-graph
unwinding, `cpu_core/instructions/`) on a real `d.nix`/ffmpeg eval found
`lex_until` as the single largest self-time symbol in the whole program,
at 7.28% -- nearly double the next entry. The dominant call path was
`asnix_parse -> parse_expr (x3) -> find_matching_rbrace -> lexcur_tok ->
lexcur_tok_slow -> lex_until`. Every `{` in the grammar is ambiguous
between a lambda-pattern formals list (`{...}: body` / `{...}@name:
body`) and an ordinary attrset-literal expression until something past
the matching `}` is examined; `find_matching_rbrace` (shipped since
before this project's milestone numbering reached double digits) resolved
that ambiguity by scanning the ENTIRE `{...}` span token-by-token,
counting brace depth (including `${`'s own depth contribution, to avoid
miscounting a formal's default-value expression that itself contains a
dynamic select), just to peek at the one token immediately following the
real closing brace.

Because the project's lexer cursor only ever lexes forward and never
re-lexes an already-produced token (`lexcur_tok`/`lexcur_tok_slow`,
`src/c/lexer.h`/`lexer.c`), this scan wasn't literally wasted work in the
sense of re-doing anything -- but it was usually the FIRST code to reach
fresh, not-yet-lexed source text (since it runs ahead of wherever the
parser's own cursor otherwise is), so it ended up attributed the bulk of
the program's real lexing cost, concentrated in one place, for every
single `{` in every imported nixpkgs file.

**The fix.** `iets` (a sibling evaluator, `~/gnix/iets/src/syntax/
parser.rs`'s `is_formals`) resolves the exact same grammar ambiguity with
a bounded lookahead at the first one or two tokens after `{`, never
scanning to the matching brace at all:
  - first token is `...` -> formals (ellipsis-leading or ellipsis-only)
  - first token is `}`, second is `:` or `@` -> formals (empty formals)
  - first token is an identifier, second is `,`/`?`/`}` -> formals (a
    formal's name, immediately followed by the next separator/default/
    close that only a formals list's grammar can produce there)
  - anything else -> an attrset literal (a bare identifier followed by
    `=` or `.`, a string/dynamic key, `inherit`, `rec`, etc. -- none of
    which share a token-level prefix with a valid formals list)

Ported directly as `is_formals_pattern(Parser*, size_t open_idx)` in
`src/c/parser.c`, replacing `find_matching_rbrace` and its single call
site. The old function's own `${`-depth special case (needed because a
formal's default-value expression can itself contain a dynamic select,
e.g. real nixpkgs's `pkgs/stdenv/linux/default.nix`'s `bootstrapFiles ?
let ... archLookupTable.${system} ... in ...`) disappears entirely --
there is nothing to miscount when only 1-2 tokens are ever inspected.
Looking 2 tokens past `open_idx` is always a safe `lexcur_tok` query: the
second lookahead only happens inside the `TOK_RBRACE`/`TOK_IDENT` branches,
both of which already confirm the first lookahead token is NOT `TOK_EOF`
(the lexer's own sentinel final token), so the second query can never
land past it. A malformed/truncated `{` at end-of-input no longer gets
its own dedicated "unterminated '{'" message -- it now surfaces the
normal "expecting '}'"-style error from whichever real parse path
(formals or attrset literal) it falls into, matching this project's
standing convention of matching an error's class, not its exact wording.

**Correctness.** Full ladder green: `make test`, `make test-e2e`, `make
test-conformance` all pass. `make test-nix-conformance
NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`: exact baseline `pass=655
fail=3 skip=148` (the same 3 pre-existing pos-tracking gaps). `make
test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. Twelve hand-written differential
cases, cross-checked byte-for-byte against real `nix-instantiate --eval
--strict`, specifically targeting the disambiguation boundary: an
ordinary attrset-literal argument (`(x: x) { a = 1; b = 2; }`), empty
formals (`{ }: ...`), ellipsis-only formals (`{ ... }: ...`), a single
bare formal (`{ a }: a`), a formal with a default (`{ a, b ? 10 }: ...`),
both `@`-binding orders (`{ a, ... }@args: ...` and `{ }@x: x`), an
attrset literal with a dotted attrpath (`{ a.b = 1; }`), `inherit` (`{
inherit (builtins) toString; }`), a dynamic-key attrset (`{ "${x}" = 1;
}`), and -- the exact hazard the old function's own comment called out
-- a formal's default value containing its own nested attrset literal
(`{ a ? let inner = { b = 1; }; in inner.b }: a`). All twelve matched
real Nix exactly, both before and after. `./asnix d.nix` output unchanged:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`, verified
byte-identical on every trial below.

**Measured** (`perf stat`, `taskset -c 0`, `cpu_core/instructions/`+
`cpu_core/cycles/`, 20 interleaved trials (before,after,before,after,...)
on the real cold `d.nix`/ffmpeg eval, output hash checked every trial,
zero mismatches):

| | instructions | cycles |
|---|---|---|
| before (M157 baseline) | 6,541,536,795 (avg) | 3,898,556,994 (avg) |
| after (M158) | 6,494,331,550 (avg) | 3,924,281,876 (avg) |
| delta | **-0.722%** (~47.2M instructions) | +0.660% |
| wins | 20/20 | n/a |

Instructions: completely non-overlapping across all 20 pairs (every
BEFORE trial 6,538.5M-6,544.5M, every AFTER trial 6,491.3M-6,498.5M) --
a small but hard, repetition-independent win by this project's own
standard for what counts as real. Cycles: flat/noisy in the usual
direction-ambiguous band for this shared, contended machine, not treated
as an independent signal.

**Honest sizing against the profile that motivated it.** The realized
win (~47.2M instructions) is well below the ~7.28%/~476M-instruction
self-time share the profile attributed to `lex_until` via this call
path. This is not a discrepancy to chase further: most of that self-time
was always going to be spent regardless of which code path first touches
a given span of source text, since every token still has to be lexed
exactly once before parsing can finish (the project's lexer cursor never
re-lexes). What this milestone actually removes is the explicit
depth-counting loop's own overhead (a `lexcur_tok` call, a branch, and an
`i++` per token across the full scanned span, for every single `{` in
every imported file) and the fact that lexing was being forced ahead of
where the parser's own position otherwise needed it yet -- both real, but
a much narrower slice than the raw self-time attribution implied. This
matches this campaign's own repeated finding (M152, M157) that
instrumented/self-time estimates reliably indicate DIRECTION but not
MAGNITUDE; only a real interleaved measurement settles the latter.

Files: `src/c/parser.c` (`find_matching_rbrace` replaced by
`is_formals_pattern`; one call site updated).

## M159: `asnix_bshared_attrs_find`'s binary search re-resolved its loop-invariant `attrs` argument on every iteration via `attrs_sym`/`attrs_count`

M155's own `attrs_find_flat_noresolve` comment explicitly flagged this as
its follow-up and declared it out of scope at the time: `attrs_find`
(`src/c/builtins_shared.c`) called `asnix_bshared_attrs_resolve(attrs)`
once up front, then `asnix_bshared_attrs_count(attrs)` to get `hi`
(another internal resolve), then `asnix_bshared_attrs_sym(attrs, mid)`
once per binary-search iteration -- and `attrs_sym` ALSO calls
`asnix_bshared_attrs_resolve(attrs)` internally on every single call,
even though `attrs` never changes across the loop and was already
resolved by the first line of `find()` itself. For a typical
nixpkgs-sized attrset that is roughly `1 (direct) + 1 (via count) +
log2(n) (via sym)` wasted `resolve()` calls per `find()`, where exactly
one `resolve()` call suffices, since the function's own first line
already guarantees `attrs` is flat (`count >= 0`) for the rest of the
function body.

**The fix.** `attrs_find_flat_noresolve` (added by M155 for a different
call path, `asnix_bshared_attrs_probe`'s leaf-walk) already implements
exactly the needed shape: given a value ALREADY known to be flat, binary-
search its raw `ASNIX_ATTRS_OFF_ENTRIES` array directly, with no further
resolve/wrapper calls inside the loop. `asnix_bshared_attrs_find` now
does one `asnix_bshared_attrs_resolve(attrs)` call and then delegates the
entire search to `attrs_find_flat_noresolve(attrs, sym)`, which was moved
above `find()` in the file (it has no other dependency on ordering) so
it could be called without a forward declaration. `attrs_count`/
`attrs_sym`/`attrs_value` themselves were deliberately left untouched --
each is a tiny standalone public wrapper used directly by many call
sites that pass values NOT already known to be resolved (e.g. iterating
a lazy union's attrset directly), so collapsing their own internal
resolve would require auditing all 35+ of those call sites individually,
same "out of scope" boundary M155's own comment already drew; only
`find()`'s own internal loop, which uniquely has the invariant-resolve
information available for free, changes here.

**Measured** (`perf stat`, `taskset -c 0`,
`cpu_core/instructions/`+`cpu_core/cycles/`, 10 interleaved trials
(before,after,before,after,...) on the real cold `d.nix`/ffmpeg eval,
both binaries built from a clean `make` at this milestone's parent
commit (M157, `4c663df`) and at this fix, output hash cross-checked
byte-identical on every trial):

| | instructions | cycles |
|---|---|---|
| before (M157) | 6,537,248,409 (avg) | 3,840,689,997 (avg) |
| after (M158) | 6,459,331,154 (avg) | 3,832,132,689 (avg) |
| delta | **-1.192%** | -0.223% |
| wins | 10/10 | 5/10 |

Instructions: completely non-overlapping ranges across all 10 trials
(every BEFORE trial 6,536.1M-6,540.8M, every AFTER trial 6,458.0M-
6,461.1M) -- the same "hard, repetition-independent fact" character this
project's measurement culture already established for a real win
(M129/M130/M146/M152/M156/M157). Cycles: weak/noisy as usual on this
shared machine (5/10 wins, -0.223% on average), consistent with every
prior milestone's finding that cycles are the noisier signal and
instructions are the one to trust.

**Honest sizing against the gap.** The handoff's own estimate was
0.7%/50,000,000 instructions. The measured result, -1.192%/~77.9M
instructions, is noticeably bigger than that estimate -- plausible
because the handoff's own per-call-count arithmetic (`~7.2 resolve()
calls where 1 would suffice`) only counted `resolve()`'s own measured
~24-instruction self-cost, not the additional call/ret and argument-
marshalling overhead of the now-eliminated `attrs_sym`/`attrs_count`
wrapper calls themselves (each one a real function call, not inlined,
across translation units), nor the loop-body register pressure those
calls previously forced.

**Correctness.** `find()`'s observable behavior is unchanged: it still
returns the same positional index into `attrs`'s own flat form for a
present `sym`, or `-1` for a missing one, with the one resolve happening
up front (correct) rather than redundantly inside the loop (also
correct, just wasteful) -- `attrs` is immutable for the duration of the
call, so caching the resolved pointer across the loop iterations changes
no semantics. Full ladder green: `make test`/`test-e2e`/
`test-conformance` all pass. `make test-nix-conformance
NIX_CONFORMANCE_DIR=/tmp/nix-conformance`: `pass=655 fail=3 skip=148`
(exact baseline, the same 3 pre-existing position-tracking failures).
`make test-nixpkgs-hash`: `pass=148 fail=0`. `d.nix` output hash
unchanged on every trial:
`/nix/store/29iacg6h530yx7rxz4k1fhvi0kxxhsam-ffmpeg-9.0.1-bin`.

**Independent verification.** A separate adversarial-verify pass fetched
this commit into its own isolated worktree, confirmed the diff's logic
directly (delegating to `attrs_find_flat_noresolve` after exactly one
`resolve()` call is semantically equivalent, since `attrs` is immutable
across the loop), re-ran the full correctness ladder fresh (not trusted
from this writeup) with identical results, and ran its OWN independent
20-trial interleaved measurement: instructions before (4c663df) avg
6,535,864,027, after (this fix) avg 6,458,737,528, delta **-1.180%**
(~77.1M instructions), 20/20 wins, completely non-overlapping ranges --
closely matching the -1.192% reported above (well within normal
trial-to-trial variance, same hard-win signature). Verdict: CONFIRMED.

Files: `src/c/builtins_shared.c` (`attrs_find_flat_noresolve` moved
above `asnix_bshared_attrs_find`; `asnix_bshared_attrs_find` rewritten to
resolve once and delegate to `attrs_find_flat_noresolve`; no other
function touched).

## M160: `nar.c`'s `copy_cache_find` was a plain linear `strcmp` scan -- given the same open-addressing hash index fix `derivation.c`'s `input_ref_add_src`/`input_ref_add_built` already got for the identical shape of anti-pattern
